* fix(membership): conjoin admission, split self-inspection, purge stale directives

Codex round 2 on PR #891 — three P1, two P2. Two of the P1s were security
regressions in the spec itself.

P1 — admission was specced as `admitted(eventId) || isOwner(...)`. Backwards.
`boards` (firestore.rules:1105) and `claims` (:1304) are owner/admin-only TODAY,
so OR-ing admission in would have given every member of an Event read access to
every other member's private Board and Claims — a regression introduced by the
change meant to harden the boundary. The shape is `admitted(eventId) && <the
rule's existing condition>`: membership only ever subtracts. Added the invariant
that any rule leaving #804 more permissive than it entered is wrong on its face.

That also falsified two neighbouring claims, both corrected: the inventory said
every listed read arm is a bare `signedIn()` (boards and claims are not), and
the `exists()` justification rested on the withdrawn OR shape — under pure
conjunction an error and a false both deny, so it is downgraded to the
robustness argument it actually is rather than left overstated.

P1 — the `memberships/{uid}` read rule used the admission predicate, which was
wrong in both directions: a revoked member could not read their OWN record (so
the promised `denied-revoked` outcome was unreachable and the client would show
a permission error), while any active member could read EVERY other member's
record including `grantedBy`, `invitationId` and the revocation audit fields.
Now `allow get: if isOwner(uid) || isAdmin(eventId)` and `allow list: if
isAdmin(eventId)`. Self-inspection is not admission, and the admission predicate
gates Event content rather than the admission record itself.

P1 — round 1's withdrawal of the create-only board shape updated the prose but
left it standing in the enforced-path inventory and in an acceptance criterion,
which is what an implementer would actually follow. Both purged; admission gates
create AND update.

P2 — `invitationId: ''` parsed as valid; `null` is the reserved no-invitation
value and an empty string is neither, losing the provenance #803 needs to
diagnose reuse. Rejected, with a test.

P2 — routed the type imports through `src/types.ts`, the stable domain-contract
entrypoint, instead of reaching into `domainTypes.d.ts` directly.

* fix(membership): budget whole batches, bind Admin revocation, close D9

Codex round 3 on PR #891 (three P1, one P2), plus Nathan's ruling on epic
Decision 9.

P1 — the 20-call BATCH aggregate was quoted and then never applied; the budget
only considered single operations. The Mark path is not one write: setMark

P1 — a revoked Admin still satisfied isAdmin(), which reads EventDoc.admins and
knows nothing about membership, so the new memberships read rule would have let

* fix(membership): Storage within two accesses, revoke by array, honest batch levers

Codex round 4 on PR #891 — three P1, one P2. All four were places round 3's
fixes were incomplete rather than wrong.

P1 — the Storage budget was mis-read. Firebase documents it as "two Firestore
documents", which this spec took literally and then spent THREE calls against:
one for the switch, plus exists()+get() for the membership. Counted as calls —
the stricter and correct reading — that overruns. The Storage membership check
is now a single firestore.get() relying on error-to-deny, which is safe there
because the Storage arms conjoin admission with isOwner/isEventAdmin rather
than falling through to them. Documented why the two rules files now
deliberately differ, and corrected the budget table, finding 3 and the
EventDoc.membershipEnforcement comment to say "accesses" throughout.

P1 — roster removal on revocation was keyed on the membership's `role`, which
misses the common case. EventDoc.admins is client-writable by any Admin while
memberships are writable by nobody, so an Admin promoted by a direct array edit
is an Admin whose record still reads role: 'member'. A role-conditioned removal
leaves exactly that uid in admins after revocation, still passing isAdmin().
Now keyed on the ARRAY. Also named the root cause — that admins is
client-writable at all — and recorded routing promotion through the server path
as the durable fix rather than something to keep compensating for.

P1 — "shrink the predicate to one call" was offered as an independent batch
remedy and is not one. The floor is TWO (a bare exists() still leaves the
enforcement-switch lookup), and a full-card reconcileEchoes repair of 25
operations exceeds the 20-call aggregate at any per-write cost. Demoted to a
multiplier reduction; proven cross-operation caching and batch splitting are
the only remedies, and repair batching must change regardless unless caching
proves out — which makes it a #807 dependency, not something #804 absorbs.

P2 — the bold lead still said Functions "must mirror it instead" while the same
paragraph forbade a hand-maintained mirror, so #803 could have followed the
heading and built the duplicate the body prohibits.

* fix(membership): conjoin admission on roster reads, thread the Storage Event fetch

Codex round 5 on PR #891 — two P1, both consequences of round 4's fixes.

P1 — binding revocation to the admins array (round 4) could never reach
PROMOTION. EventDoc.admins is client-writable, so an Admin who adds a UID to it
after enforcement creates a privileged account with NO membership, which
immediately passed `allow list: if isAdmin(eventId)` and could read the whole
roster including grantedBy, invitationId and the revocation audit fields.

Both roster branches now conjoin admission: `allow get: if isOwner(uid) ||
(admitted(eventId) && isAdmin(eventId))` and `allow list: if admitted(eventId)
&& isAdmin(eventId)`. This REVERSES the position taken in round 4, which
rejected exactly this remedy. Both objections were wrong: the cost is one get()
on a path that is neither batched nor hot, and there is no circularity because
rules do not recurse and the reader's own membership is a different document
from the one being read. Special-casing the admin branches was the anomaly —
every other gated path already conjoins. The atomic array removal stays as
defence in depth rather than the sole protection.

P1 — with admission conjoined, the Storage delete arm costs the switch read,
the membership read AND isEventAdmin()'s own Event read: three accesses against
a limit of two, denying every admin moderation delete on an enforced Event.
#806 must thread ONE Event fetch through both the switch and the admin check —
the same hoist already prescribed for the boards clause, since rules have no
`let`. Call-site shape written out explicitly, budget table row corrected to

Codex round 6 on PR #891 — two P1, two P2.

P1 — the inventory gated `events/{eventId}` READ and left update (:796) and
delete (:917) open. Both are isAdmin-gated and EventDoc.admins is
client-writable, so an Admin promoting a UID by array edit creates a privileged

provisioner's Admin-SDK path, whose client arm is already unsatisfiable. Both

#850 shows is over the expression cap, so #850 is the prerequisite two separate

P1 — a real outage window between #802 and #804. The field exists in the
contract now while the Event update arm still accepts arbitrary writes to it, so
an Admin can set 'enforced' today. Shipping the freeze and the gate in one
deploy would freeze that pre-set value AND immediately honour it, enforcing an

switch exists to prevent, delivered by the deploy meant to be a no-op. Rollout

active record carrying stale ones — both of which readMembership rejects, letting
a writer using the canonical contract persist unparseable data. Now a
discriminated union: ActiveMembership (`revokedAt?: never`) | RevokedMembership
(both required).

* fix(membership): bind admission at every privileged surface, incl. callables

Codex round 7 on PR #891 — one P1, three P2.

P1 — the invitation callable was specced to authorize from the live admins
roster alone. Firestore rules do not run on an Admin-SDK callable, so every

invitation callable, revocation itself — because EventDoc.admins is
client-writable and each surface checked the array without checking admission.
The rule is now stated once: anything that consults EventDoc.admins to
authorize an action conjoins an active-membership check, whether it is a

client-writable — is D-A's territory and remains OPEN; this conjunction is the
compensating control until it is settled.

from exactly the revoked user whose outcome depends on it, making the promised

would show a bare permission error instead). The read arm now admits a caller
holding any membership document at their own uid, active or revoked; the write
arms do not.

P2 — schemaVersion was `number`, so a writer using the canonical contract could

* fix(membership): admits() gates access, never grant authority — add mayAdministerMembership()

Phase 4b P1, round 4, and it lands on a claim I made in round 3 rather
than on a new surface.

Round 3 scoped D-A's bypass out of #803's invitation callable and
asserted the callable was therefore safe because it calls admits()
without the flag. The scoping was right; the predicate behind it was not.
admits() returns 'admitted-unenforced' BEFORE inspecting membership
whenever enforcement is not 'enforced' — and Rollout step 3 runs that
callable while every Event is still 'off'. So authorizing from admits()
required no membership at all, and a UID added to the client-writable
EventDoc.admins array could mint invitations whose memberships remain,
and become decisive, after the flip to 'enforced'. A transient
permissiveness would have written a permanent admission.

The round-3 test that was supposed to pin this used enforcement:
'enforced' — the one posture the callable never runs in — so it asserted
the safe case and left the live one untested. Replaced rather than
amended.

The distinction, stated once: admits() gates ACCESS, never GRANT
authority. An access decision is confined to the window it happens in,
which is why admits() may be and deliberately is permissive while an
Event is unenforced. A grant is not so confined. Anything that MINTS or
REVOKES admission now asks mayAdministerMembership(): authenticated,
present in the LIVE admins roster, holding an ACTIVE membership, all
conjoined. It takes no enforcement input at all — not ignored, absent —
because there is no state of the switch in which minting admission
without holding it is acceptable. D-A's bypass is deliberately absent
there for the same reason.

This failure is subtle precisely because admits() returns true in the
vulnerable case: the permissive answer is correct for the question
admits() was asked and wrong for the question the caller meant.

committing transaction; issuance and revocation were not. Same reasoning
applies verbatim -- the Admin SDK bypasses rules, nothing re-evaluates at
commit, and a caller demoted from admins or revoked between a pre-flight
check and the write still mints a durable invitation or still revokes
another member. Requiring it in one place and not the other was an
inconsistency, not a distinction.

grant paths -- a grant writes only where no document exists, with the
existence check inside the transaction that writes. The provisioner's
case is vacuous today (it creates the Event in the same operation, so
nothing can pre-exist) but is held to the rule rather than exempted,

contract, and a re-provision would otherwise be the one path allowed to

and the finality of a revocation. A blind write destroys the first and

- **`WireEnumTest`** drives off the enum constants themselves, so a new value is covered the moment it is added: round-tripping, unique lowercase wire forms, case and whitespace tolerance, and empty (never an exception) for null, blank, unknown and injection-shaped input.
- **`EnumSchemaAlignmentTest`** reads the allowed values out of `pg_constraint` and compares them to the enum, then writes every value to the real table. The enum and the CHECK constraint are two declarations of one fact in different languages; nothing but this keeps them honest. Add a value to one and not the other and it fails, naming the constraint.

## Compile

`packages/compile` turns ProseMirror documents into the formats Core ships (`txt`, `md`, `html`). `ExportProvider` on the Java side reports the same boundary; a commercial module contributes the remaining formats by supplying another implementation, and Core must keep working with only its own provider present.

### binder_item

The tree structure — folders, documents, trash. This is the Scrivener "binder."

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

| type | enum | `folder` \| `document` \| `trash` |
| title | text | |
| order_index | float | fractional indexing — lets you reorder/insert without rewriting siblings *(superseded — see A4)* |
| icon | text, nullable | optional custom icon (Scrivener-style) |
| deleted_at | timestamptz, nullable | soft delete — needed for sync tombstones |
| version | bigint | monotonic, incremented on every change |
| updated_by_device_id | uuid | for conflict attribution |

| id | uuid | same as binder_item.id, or separate FK — recommend same id for simplicity |
| content | jsonb | ProseMirror doc JSON |
| word_count | int | derived, cached for fast binder display |
| synopsis | text, nullable | the Scrivener index-card text |
| notes | text, nullable | document notes (rich text or plain) |
| version | bigint | incremented per content save |
| updated_at | timestamptz | |

### snapshot

Manual or auto point-in-time captures of a document's content (Scrivener's snapshot feature).

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

### label / status

Scrivener-style metadata taxonomies, per project.

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

### custom_metadata_field + custom_metadata_value

For arbitrary principal-defined metadata (Scrivener's custom meta-data pane). Field defs at the project level, values keyed per binder_item.

### collection

- Each entity carries a version integer, bumped on every write.
- Client pushes a batch: {entity, base_version, new_data} for each locally-changed record since last sync.
- Server accepts if base_version matches current server version (no one else changed it since the client last knew about it). Otherwise it's a conflict.
- On conflict for document content: don't try to merge rich text — create a sibling binder_item titled "<original title> (Conflicted Copy, <device>, <timestamp>)" containing the client's version, and let the principal manually reconcile. This mirrors Dropbox/Scrivener'
explanation:
Allowlist link schemes, sweep every route for IDOR, drop product names

Fixes a real cross-site scripting hole in compiled output. Link hrefs were
escaped but their scheme was never checked, so a document containing
javascript:alert(1) produced a working anchor in every format that carries
links. Escaping cannot help there: the payload contains nothing that needs
escaping. isSafeHref now allowlists http, https, mailto and relative
references, normalising away case, whitespace and control characters first so
JaVaScRiPt: and an embedded tab do not slip past, and failing closed on schemes
nobody has listed. An unsafe link loses its anchor, keeps its text, and warns.
Markdown gets the same treatment, since markdown links execute in renderers.

IdorSweepTest enumerates every route from the handler mapping and drives each
one with a stranger's token. Routes naming another account's resource must not
answer 2xx; caller-scoped collections may, but must not contain the victim's

Authentication Bypass For Endpoints With Anonymous Access

Using a remember-me cookie with an arbitrary username can cause Opencast
to assume proper authentication for that user even if the remember-me
cookie was incorrect given that the attacked endpoint also allows
anonymous access.

This way, an attacker can, for example, fake a remember-me token, assume
the identity of the global system administrator and request non-public
content from the search service without ever providing any proper
authentication.

The reason for this problem is that using a remember-me cookie will
always cause the user in the request context to be populated, even if
the cookie is invalid by now. This is usually no problem, except in
combination with anonymous access where anonymous authentication is
granted and the request may continue.

In such a case, Opencast's security service would just check that a user
existed in the request context and assume proper authentication of this
user, never checking if it's actually anonymous authentication.

This patch adds this additional check, falling back to the anonymous
user in case of anonymous authentication.

feat(discovery): site discovery — a scan that cannot change your plant (#161)

* feat(discovery): scan types, industrial port allowlist, and safety profiles

The base of the site-discovery ladder — pure data and types, no sockets yet.

The allowlist is the safety argument in code: a fixed ~16-entry table with a
per-port rationale, a NEVER_SCAN table naming the damage each forbidden probe
would do, and NEVER_IDENTIFIED for protocols a sweep must never speak at all.
secsgem is the load-bearing case — a fab tool typically accepts ONE host
connection, so an HSMS session opened to 'identify' it can evict the real MES
host. Port 5000 stays scannable for MTConnect (HTTP is refused harmlessly by an
HSMS listener); the protocol does not.

Profiles bind stages + ports + pacing together so a cautious posture cannot be
half-applied. 'passive' emits nothing; 'legacy-safe' sweeps only, one host at a
time, for 1990s controllers where even a well-formed identify is a risk.

Found in review, not by a failing test: PacingPolicy's hard ceilings were
annotated Final, which still makes them dataclass FIELDS — a caller could pass
HARD_MAX_CPS=9999 and lift their own limit, defeating the one thing the class
promises. Now ClassVar, mutation-checked by a guard test.

* feat(discovery): pacing brakes, the wire log, and the no-write guard

Lands before any socket code, deliberately — these are what make the scan's
safety claim checkable rather than promised.

Pacing has four independent brakes because they fail differently: a global token
bucket, a concurrency cap, a per-host gate (one in-flight probe per host — rate
limiting alone still permits 20 connects/s all aimed at one fragile controller),
and segment health that drops a repeatedly-failing host and aborts a run whose
whole segment is failing, on the assumption that we are the cause. Host order is
a seeded shuffle: a march up the subnet concentrates every connect on one
switch's port group, which is what an IDS is tuned to notice.

WireLog only accepts a DECLARED packet class. A stage that starts emitting
something new has to add it to KNOWN_KINDS, next to every other thing this
product is willing to put on an OT network — so the report's counts, and its
'never done' list, stay true by construction rather than by memory.

The guard reads the package's own AST and fails if a write becomes reachable.
Two checks, because they catch different mistakes: an exact import check (which
is how the generically-named BAS write, , is caught without flagging
every local variable of that name) and an identifier scan for the unambiguous
ones. A sync test against the MCP write manifest means an 11th upstream write
tool fails the build instead of quietly falling outside the list.

Two bugs found while testing, both by the tests hanging rather than failing:
- TokenBucket compared refilled tokens with a strict >=, so a sleep of
  deficit/rate landed a few float ulps short and the loop span forever on
  ever-smaller sleeps. Now compared with a tolerance, mutation-checked.
- A hung limiter is a hung scanner, and on a plant floor a stuck process beats
  no error only in the worst sense. The refill loop now raises after a bounded
  number of rounds instead of spinning.

* feat(discovery): the dry-run preview — exhaustive, signable, zero emissions

The first thing anyone can run against a plant network is now the thing that
puts no packets on it. Given a plan, this derives the exact host list, the exact
ports with the identify call permitted on each, the worst-case duration under
the rate limits, and — as prominently as the rest — the list of what the scan
will never do. That page is what a controls engineer signs before the first
packet, and its whole value is that it needs nothing touched to produce.

Honesty properties, each pinned: the preview's declared per-stage packet classes
are checked to be real wire-log classes, so what it promises and what the report
later proves come from one vocabulary; a profile needing sign-off reports
authorized:false rather than looking ready; network and broadcast addresses are
dropped automatically, since a broadcast address is the one address a scan must
never connect to. 'Emits nothing' is proven by running it with every socket
entry point monkeypatched to raise, not asserted in a docstring.

Two refusals rather than best-effort: a prefix shorter than /16 is a mistyped
prefix until acknowledged on the plan, and 4096 hosts is the cap for one run.

Found while testing: the scope was expanded before the cap was checked, so a /8
materialised 16.7M address strings on the way to being rejected — 11s in the
suite, and an out-of-memory on an edge box. The cap is now decided by address
arithmetic (exclusions included, or a legitimately-narrowed large scope would be
refused); the same tests run in 0.05s.

* feat(discovery): L1 — the gentle TCP sweep

The first code here that puts a packet on a wire, and deliberately the least a
scanner can do while still learning something: one ordinary TCP connect per
allowlisted port, orderly shutdown, close. No payload, no raw socket, no
half-open SYN, no ICMP, no retry storm — a full handshake from the kernel's own
stack is what any client does, and the one thing a device cannot mistake for an
attack. Shutdown before close because some embedded stacks hold a connection
slot until they see the FIN.

The verdict is three-valued and the values never merge. 'refused' proves the
host is ALIVE and simply runs no industrial service — a positive finding, not an
absence — while 'filtered' means a silent drop, usually an ACL. A host-unreachable
errno is filtered too, not alive: a router answered on the host's behalf, so the
host itself said nothing. diagnose_empty_sweep() reports these separately because
they look identical in a summary and are completely different to act on, and a
silent empty list is never returned.

Tested in two layers: a scripted connector drives every verdict exactly
(including errnos a laptop cannot produce on demand), and a real socket listener
matrix proves the connect path against the kernel rather than against our idea of
it. A genuine 'filtered' needs a real DROP rule, so that one is left for the
Linux verification run rather than faked and called verified.

Found by measuring rather than reading: work was submitted host-major, so one
host's ports queued back to back, the host gate serialised them, and they held
the whole concurrency budget while blocked — 2.05s for a run that should take
0.62s, and worse on the deep profile's 13 ports. Two fixes: submit port-major so
consecutive probes are different hosts (also gentler per device than bursting six
ports at one), and take the host gate BEFORE the concurrency slot so a thread
waiting out a gap holds neither a slot nor a spent token. The preview's duration
estimate is what an operator agreed a maintenance window on, so it has to stay
true. Both pinned, the ordering one mutation-checked.

* feat(modbus): FC43 device identification — identify without touching a register

The scan needs to ask a Modbus slave 'what are you'. The obvious way, reading
holding register 0, is a data-plane request against an address the device may not
map, and legacy slaves answer an unmapped address by raising, dropping the
session, or faulting. FC43/MEI-14 asks the protocol layer instead, so nothing in
the process image is touched — proven by a test that makes every register read on
the connector explode and requires identification to still succeed.

Honest degradation is the point, not the happy path. Many simple slaves do not
implement FC43 and answer 'illegal function' — the device ANSWERED, so it is
alive and reachable, which is exactly what OTProtocolError means here and lets
the caller record 'identified by port only' instead of inventing a vendor. A
server that answers FC43 with an empty object set is identified as
Modbus-speaking and nothing more; the vendor field stays empty rather than
becoming 'Unknown'. more_follows is reported and never chased — continuations
cost extra packets and identification does not need them.

Verified against a real pymodbus server, not only a fake, and that is what caught
the actual bug: the decoder tried ASCII first, so 汇川 / 三菱電機 / Müller — entirely
ordinary vendor names in this market — were all flagged 'undecodable'. A
corruption warning on a good asset-register row teaches the reader to ignore the
flag. UTF-8 is now tried first and only genuinely non-UTF-8 bytes fall back to
latin-1 and get flagged, since latin-1 never raises and so can silently
mis-render. Every fake had used ASCII bytes, so the fake and the decoder agreed
and were both wrong; the non-ASCII vendor name in the LIVE fixture is what
exposed it.

Also recorded in the live fixture: pymodbus keeps device identity in
process-wide state, so a server started with identity=None still answers with a
previously-constructed identity. Checked in a clean process — identity=None
returns information={}, an empty answer rather than an exception.

* feat(opcua): identify a server via GetEndpoints, without opening a session

The scan needs to identify an OPC-UA server. server_info goes through
opcua_session and therefore takes one of the server's session slots — embedded
servers commonly allow only two to five, so an unattended re-scan can evict the
plant's real SCADA client from its own PLC. GetEndpoints runs on the secure
channel before any session exists, so it costs the server nothing it counts.
Pinned by probing eight times in a row against a real server and then requiring a
genuine session to still be available.

The security policies come back too, which makes this useful beyond naming the
device: 'still offers SecurityPolicy None with Anonymous tokens' is a finding an
IEC 62443 review acts on, and it is visible without authenticating. Reported as
plain booleans, flagged on the WEAKEST endpoint — an attacker picks that one, so
a mixed server must not average it away.

Verified against a real asyncua server, not only a fake, because the fake's
attribute names were mine to choose and that is exactly how a fake and its parser
agree while both being wrong. The real objects confirm each guess:
SecurityPolicyUri does carry the '#None' fragment, SecurityMode is an enum whose
value is an int, Server.ApplicationName is a LocalizedText needing .Text, and
UserIdentityTokens are UserTokenPolicy objects.

The teardown is load-bearing in a way worth spelling out: asyncua's sync Client
starts a NON-DAEMON ThreadLoop in its CONSTRUCTOR, so a probe that skips
disconnect leaks a thread every time and the process then never exits. Removing
that line does not turn the leak tests red — it HANGS the run, which is how the
mutation check proved it. Both the success and the failure path are covered; the
failure path is the one that bites, since a dead endpoint has the loop already
running by the time the connect fails.

* test(discovery): prove the filtered verdict against a real firewall rule

refused and filtered are the two findings this scanner refuses to merge — one
proves the host is ALIVE and simply runs no industrial service, the other usually
means an ACL between here and it, and they are completely different to act on.
Until now the timeout path was only ever driven by a stub raising TimeoutError
because the test told it to, which proves the branch is wired, not that the
kernel behaves that way.

This installs an actual iptables DROP inside a container's own network namespace
and probes that container's loopback: a real listener, a real refused port, and a
real silently-dropped one, all three verdicts asserted at once. Nothing outside
the container is contacted, and no host firewall is touched.

Verified on a Linux box with a container runtime — 9001 open in 0.01s, 9002
refused in 0.00s with alive=True, 9003 filtered after burning the full 2.00s
timeout with alive=False. Skips where Docker is absent, so a laptop still runs
the rest of the suite.

Also removes a comment in test_discovery_sweep.py that said this case was 'left
for the Linux verification run'. It no longer is, and a docstring promising work
that has since been done is the kind of stale claim this codebase keeps proving
costly.

* feat(discovery): L2 identification — one safe question per candidate protocol

L1 says a port is open. That is not an answer: TCP 502 open means "probably
Modbus", and an inventory built on "probably" is one a controls engineer throws
out on the first wrong row. This stage asks each device what it is, using the
cheapest question its protocol defines and never a data-plane read.

The table exists to route around four probes that would earn this product a
site ban. The diagnostic probes elsewhere in this repo were written for
endpoints an operator had already configured and consented to; pointed at
unknown hosts they are hazards:

  * Modbus — the obvious probe reads holding register 0, an address the slave
    may not map. Uses FC43/MEI-14 instead: a protocol-layer question that
    touches nothing in the process image.
  * OPC-UA — the obvious probe opens a SESSION, and embedded servers allow two
    to five. Uses GetEndpoints, which runs before any session exists.
  * SECS/GEM — never attempted at all. A fab tool typically accepts ONE host
    connection; taking it stops a production tool.
  * MQTT — a client-id collision disconnects the broker's real subscriber. Not
    part of automatic identification.

Two judgements are load-bearing and both are pinned by tests:

  * A rejection is a confirmation. A device answering FC43 with "illegal
    function" has spoken Modbus — it is CONFIRMED with an unknown identity.
    A transport failure is not, and leaves the port at port_only with NO
    vendor. Inverting these two produces an inventory full of invented rows.
  * A missing extra is a finding about this machine, not the device. Saying
    "could not identify" would blame a host that was never asked.

S7 is the only probe that sends twice: slot 1 then slot 2, because
S7-1200/1500 and S7-300/400 differ and one guess mis-reports half the installed
base. Both attempts are counted on the wire log, and an in-protocol refusal
stops the retry — the slot was right.

The preview's L2 emission list is now DERIVED from this table rather than
hand-written, so the document an operator signs cannot drift from the probes
that will run. The plan's invariants (no forbidden protocol, no undeclared
packet class, no protocol both probeable and not) are checked at import, so a
bad edit fails on load rather than in a plant.

56 tests. Four guarantees mutation-checked: the refusal/failure distinction,
open-ports-only, the S7 retry stop, and the identify gap. A fifth test caught a
real TypeError — host/port are TargetConfig FIELDS and collided with _target's
positional parameters, so four probes were dead against every live device while
every faked test stayed green; there is now a per-probe test that walks the
whole table and would catch it for probes added later.

* feat(discovery): L0 passive — read the kernel's ARP cache, emit nothing

The kernel already knows part of the answer. Every host this machine has
spoken to recently sits in the ARP/neighbour cache, and reading it costs
exactly zero packets — which is the entire content of the `passive` profile
and the only honest first move on a network nobody has authorised yet.

Three things decide whether "emits nothing" is actually true, and each is a
test rather than a comment:

  * `arp -n`, never `arp -a`. Without -n the BSD/macOS tool reverse-resolves
    every address it prints, putting a DNS query on the network per entry —
    which would make the one profile whose whole promise is silence emit
    something. Linux reads /proc/net/arp directly and the question is moot.
  * `(incomplete)` entries are dropped. An incomplete entry is an ARP request
    that went UNANSWERED — the exact opposite of evidence a host exists.
  * Broadcast and multicast are not devices. Every cache holds the subnet
    broadcast; listing it would put 192.168.60.255 in an inventory as though
    someone could go find it in a cabinet. One bit separates all three cases.

MAC addresses are normalized because two kernels print the same NIC
differently — Linux writes 48:21:0b:33:57:94, macOS writes 48:21:b:33:57:94.
Left alone, one device becomes two assets the moment a survey is run from a
different laptop. Verified against both real kernels: after normalization the
two machines agree exactly on the devices they share.

An unreadable cache produces a NOTE, never a silent empty table — "nothing is
on this network" and "I could not look" are different answers and only one of
them is about the network. Same for an unsupported platform.

24 unit tests over fixture text copied verbatim from both real kernels, plus a
docker-gated live test that sends a genuinely unanswered ARP inside a
container's own netns (an unused address on its docker bridge, so nothing on
the host network is contacted) and asserts the kernel's real incomplete row is
not reported as a device — with the complement asserted too, so a filter that
discarded everything could not pass by accident.

* feat(discovery): the scan runner — a plan in, an honest ScanResult out

Each stage was already careful on its own. What this level adds is the chance
to lose that, so the rules it enforces are all about the result never being
quieter than the run:

  * A stage the plan asked for that this build cannot run is NAMED in the
    notes. Silently running four stages when the operator authorised six is
    how a report comes to claim coverage it does not have.
  * An empty result is a verdict with a diagnosis. "No device answered",
    "every port was silently dropped", and "the hosts are right there and run
    nothing we speak" look identical in a summary and are acted on completely
    differently, so they stay apart — VERDICT_PARTIAL exists precisely for the
    third, which is the common answer on an IT segment.
  * The wire summary is taken from the log, so probes that FAILED are counted
    too. A trust page that tallied only successful requests would understate
    exactly the traffic an operator is worried about.

Authorization is enforced in the library rather than the CLI — checked before
a single packet, and asserted as such — so calling run_scan directly cannot
route around it.

Two fixes fell out of running it end to end for the first time:

  * A host dropped by the backoff now records that fact in its OWN row, not
    only in a run-level note. Its row has fewer ports than its neighbours',
    and without the per-host line that reads as an inconsistent scan rather
    than a careful one.
  * run_scan gained an identify_plan injection point. Without it the identify
    stage always reached the real network, which made the first smoke run
    emit genuine packets at a range it was only pretending to scan.

Hosts sort numerically (10.0.0.9 before 10.0.0.10) because a person reads this.

23 tests, including the one that matters most: the `passive` profile emits
literally zero packets even when a host in scope has an open port.

* feat(sink): on-box scan store — the tables the device inventory is read from

Sits beside the existing `samples` table in the same local database and never
touches it: a survey and a data collection are two products of the same box,
and one filling up must not corrupt the other.

Stores both shapes on purpose. The full result as JSON, so nothing observed is
lost to a schema that did not anticipate it — and flat columns (ip, mac,
vendor, model, serial, firmware, open_ports, confirmed) so the device table a
person reads is a SELECT rather than a program.

The judgement that needed a rule: where a host speaks two protocols, the flat
columns come from ONE of them and `identity_from` names which. A row that put
a Modbus vendor next to an OPC-UA model would describe a device that does not
exist, and a gateway speaking both is ordinary, not an anomaly. Both identities
survive in JSON regardless. Likewise an unconfirmed protocol supplies nothing:
port_only means nobody said what it is, so the columns stay blank rather than
borrowing a guess.

Saving is idempotent, keyed on a content-addressed id. A survey stored twice is
one survey — a store that appended would make the next comparison report change
that never happened, which is the most damaging thing a change-detection
product can do.

Nothing is pruned by default and there is no retention ceiling. `prune_scans`
is offered and never applied on its own: an on-box store that silently
discarded last month's survey is worse than one that grows, and it returns the
count so the decision stays visible. Keeping zero is refused outright.

25 tests. Four rules mutation-checked; one of them exposed a hollow test —
the port_only case had an EMPTY identity dict, so it would have passed even if
unconfirmed protocols were promoted, because there was nothing to promote. The
fixture now carries fields the store has to actively refuse.

* feat(discovery): the scan report — one self-contained file that opens with what it did

The section order is the argument. Most scanners open with findings; this one
opens with **what it touched**, because the reader of a first survey is usually
the person who has to defend having let it run. "We made 1,524 TCP connections
and 12 Modbus device-ID requests, and here is everything we never do" is
checkable against a packet capture. "The scan was safe" is not. The trust page
is section one and cannot be moved by configuration.

Two constraints are load-bearing:

  * Nothing is loaded from anywhere. No CDN, no web font, no remote image, no
    fetch, no stylesheet link. The file opens on an air-gapped laptop in a
    plant office and renders identically — a report that phoned home to render
    would contradict the product it documents.
  * Everything is escaped. A Modbus vendor field, an OPC-UA ApplicationName and
    an MTConnect device name are all free text chosen by the DEVICE, and a
    device on an unknown network is not a trusted source. Rendering any of them
    raw would turn a survey of a hostile segment into script execution on the
    surveyor's laptop.

A blank cell is rendered as a dash and marked as blank: the device did not
report that field, and it is never filled by inference. Where a host speaks two
protocols the table says which one supplied the row and leaves the rest to the
appendix, rather than describing a device that does not exist.

`host_to_dict` gives the runner's output the same shape the store returns, so a
report renders identically whether the scan came off disk or straight out of
the run — asserted key-for-key, because a renderer that quietly worked on only
one of them would go unnoticed until someone asked for a report of an unsaved
scan.

30 tests. Five properties mutation-checked, and one of them exposed a second
hollow test: "an absent field renders as a dash" searched the whole page, and
the HEADER renders a dash too — so it passed even with every table cell left
empty. It now asserts the marker only the cell renderer emits, plus the
complement, so a filter that marked everything blank could not pass either.

* test(discovery): the whole pipeline against a real Modbus device

Every other test drives one stage with the next one faked. This runs the actual
product end to end — a real pymodbus server answering a real FC43 identification
over a real socket, swept by the real sweeper, identified by the real probe,
written to real SQLite, rendered into the real HTML — and asserts that a vendor
name typed into the server's identity block comes out the far end in the report.

It needs a container for one reason: the allowlist permits 502 and nothing else,
and binding 502 needs root. That constraint is the product working as designed,
so the test bends rather than the allowlist.

Verified on the Linux box:
    VERDICT ok
    WIRE {'modbus_fc43': 1, 'tcp_connect': 6}
    HOST 127.0.0.1 [(102,'refused'),(502,'open'),(4840,'refused'),
                    (4843,'refused'),(5007,'refused'),(44818,'refused')]
    CANDIDATE modbus confirmed modbus_fc43 | vendor=汇川 Inovance,
              model=AM401-CPU1608TP, firmware=2.1.7

The vendor is deliberately non-ASCII. The one real decoding bug found in this
work was an ASCII-first identity decoder that flagged 汇川 as undecodable, and
it survived every test whose fixtures were ASCII, because the fake and the
parser agreed with each other and were both wrong.

Bringing it up exposed a misleading message in the product itself. The probe
reported "modbus extra not installed" when the module actually missing was
`cryptography` — a BASE dependency the connector reaches through the config
layer. That sends a field engineer to `pip install iaiops[modbus]`, which
changes nothing, on a plant floor where there may be no second visit. The
message now names the module that is actually missing and says whether it is a
driver or an incomplete install. Four tests pin it.

The scenario also prints its diagnostics BEFORE asserting: "partial" alone does
not distinguish a silent device from a probe that could not load, and those are
opposite diagnoses.

* fix(discovery): a sub-1/s rate must still grant a whole token

The token bucket sized its capacity to the refill rate, so any policy
below 1.0 connects/second saturated under the single token acquire()
asks for. PacingPolicy accepts anything in (0, 100] — and a rate that
gentle is exactly what a fragile controller deserves — so the gentlest
settings the ceiling allows would sleep out all 1000 refill rounds and
then raise, blaming the limiter for what was a sizing bug.

Capacity now floors at one whole token.

* fix(discovery): a hint narrows the port set, it never widens it

Passing any protocol or port hint flipped include_optional on, which
pulled in ports the chosen profile had deliberately left out. So
"scan only MTConnect" turned a six-port inventory sweep into one that
also connected to 80 and 8080 — ports the allowlist itself marks as
ambiguous with IT. Asking for less reached further, and reached at
ordinary web servers on the OT VLAN.

include_optional is now the profile's decision alone. When a hint
selects only opt-in ports the call is refused with the ports and their
notes, rather than resolving to an empty set and sweeping nothing while
reporting a sweep.

* fix(discovery): a hint that names nothing must say so

ports_for_protocols returns an empty set for a name it does not serve —
the right contract for a narrowing primitive, and pinned by its own
test. At plan level that silence was the whole failure: resolve_ports
handed back no ports, the runner's `and ports` guard skipped the sweep
without a note, and diagnose_empty_sweep then told the operator to
check their VLAN and CIDR while wire_summary showed not one packet had
been sent.

So a misspelling ("modbuss") and a protocol a TCP sweep structurally
cannot find (BACnet, FINS and HART are UDP) both came back as "your
network is wrong". resolve_ports now refuses either, names which it
was, and lists what is sweepable.

* fix(discovery): carry the abort as a flag, and cancel where it counts

Two problems in one path.

The verdict searched the notes for the word "aborting". That word lives
in a sentence in pacing.py, so rewording it — a change no test would
catch, since the tests assert behaviour and not prose — would have made
an aborted, possibly plant-disturbing scan report itself as ok. Any
future note containing the word would have flipped a healthy run the
other way. sweep_hosts now returns the abort as a third value and
_verdict takes it as an argument.

The cancel loop also sat outside the executor's context, so
shutdown(wait=True) had already drained every queued future by the time
it ran. No packets escaped — Pacer.probe re-checks segment health first
and _consecutive never resets, so each remaining future raised before
touching the network — but the code read like a brake that did nothing.
It now cancels inside the block, before the drain.

Add multi-tenant support: multiple restaurants, one system

Every restaurant's data is now isolated by a new Restaurant model —
tables, comandas, menu, orders, payments, coupons, help calls, audit
log and staff all carry a restaurantId and are scoped by it end to
end. This is the foundation for self-service onboarding ("reach the
market") and for a future iFood/delivery-platform channel to slot in
next to KIOSK/DELIVERY/SCHEDULED.

Architecture:
- New `Restaurant` model (id, slug, createdAt). `Settings` keyed by
  restaurantId instead of a hardcoded "singleton" row.
- QR tokens (table/comanda) and the Checkout id stay globally unique
  on purpose — that's how an anonymous QR scan resolves its own
  restaurant with no slug/login needed. Human-facing numbers (table
  number, comanda number, order number/pickup ticket, coupon code)
  become unique per restaurant instead of globally.
- User.email stays globally unique (keeps /login simple: no
  restaurant selection before the password prompt).
- Every by-id staff mutation (delete/update) now scopes on
  {id, restaurantId} via deleteMany/updateMany + a count check,
  instead of trusting a bare id — closes an IDOR class of bug that a
  single-tenant system never had to worry about.
- Realtime SSE topics ("kitchen"/"pdv") are now per-restaurant
  (`kitchen:${restaurantId}`) so one restaurant's live board never
  sees another's events.
- /totem and /pedir move to /totem/[slug] and /pedir/[slug] — the only
  public screens with no QR Code to resolve a restaurant from. New
  /signup does self-service onboarding (Restaurant + Settings + first
  ADMIN user, auto-login), also used as the isolation test's own
  second-tenant fixture.
- Data migration backfills all pre-existing rows onto one
  'rst_default' restaurant (slug "principal") — the real restaurant
  already in production, preserved verbatim.

Found and fixed during isolation testing: the order-number Counter
row wasn't migrated to its new per-restaurant key, so the first order
placed after the migration collided with an existing order number
(unique constraint violation). Added a small follow-up migration that
renames the counter key, preserving the existing sequence.

Verified: full TypeScript + lint clean, production build clean. A
12-point isolation test (via /signup, creating a real second
restaurant on an isolated DB copy) confirms: empty dashboards for a
new tenant, 404 on cross-tenant IDOR attempts by id, independent
per-restaurant numbering/coupons/audit log, SSE events never leaking
across restaurants, and /totem/[slug] serving only its own menu.
Separately reran the full real-restaurant regression (QR order → PDV
payment → totem → painel → reports) after the fix.

        """

Strict meta channel recognition in server

This addresses a security vulnerability affecting user-added extensions
that implement access control for channels. These extensions typically
work by checking incoming messages whose channel is `/meta/subscribe`
and then performing some authentication routine before allowing the
message through.

However, the Server parses channels in a way that means any channel
namespaced under `/meta/subscribe` will also work as a subscription
request. For example if the client sends a message to the channel
`/meta/subscribe/x`, that will bypass most authentication extensions but
will still be interpreted by the server as a subscription request, and
the client will be subscribed to the requested channel. The client has
thus bypassed the user's access control policy.

Here we prevent this by using a strict equality check; only messages
whose channel is exactly `/meta/subscribe` will be interpreted as
subscription requests. The same pattern is applied to all other meta
channels.

explanation:
merge: sync official main with ChatArch feature review (#39)

* Surface warning when context exceeds compression threshold but compression is blocked

Previously, when a session crossed the compression threshold but compression
was skipped (summary-LLM cooldown, #11529, or anti-thrashing, #40803), the
model kept accumulating context until it hit the hard provider token limit and
silently stopped answering — with no signal to the user about why.

Changes:
- context_compressor.should_compress_info() returns a (should_compress, reason)
  tuple. reason is 'cooldown:<seconds>' or 'ineffective' when compression is
  needed but blocked. should_compress() keeps its bool contract so existing
  callers (conversation_loop.py) and regression #29335 are unaffected.
- turn_context.build_turn_context() emits a deduped _emit_warning when the
  context is over threshold but compression is blocked, advising /new or
  /compress. Dedup keys on the block *kind* (cooldown/ineffective), not the
  ticking countdown, so a cooldown doesn't re-fire the warning every turn.
- Adds tests/agent/test_turn_context_overflow_warning.py covering the tuple
  shape, both block kinds, dedup, and re-fire-after-clear.

* Address sweeper review: safe should_compress_info + cover all guards

- ContextEngine.should_compress_info() default impl so plugin engines
  (e.g. _StubEngine) don't raise AttributeError at the call site.
- Centralise warning/reset in AIAgent._warn_context_overflow_blocked /
  _clear_context_overflow_warn so turn-context and conversation-loop guards
  share identical dedup logic and reset on the real compression boundary.
- Cover conversation_loop.py pre-API (~L1007) and loop-compaction (~L4774)
  guards, not just the turn-context preflight.
- _FakeAgent mirrors the two helpers; test suite green (219 passed).

Fixes #62708

* fix(compression): reset blocked-overflow dedup on every compression path + noise-filter survival pins

Follow-up fixes for the #62625 salvage:

- Dedup-reset gap (sweeper review): when the block clears while the
  context is STILL over threshold, execution enters the compression
  branch — the PR's 'else' reset never ran, so the warning stayed
  suppressed forever after the first block. _clear_context_overflow_warn()
  now fires on every automatic compression path: turn-context preflight,
  conversation_loop pre-API gate, and the post-tool loop-compaction gate.
- should_compress_info on current main: main refactored should_compress
  into _automatic_compression_blocked()/_locally(); the tuple variant now
  derives its reason from the same in-memory state via
  _compression_block_reason(), keeping cooldown:<s>/ineffective shapes.
- ContextEngine.should_compress_info ABC default now actually returns
  (should_compress(tokens), None) — the PR's default had a docstring but
  no return (returned None, would crash tuple-unpacking call sites).
- Below-threshold guard: the turn-context persisted-cooldown branch and
  the conversation_loop pre-API cooldown branch no longer warn when the
  estimate is under threshold (should_compress_info returns a None
  reason; the preflight pre-check is not a threshold guarantee). The
  pre-API guard also honors compression.max_attempts instead of a
  hardcoded 3, and no longer fabricates a cooldown reason.
- Noise-filter survival (#69550 composition): warning text is now a
  template constant (CONTEXT_OVERFLOW_BLOCKED_WARNING_TEMPLATE) marked
  FAILURE-CLASS, pinned un-swallowed in VISIBLE_COMPRESSION_MESSAGES and
  in new tests that execute the real _TELEGRAM_NOISY_STATUS_RE +
  _prepare_gateway_status_message.
- Contributor mapping for stanislav@local -> sl4m3.

* fix(compression): guard overflow-warn dedup reset against minimal test doubles

The dedup-reset calls assumed a full AIAgent; gateway/loop test doubles
built via object.__new__ lack _clear_context_overflow_warn and crashed
in build_turn_context (caught by test_api_content_sidecar on CI slice 3).
getattr-guard all four call sites per the established test-double pitfall
pattern (AGENTS.md #17).

* fix(compression): compose the blocked-warning probe with engine preflight

Two composition fixes vs the merged #69865 engine-preflight arm:
1. should_compress_info probe getattr-guarded — minimal compressor
   doubles (SimpleNamespace) and plugin engines lack it; absence means
   no block reason, no warning.
2. Engine maintenance hook stays un-consulted when any skip-branch
   fired (failure cooldown / deferred estimate / codex-native) —
   restoring the #20316 contract the warn-chain restructure broke.

* fix(credential-pool): exhaust all entries sharing a failed API key on 402

A 402/429/401 is an API-key–level failure (account out of balance,
rate-limited, or key rejected), but the same key can back more than one
pool entry — e.g. an explicit pool entry plus a `model_config` entry
auto-seeded from `model.api_key`, both carrying the identical
`runtime_api_key`.

`mark_exhausted_and_rotate(api_key_hint=...)` only marked the *first*
matching entry, leaving the sibling OK. `_select_unlocked()` then kept
handing back the same depleted key, so the billing-recovery `continue`
loop in the conversation retry path never converged: the request hung
until the client disconnected (~2.5min observed against DeepSeek),
emitting only `response.created` with no 402 ever surfaced to the user.

Mark every entry sharing the failed key so the pool can reach the
"no available entries" state and let the error propagate immediately.

Adds a regression test covering two entries backed by the same key.

* perf(credential-pool): persist same-key sibling exhaustion once

Follow-up to the #68565 salvage: batch the sibling _mark_exhausted calls
behind a single _persist() instead of one auth.json write per sibling.

* chore(contributors): add email mapping for airclear

* fix(update): survive undeletable untracked files during autostash (#70161)

git stash push --include-untracked exits non-zero when it saved
everything but could not DELETE some swept untracked files from the
working tree (e.g. a root-owned packaging/ directory left behind by a
sudo'd build: 'warning: failed to remove ...: Permission denied').
The updater ran the push with check=True, so this benign partial
failure raised CalledProcessError and aborted the whole update before
it even fetched — reliably, on every run, for any user with an
undeletable untracked path in the checkout.

Fix, both ends of the class:
- _stash_local_changes_if_needed: probe refs/stash before/after the
  push. Non-zero push + fresh stash entry = changes are saved; warn,

* fix(credential-pool): stop lost-update cooldown erasure and wrong-key quarantine

Two related races in credential-pool cooldown state:

1. Lost update across processes: write_credential_pool merged only
   entries missing from the caller's snapshot; for entries present on
   both sides the caller's in-memory copy won wholesale. A process
   holding a snapshot taken before another process marked a key
   exhausted would, on its next persist (e.g. a round-robin rotation),
   write the key back as healthy — erasing the cooldown so every
   process resumes hammering a rate-limited key. Merge status fields by
   last_status_at recency: adopt the on-disk status only when it is
   strictly newer AND still binding (DEAD, or EXHAUSTED with an
   unexpired cooldown), and never onto re-authed (token-changed)
   entries, so legitimate expiry-clears and fresh logins are preserved.

2. Wrong-key quarantine: when mark_exhausted_and_rotate received an
   api_key_hint that matched no entry, it fell through to
   current()/_select_unlocked() — on a freshly loaded pool that selects
   the NEXT healthy key and benches it for the full cooldown TTL,
   punishing an innocent credential. When a hint is provided but
   unmatched, rotate without marking anything instead of guessing.

Includes regression tests.

* fix(credential_pool): acquire the pool lock in has_available/peek/current/entries

`has_available()`, `peek()`, `current()` and `entries()` read (and, via
`_available_entries()`, mutate and persist) `self._entries` without holding
`self._lock`, while every other entry point — `select()`,
`mark_exhausted_and_rotate()`, `acquire_lease()`, `try_refresh_current()` —
guards the exact same access with the lock.

`_available_entries()` is not read-only: it prunes aged-out DEAD manual
entries (rebinding `self._entries` at the prune step) and calls `_persist()`
(writes auth.json). The gateway runs platform adapters in threads and cron
runs jobs in a ThreadPoolExecutor, so a status probe via `has_available()`
or `peek()` can race a concurrent `select()`/rotation: torn iteration of
`self._entries`, interleaved auth.json writes, or a lost token rotation.

Fix: take `self._lock` in all four query methods. Because the lock is
non-reentrant and `peek()` composes `current()` + `_available_entries()`,
add a lock-free `_current_unlocked()` helper and route the already-locked
internal callers (`_select_unlocked`, `mark_exhausted_and_rotate`,
`_try_refresh_current_unlocked`) through it to avoid self-deadlock.

Added regression tests: a no-deadlock check (peek re-entrancy) and a
lock-held-blocks-the-call check for each of the four methods.

* fix(credential_pool): complete the locking boundary across the public pool surface

Follow-up to review feedback:

- Acquire self._lock in the remaining public pool-state methods:
  has_credentials, reset_statuses, remove_index, resolve_target, and
  add_entry. All of them read or rebind self._entries (and the mutating
  ones persist auth.json), so they now hold the same lock as select()
  and the query methods. None are called from within the lock, so no
  unlocked helpers are needed.
- Make the blocking test deterministic: an instrumented lock records the
  acquire attempt, and the test first waits for the worker to actually
  reach self._lock before asserting it blocks. Previously an unlocked
  method could pass if the worker thread was scheduled late.
- Extend the lock test matrix to all nine public methods; the five newly

* fix(slack): add catch-all event handler to prevent Slack auto-disabling Event Subscriptions

Without a catch-all handler, slack-bolt returns HTTP 404 for every
unhandled bot event (user_change, user_huddle_changed, reaction_added,
etc.) and never sends the Socket Mode ack. On active Slack workspaces
where the app is subscribed to high-volume events, this produces a
near-100% un-acked failure rate that crosses Slack's >95%/60-min
threshold and triggers automatic disabling of the app's Event
Subscriptions — silently killing all inbound event delivery.

Place a catch-all re.compile(r".*") handler AFTER the specific event
handlers so bolt's router matches those first. Truly unhandled events
are silently acked (200) and logged at DEBUG. The failure rate stays
near 0% regardless of which events the Slack app manifest subscribes to.

* fix(slack): neutralize prompt injection in thread-context backfill

`SlackAdapter._fetch_thread_context` formats each prior thread message as
`{name}: {msg_text}` and joins them with newlines into the block the call
site prepends *raw* into the model turn (`text = thread_context + text`).
Both fields are attacker-influenceable — any thread participant sets their
own Slack display name and message text — and neither was neutralized, so
an embedded newline let a thread message break out of its line and pose as
a fresh markdown section (a fake "## SYSTEM" / "## Override" heading) inside
the context the model reads when first mentioned mid-thread.

This is the same indirect-prompt-injection vector already closed for the
sibling untrusted sinks: the sender-name prefix
(`neutralize_untrusted_inline_text`), the reply quote, and the relay
channel-context renderer. The Slack thread-context backfill — the default
whenever the bot is mentioned in a thread with no active session — was the
missed sink. (The existing `[unverified]` tagging marks *who* a message is
from; it does nothing about newline structure, so an authorized sender can
inject just as easily.)

Flatten both fields with `neutralize_untrusted_inline_text` before
interpolation. The body uses `max_chars=0` so message text is not truncated
(thread context caps the message *count*, never per-message length); the
display name keeps the default bound. `parent_text` keeps the raw message
(its own reply-context sink neutralizes separately). A well-behaved message
is preserved byte-for-byte.

Adds a regression test covering a hostile display name, a hostile message
body, benign passthrough, and the no-truncation guarantee.

* fix(slack): warn when slack_tokens.json is group/world-readable

enforcement — a default umask 022 makes it world-readable.

* fix(slack): stop double-decoding HTML entities when escaping message text

format_message unescapes already-escaped input before re-escaping, so that
pre-escaped text doesn't get double-escaped. That unescape was three
sequential str.replace calls, which re-scan each other's output:

    "&lt;"  --(& -> &)-->  "<"  --(< -> <)-->  "<"

The & produced by the first replace pairs with the following "lt;" and
decodes a second time. "&lt;" is the wire form of the literal text
"<", so the text is silently destroyed: Slack receives "<" and renders
"<". Anyone writing about HTML or markup ("&lt;b&gt;" -> "<b>")
loses their literal text, with no error.

re.sub scans left-to-right and never re-scans its own replacements, so a
single pass fixes it. The escape pass on the next line is left untouched --
it is correctly ordered (& first, so the &s it inserts aren't re-escaped).

Only the double-decode cases change; every other input is byte-identical
before and after. This is the same round-trip invariant the neighbouring
test_pre_escaped_{ampersand,lt,gt}_not_double_escaped tests already assert,
extended to the case they miss. Affects the plain mrkdwn path (send,
edit_message) and Block Kit sections, which route section text through
format_message.

* fix(gateway): strip language tag from Slack fenced code blocks

Slack's mrkdwn does not strip the optional language tag from fenced
code blocks like GitHub-flavored markdown does — it renders
```text\nfoo\n``` as a code block whose literal first line is "text".
The agent emitted ```text fences around raw command output, which
surfaced "text" as the first line of every such block.

Drop the tag from the opening fence in format_message() before stashing
the block behind a placeholder. Stripping only fires for a genuine
opening fence — a ``` at the start of a line, tagged with a single
token (no spaces or backticks) — and the original line ending is
preserved. The fence-protection regex deliberately matches loosely, so
a mid-line ``` (e.g. an inline ```span``` wrapping across a newline)
can be grouped as an "opening fence" whose first line is real content;
differential fuzzing against the pre-change formatter (40k generated
messages) confirms the only behavioral delta is the tag strip itself.

The Block Kit renderer is unaffected: render_blocks() intercepts fences
itself before mrkdwn_fn is applied, so this only changes the mrkdwn
surfaces that still go through format_message() — the plain-text
fallback field (notifications, search indexing, accessibility),
slash-command ephemeral replies, and standalone cron delivery.

* fix(slack): add bold-text zero-width-space guard for trailing non-word chars

* fix: also close orphaned single-backtick inline-code spans

(```) code-block fences. Single backtick (`) inline-code spans have

fix(api): gate runner-KYC reads + close auth-recovery lockout & OTP email-flood

Three verified findings from the authz/abuse sweep:

1) Runner KYC read routes over-exposed (IDOR). GET /admin/runners/pending and
   /admin/runners/{userId}/documents sat under the bare 'admin' alias (any active
   admin) while their approve/reject siblings and the byte-stream route require
   canModerate. finance/support admins — who by design never see runner KYC —
   could read government-ID/selfie metadata and, for any un-migrated legacy row,
   a raw public-disk file_url. Gated both reads with admin.can:moderate
   (super_admin/admin/ops), matching the rest of the KYC surface. Same class as
   3891604, on the two read routes that sweep missed.

2) Account-recovery lockout (AUTHX-3 class). verify-otp and reset-password shared
   the credential-ONLY 'auth' limiter, so 5 junk requests for a victim's
   phone/email locked the legitimate user out of COMPLETING recovery for the
   window — from any IP. Added an 'auth-verify' limiter keyed on credential+IP
   (like 'login') and moved those two completion paths onto it; forgot-password
   stays on 'auth' so outbound reset-email bombing remains globally capped per
   credential.

3) send-otp email flood. The 'otp' limiter had only a per-recipient 3/hr bucket
   and no per-IP cap, so one source could rotate through unlimited distinct
   recipient addresses and fan out real verification emails (only the anon 20/min
   api cap applied → ~1200 emails/hr to arbitrary inboxes). Added a per-IP 30/hr
   aggregate bucket, mirroring the secondary cap 'auth'/'login' already carry.

Tests: finance/support 403 & ops 200 on the KYC reads; cross-IP recovery is not
locked out while single-IP stays capped; send-otp is capped across distinct
recipients per IP. 665 pass on SQLite and MySQL 8.

Generate new passwords in a secure way

Previously, lost passwords were generated via
org.apache.commons.lang.RandomStringUtils,
which is using java.util.Random internally.

This PRNG is has a 48-bit seed, that can easily be bruteforced
if an attacker is able to get the PRNG's output, for example
but resetting their own account multiple times,
leading to trivial privileges escalation attacks.

This commit makes use of java.security.SecureRandom
instead.

## Broken leg
The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Not authorized to reprice this booking' });
    }

Unauth callers ate a wasted bookingRequests SELECT before hitting a
MISLEADING 403 that suggested a permissions problem, not a
credentials problem. The audit agent classified this as "risky-cosmetic"
because it's a 403→401 client-behavior change; on inspection the reprice
client is always an authenticated logged-in customer, so a 401 only fires
for callers that shouldn't be reaching the endpoint at all.

## Fix (server-only, split into two clean checks)
1. Explicit 401 at the door — before the DB fetch — with an honest
   'Authentication required' message.
2. Ownership check no longer needs the !userId branch — reads cleanly
   as "owner OR verified admin".

Both branches unchanged behaviorally for legitimate callers.

## Test
server/tests/reprice-401-hygiene.regression.test.ts — 3 pins:
  ✓ returns 401 explicitly when there is no userId
  ✓ 401 guard sits BEFORE the first db.select() (no wasted round-trip)
  ✓ ownership check no longer folds !userId into the 403 branch

    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  3 passed (3)

## Dependency
None. Completes the auth-slippage sweep on booking-requests.ts —
prior sweep PRs #1904 (confirm), #1911 (7 POSTs), #1912 (GET). This
covers the last remaining router-mounted handler with the same shape.

## Risk
Very low. 401 replaces 403 for anon callers only (a case that already
denied). Legitimate customer + admin repricing unchanged.

## Do not merge
Per standing CEO directive.

explanation:
Ship the evidence layer, and say which controls it satisfies

An enterprise checklist arrived covering auditability, security posture, data
governance, reliability and procurement fit. Mapping it against the 28-question
ledger showed the two were asking different things: the ledger asks whether the
system does the right thing, and most of the checklist asks whether you can
*prove* it did, continuously, to someone who will not take your word for it.

Three of the gaps turned out to be specific and verifiable rather than vague.

**The audit log had no integrity protection.** "Append-only" was a property of
the application -- the resource offered only `:read` -- and said nothing about
what a `psql` connection could do. It now has two mechanisms doing different
jobs. A trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE, which is total until someone can
`ALTER TABLE`. And every event carries the SHA-256 of its contents chained to
the previous event's, so an operator privileged enough to drop the trigger still
cannot make an edit look untouched. The suite proves it by tampering: it
disables each trigger in turn, alters a row, removes a row, forges an event, and
asserts each is found.

The chain is per tenant, which is cheaper *and* better. AshEvents already takes
`pg_advisory_xact_lock` keyed by the written resource's tenant, so the
serialization a chain needs is already held -- a global chain would serialize
every tenant against every other for nothing. And a customer can verify their
own chain without being shown anyone else's.

**`audit_events` had no tenant column.** Reading the log required a `:global`
grant, necessarily -- the log has no owner and no business unit, so every
narrower depth reaches nothing on it. So a customer could not see their own
audit trail at all, and no column existed that would have let them. The first
fix here was a bespoke policy check; it worked and it was wrong, because it
answered a tenancy question with an authorization mechanism. The log is now
attribute-multitenant like everything else, and the check is deleted.

**Nothing had ever written to the provenance columns.** SystemAttributes
declares Dataverse's `created_by_id`, `modified_by_id` and the two
`*_on_behalf_by` columns on every platform resource; a grep for `created_by_id`
outside the transformer that declares them returned nothing. Every row carried
four nulls describing who was responsible for it. They are filled now, and the
on-behalf pair is what makes impersonation representable: the customer stays the
actor, so authorization is exactly what they could have done unaided, and the
operator is recorded alongside on the record and in every audit event.

Also: `mix ash_enterprise.audit.export`, the CSV an auditor actually asks for --
in chain order, carrying `sequence`, `previous_hash` and `hash` so the recipient
can re-verify it rather than take it on trust.

**The ledger grows from 28 questions to 51**, with a sixth section for the
evidence axis. Read the per-section rollup rather than the total: evidence is
8/11 shipped, identity 4/10, assurance 0/6. One ratio across 51 questions
reports the project as uniformly half-finished and hides which half, which is
why the site and the README now render both.

**`docs/controls.json` maps SOC 2, ISO 27001 and GDPR controls** to those
questions and through them to the test that proves each, rendered by the same
task and gated by the same `--check` as the roadmap tables. It claims technical
prerequisites and says so in its first paragraph, because certification is an
auditor's judgement about policy and process over a twelve-month window and
claiming otherwise would make the honesty mechanism the rest of this repository
runs on worthless. A control is scored by its *weakest* question -- an early
version used `min_by` where it needed `max_by` and cheerfully reported a control
with an open question as shipped, which is precisely the failure this file
exists to prevent.

Writing the map found two things that had been invisible: evidence of review had
no question at all, and cryptography appears in exactly one place in the whole
repository.

ADRs 0020-0023 are `accepted` and describe the above. 0024-0026 are `proposed`:
retention and erasure (the least reversible decision in the set -- an
append-only log that refuses DELETE collides head-on with Article 17, and the
resolution is to destroy keys rather than rows), log shipping and evidence of
review, and AI governance as disclosure rather than a second authorization
model.

**The site tells it as a sequence now.** It had all the ingredients and told
none of it as a story: every section was a thesis or a feature, and the
strangler -- the on-ramp the whole argument depends on -- sat fifth, between two
capability sections. It is three acts now (the on-ramp, what you get, the
evidence), plus a `/vision/` page that puts it on a week-one-to-month-three
timeline with a "where it actually is" note wherever the package ships but the
demonstration does not, and a `/controls/` page rendering the control map with
the disclaimer first. The hero leads with the outcome rather than the thesis and
shows the Clarity ER diagram above the fold, which was previously below it.

**`og:image` was missing entirely.** The layout has always set
`twitter:card=summary_large_image` and never supplied an image, so every share
on Slack, LinkedIn or X rendered a blank rectangle. `scripts/build-og.mjs`
composes the card from `docs/roadmap.json` and rasterises it with sharp, which
Astro already depends on -- so a stranger's first impression is the current
scoreboard, and it cannot go stale while the ledger moves.

`COMPLIANCE.md` also had to be added to `ROOT_FILES` in the sync script, or the
hand-written link from `/controls/` would have 404'd: the dead-link check covers
links inside synced docs, not links written by hand in `src/pages/`.

--check, sobelow, hex.audit and 132 tests (up from 102) all pass; the site
builds to 50 pages with no dead links and `astro check` is clean. CI gains
`--skip` on sobelow, for the one documented `@sobelow_skip` in the codebase.

fix(api): close the agent-token gaps found by the codex gate

Critical: the MCP-only rule was scoped to the /api/v1 prefix, so POST /logout —
the one root-level auth:sanctum route — still accepted agent bearers, giving an
agent a human-only action and a token-validity oracle. The refusal now sits on
both route groups; accepting a token is a positive capability exactly one
surface will opt into (#135). The IDOR sweep enumerates every registered route
instead of a prefix, and proves its two exemptions authenticate nothing.

High: Sanctum's provider hoists EnsureFrontendRequestsAreStateful to the front
of the middleware priority list at boot, which sorted the session/CSRF stack
ahead of the refusal — a bearer with a first-party Origin opened a database
session and hit 419 before being refused. AppServiceProvider now hoists the
refusal after Sanctum's provider; asserted on pipeline order and as zero
queries on a rejected request. Mint and its audit record are one transaction;
revoke records through recordSafely and only the request that removed the row
records an event; the Policy trait fails closed on any persistent token that is
not an AgentToken.

Also: no-store on the mint response, a dismiss action for the revealed value,
error-vs-empty on the settings list, deny-as-not-found for a foreign token id,
and a per-member token cap that bounds the unpaginated list.

· `diffSummary` · `--observe` 를 줬으면 `environmentObservation`.

### 2. 승인

```bash
python3 scripts/authorize.py --plan compiled.json \
  --authority HERMES --actor "hermes:ceo" > authorization.json
```

**`apply` 와 다른 명령인 것이 요점이다.** 승인이 Plan 안의 필드였을 때는 그 필드를 고치고
다시 digest 한 Plan 이 스스로를 승인한 것과 구별되지 않았다. 영수증은 **어떤 digest 를**
승인했는지 말하므로, Plan 이 한 바이트라도 바뀌면 그 승인이 더 이상 그 Plan 을 안 가리킨다.
통합 구성에서는 이 문서를 제어평면이 만든다.

서명은 아니다. 이 파일을 쓸 수 있는 사람은 승인을 주장할 수 있다. 사는 것은 주장이 별개의
아티팩트가 되고 행위자·시각·묶인 digest 를 갖는다는 것이다.

### 3. 외부 쓰기

```bash
python3 scripts/apply.py --plan compiled.json --ledger receipts.json \
  --phase before-files --authorization authorization.json [--dry-run]
```

`--authorization` 없이는 어떤 원격 읽기보다 먼저 거부한다. `--dry-run` 은 그 게이트에
닿기 전에 반환하므로, dry-run 이 도는 것은 실행 경로가 산다는 증거가 아니다.

각 Operation 은 자기가 만들 것을 `desiredState` 로 싣고 있다. 생성 파라미터가 Plan
밖에서 오면 승인된 digest 가 실행될 effect 를 결정하지 못한다 — private 으로 승인된
Plan 이 public 저장소를 만들어도 digest 는 같다.

쓰고 나서 다시 읽고, **승인된 상태와 대조**한다. 존재만 확인하면 `disabled` 로 만들어진
ruleset 이 `active` 로 만들어진 것과 같은 통과를 받는다.

### 4. genesis 커밋

```bash
python3 scripts/publish.py --plan compiled.json --workdir /tmp/genesis \

커밋에 세션 식별자를 남기지 않는다. 생성 저장소는 공개일 수 있고, 그 경우 트레일러는
저장소 안에 운영 정보를 넣는 것이 된다.

### 5. Result

```bash
python3 scripts/result.py --input result-input.json \
  --verification verification.json
```

`--verification` 은 Plan 을 컴파일할 때 쓴 그 목록이다. Plan 은 digest 만 싣기 때문에,
Result 를 조립하는 쪽이 원본을 다시 대야 하고 그것이 승인된 계약과 같은지를 여기서
대조한다. 다른 목록을 대면 거부한다.

원장을 그대로 넘긴다 — genesis 영수증까지. 파일을 올린 push 는 외부 쓰기이고, 그 행을
빼고 세면 파일이 한 번도 안 올라간 부트스트랩이 완료로 보고된다.

제어평면이 받는 문서다. **활성화를 주장하지 않는다** — 공장은 저장소를 만들었을 뿐
그 저장소가 제어평면 위에서 돈다고 말할 수 있는 위치에 있지 않다. 받는 쪽이
그런 주장을 키 존재만으로 거부한다.

fix(reprice): P1 — split !userId (401) from ownership check (403) on POST /:requestId/reprice (#1913)

## Broken leg
The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Not authorized to reprice this booking' });
    }

Unauth callers ate a wasted bookingRequests SELECT before hitting a
MISLEADING 403 that suggested a permissions problem, not a
credentials problem. The audit agent classified this as "risky-cosmetic"
because it's a 403→401 client-behavior change; on inspection the reprice
client is always an authenticated logged-in customer, so a 401 only fires
for callers that shouldn't be reaching the endpoint at all.

## Fix (server-only, split into two clean checks)
1. Explicit 401 at the door — before the DB fetch — with an honest
   'Authentication required' message.
2. Ownership check no longer needs the !userId branch — reads cleanly
   as "owner OR verified admin".

Both branches unchanged behaviorally for legitimate callers.

## Test
server/tests/reprice-401-hygiene.regression.test.ts — 3 pins:
  ✓ returns 401 explicitly when there is no userId
  ✓ 401 guard sits BEFORE the first db.select() (no wasted round-trip)
  ✓ ownership check no longer folds !userId into the 403 branch

    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  3 passed (3)

## Dependency
None. Completes the auth-slippage sweep on booking-requests.ts —
prior sweep PRs #1904 (confirm), #1911 (7 POSTs), #1912 (GET). This
covers the last remaining router-mounted handler with the same shape.

## Risk
Very low. 401 replaces 403 for anon callers only (a case that already
denied). Legitimate customer + admin repricing unchanged.

## Do not merge
Per standing CEO directive.
