### Added

- **Direct-to-S3 song upload via presigned URLs.** The API no longer accepts audio as `byte[]` or
  `MultipartFile`. `POST /api/v1/albums/{albumId}/songs` (`ROLE_ARTIST`) validates content type
  and size (max 500 MB), persists song metadata, and returns short-lived (10 min) presigned PUT
  URL(s). Files larger than 100 MB receive S3 multipart part URLs. The client uploads directly to
  S3; `POST /api/v1/albums/{albumId}/songs/{songId}/confirm` verifies the object (or completes
  multipart with part ETags). Domain `SongStoragePort` exposes `generateUploadUrl` /
  `confirmUpload` with pure value objects (`SongUploadCommand`, `PresignedUploadResult`,
  `ConfirmUploadCommand`). AWS SDK v2 stays in `S3SongStorageAdapter`.
- **Twelve-Factor compliance hardening.**
  - Factor 3 — production config contract: `application-prod.yaml` binds every env-specific value
    from env vars and `ProdConfigValidator` (prod profile only) aborts startup with a clear message

### Fixed

- **Playlist IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) eliminated.** All four playlist mutation
  use cases (`UpdatePlaylistDetailsService`, `DeletePlaylistService`, `AddSongToPlaylistService`,
  `RemoveSongFromPlaylistService`) now enforce ownership via `PlaylistOwnershipGuard`, which throws
  `ForbiddenException` (mapped to HTTP 403) when the authenticated user is not the playlist owner.
  The `currentUserId` is injected from the security context in every controller mutation path — never
  trusted from the request body. Covered by unit tests (per-service forbidden/not-found cases) and
  E2E A-versus-B tests in `PlaylistFlowIT`.
- **DynamoDB empty-page crashes.** `findByProfileEmail` used `page.items().get(0)` and the
  playlist/like queries used `iterator().next()`; all now stream empty pages safely
  (`IndexOutOfBoundsException` / `NoSuchElementException` on fresh tables).

- Production environment shape (`application-prod.yaml` empty; JWT secret, AWS endpoints and
  Redis host from env vars in real deployments).
- Pagination on more list endpoints; rate limiting; email verification and password recovery.

facilitator, still present in the latest published version 2.23.0):
ALGORAND_MAINNET_CAIP2/ALGORAND_TESTNET_CAIP2 are truncated to 32 base64
chars of the genesis hash instead of the full 44, which made every x402
resource server hard-fail at startup (missing_facilitator). Built the
correct CAIP-2 string from the package's own correct GENESIS_HASH exports
instead. Manus independently found and patched the same bug in the
running Intermezzo container the same day (2026-08-18/19) — this is the
durable source-level fix their own notes asked for.

X-Klendoo-API-Key — Manus's own docs disagree with themselves on which
header the gateway checks; sending both avoids guessing wrong on a launch
night (see BACKLOG.md).

feat(observability): alert when Kubescape posture data goes stale (#3237)

* feat(observability): alert when Kubescape posture data goes stale

A broken posture scanner and a compliant cluster read identically: when the
scan aborts it persists nothing, and every consumer sees "no new findings".

Measured on prod while picking this up: the newest stored
workloadconfigurationscan was 2026-06-27 — posture had been frozen for 53 days
with no signal on any surface. The scheduler CronJob kept reporting
lastSuccessfulTime daily (it only POSTs the request; it never observes the
outcome) and the CI posture gate stayed green (it scans manifests, not the
cluster). Control: applicationprofiles and vulnerabilitymanifestsummaries,
served by the same aggregated API, were fresh to the same day — so this is the
configuration scan specifically, not the storage layer.

Keys on data AGE rather than any particular failure, because #2933's original
cause was already fixed and the scan was failing a third way by the time this
was written; a rule watching for a known error string would have gone quiet
exactly when it mattered.

Paginates deliberately: the aggregated API returns a continue token, and the
collection is 1542 objects over 4 pages, so a single unpaginated GET would
report one page's newest timestamp as the collection's. An empty collection
alerts rather than passes — that is the silent zero this check exists to catch.

needs re-approval.

rendered from both trees and the grant-bearing document IDENTITIES diffed.
74 -> 77, additive only — added ServiceAccount observability/posture-staleness-alert,

removed-set EMPTY; Role and RoleBinding counts unchanged. The render of main
independently reproduces the membership already recorded in this file, which
corroborates the extraction rather than assuming it.

main is green against the old constant, so the base surface is approved and the

The new value was read from the required job's own output on the approved
renderer (run 32215442664); the local toolchain is refused as unapproved
(kubectl v1.36.1 vs an approved v1.36.2), the same single-renderer caveat the
previous value carries. The previous digest is preserved in the comment.

Part of #3024

* fix(observability): close two silent-failure paths in the staleness alert

Both found by self-review before requesting an external review, and both are
cases where a BROKEN check reports success — the exact failure class this check
exists to catch.

1. An EMPTY MAX_AGE_SECONDS made the job post a false "posture is stale" alert
   for fresh data and exit 0. `set -u` catches an unset variable, but Flux
   envsubst produces an empty one, and `[ "$age" -le "" ]` errors inside an `if`
   CONDITION where `set -e` cannot fire, so the else branch was taken. That is
   strictly worse than the sibling alert's failure mode, whose blanked variable
   at least exits 1. Now validated up front and fails closed.

2. A 404 exited 1, which contradicted this file's own header claim that local/CI
   stays quiet by design: the docker overlay comments coroot and kubescape out
   independently, so enabling coroot alone would have produced a permanently
   failing Job every 6h that never reaches the placeholder-webhook skip. Now
   exits 0 like the sibling's missing-CRD branch, with the prod trade-off stated.

Part of #3024

* fix(observability): alert on a vanished scan API, reject a zero threshold, encode the page token

Addresses three CodeRabbit findings on this PR.

A 404 from the configuration-scan API exited 0, so in prod a scanner whose
aggregated API had gone away reported success — the silent-healthy reading this
Job exists to catch. It now routes through the alert path; the placeholder-webhook
branch already keeps local and CI clusters quiet, so the trade-off the old comment
accepted was not necessary.

A zero MAX_AGE_SECONDS passed validation although the message promises a positive
integer, and would mark every scan stale. Rejects the zero value, so 00 and 000
are caught too, not just the literal 0.

The opaque continuation token was interpolated into the query string, where a
'+' decodes server-side as a space and corrupts pagination. curl encodes it now.

    result. But it doesn't define how to set that cookie.

    from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
    from fastapi.security import APIKeyCookie

    app = FastAPI()

    cookie_scheme = APIKeyCookie(name="session")

explanation:
Fix real vulnerabilities found in a dedicated security audit

Three parallel audits (auth/authz, injection/input-handling, secrets/
infrastructure) covering the whole app, adversarial lens. Fixes:

CRITICAL
- MFA was completely bypassable: the 5-minute "mfa_pending" challenge
  token issued by /auth/login (before a TOTP/backup code is ever
  checked) decoded and passed get_current_user()'s checks exactly like
  a real session token -- anyone with just a password (the one thing
  MFA exists to add a second factor against) could call any
  authenticated endpoint directly with it, no code required, for the
  full 5-minute window. Now explicitly rejected, same pattern as the
  existing "purpose" claim check.

HIGH
- Twilio webhook signature verification failed OPEN (skipped, request
  allowed through) when TWILIO_TOKEN/PUBLIC_BASE_URL were unset --
  now fails closed (503), matching the pattern already used correctly
  for CRON_SECRET/EMAIL_WORKER_SECRET.
- SECRET_KEY/JWT_SECRET ship with hardcoded, publicly-known placeholder
  defaults with no code-level guard against running with them in
  production (only Render's generateValue: true prevented this on the
  documented deploy path). App now refuses to boot with DEBUG=false if
  either is still its literal default.

MODERATE
- Three IDOR gaps: POST /communications/send's maintenance_update
  template, POST /maintenance/'s unit_id/tenant_id, and POST
  /accounting/expenses' vendor_id all accepted a foreign org's UUID
  with no ownership check, leaking that resource's name/title/status
  back in the response. All now validated against the caller's org.
- Unescaped HTML injection in three outreach-email templates
  (services/lead_service.py) -- lead fields (scraped from public,
  attacker-editable Google Business Profile data, or typed into
  POST /leads with no sanitization) were interpolated into HTML emails
  with no output encoding. Now html.escape()'d for the HTML body
  specifically (plain-text body unaffected).
- SSRF in the lead-scraper's email-discovery fetch
  (workers/tasks/lead_scraping.py) -- a Places listing's self-reported
  website URL was fetched with no scheme/private-IP allowlist and
  followed redirects blindly, so a listing pointed at an internal
  address or a cloud metadata endpoint would have the server fetch it.
  Added an SSRF guard checked on the initial URL and re-checked on
  every redirect hop.
- FastAPI backend sent no security headers at all (X-Frame-Options,
  X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) --
  only the Next.js frontend did, despite security.tsx's copy claiming
  this applies to "every response." Left /docs and /redoc unprotected
  against framing. Added a headers middleware.
- ALLOWED_ORIGINS="*" combined with allow_credentials=True (a plausible
  operator typo in Render's env vars) would silently make CORS reflect
  any origin with credentials -- app now refuses to boot with that
  combination instead.
- Three endpoints doing real, billed AI/scraping work (inspection photo
  AI analysis, the Claude marketing-copy generator, the lead-scrape
  trigger) had zero rate limiting or cost cap beyond role/plan gating --
  a compromised privileged account or a buggy retry loop had no
  built-in ceiling on Anthropic/OpenAI/Google Places billing, and on
  this single-worker server a burst could also stall every other
  tenant's requests. Added reasonable per-minute limits to all three.

Not fixed here, flagged for a follow-up decision (both require either
a schema migration or a product/UX tradeoff, not a mechanical fix):
- Password reset tokens (staff-side /auth/reset-password) are replayable
  within their 30-minute window -- not marked single-use like the
  tenant-portal equivalent already is.
- Rate limiting on login/reset/2FA is per-IP only, no per-account
  lockout/backoff -- a distributed credential-stuffing attempt across
  many source IPs isn't meaningfully throttled today.
- API keys are stored and compared in plaintext (high-entropy,
  infeasible to brute-force, but a DB-level compromise would expose
  live keys directly rather than hashes) -- hashing at rest would need
  a rotation flow since existing keys can't be un-hashed.

The native comms platform (Slices 1–6) extends the CRM in-place under `src/lib/comms/` and `/app/comms` — it is **not** a parallel marketing platform, and GoHighLevel stays **frozen** (not extended, not removed). Campaign/enrollment plumbing lives here; the *send-path compliance* details live in **twilio-a2p-compliance**.

- **Enrollment lifecycle drives the drips.** `comm_campaign_enrollments` carries a status (`enrolled`, `paused_for_conversation`, …). The drip runner (`campaign-run.ts` `dripAdvance`) selects **only** `status='enrolled'`, so pausing an enrollment removes it from the population entirely — a *structural* guarantee, not a heuristic. Reuse this lifecycle; do not build a second scheduler.
- **A reply pauses promotional automation (§10).** On a genuine inbound reply, `inbound.ts` sets that member's `enrolled` enrollments to `paused_for_conversation` (audited). This is why FSOS never sends a "haven't heard back" follow-up after a customer has engaged. Resume is deferred: the `resume-paused` cron runs the pure `evaluateResume` (`conversation-mode.ts`) against the editable `comm_conversation_policy` (quiet-period is a config default, `is_assumption`) and returns eligible enrollments to `enrolled` — on a manual resume, a resolved/closed conversation, or the customer going quiet ≥ the configured window.
- **Simulation is required before activation (§14).** A campaign cannot activate without a recent read-only simulation pass on record (`comm_campaigns.simulated_at`; activate returns **422 `simulation_required`** otherwise). Treat activation as gated on a dry-run — see **twilio-a2p-compliance** for the simulator.
- **Delegated agency-owner outreach.** Outreach on behalf of an agency owner carries an actual-sender vs represented-party model and requires an ACTIVE, in-scope delegation; unresolved ownership routes to an assignment-review queue rather than sending (ADR-015/§6). The authority check is enforced in the gate (`delegation`/`ownership` steps); the campaign/enrollment side just supplies the represented agency.

explanation:
fix(comms): production-readiness review — compliance, security, correctness & docs

Comprehensive review of the AI Communications Center (6 parallel reviewers,
adversarially verified). Fixes every confirmed Critical/Important finding plus
high-value Minors, with regression tests and full docs reconciliation.

Compliance / guardrails
- Gate ordering (CRITICAL): move business_hours (a non-escalating operational
  deferral) to the deferral tail so a firewall / DNC / recommendation / delegation /
  data-confidence trip evaluated outside operating hours still escalates on its own
  step instead of being masked as a benign "held for hours" deferral (§13.9).
  Regression test added.
- Securities firewall: send.ts now OR-resolves is_security server-side from the stored
  conversation/household flag, so the one-off send route can no longer bypass the
  firewall with a client-supplied flag (defense in depth at every call site).
- DNC opt-out (CRITICAL): match tolerantly by digit suffix for SMS so a STOP stored as
  +1XXXXXXXXXX still blocks an outbound to XXXXXXXXXX (TCPA opt-out bypass).
- Consent: a channel-wide revoke is now a hard FLOOR a purpose-scoped grant cannot
  override, and STOP cascades to revoke purpose-scoped consent rows (stores stay
  consistent). Fixed the marketing-email frequency filter (.in vs raw string) that
  silently zeroed the marketing caps.
- AI authority (§11): the authority matrix + §12 evaluations now run for EVERY
  aiGenerated send, so an unclassified AI message fails safe to draft-for-human-review
  and can't bypass by omitting the class.

Security
- HTML-escape recipient-controlled merge values on the email channel (stored-XSS /
  injection defense); SMS/plaintext unchanged.
- Sign click-tracking redirect targets (HMAC, bound to the message id) and verify at
  click time — closes the open-redirect on the tracking endpoint.

Correctness / API
- Safe DB error responses across all comms routes (no raw error strings; generic
  message + server-side log) via a shared dbErrorResponse helper.
- Campaign activate: dispatch first, mark active only on success (+ re-activation
  guard) so a dispatch failure never leaves a campaign active with nothing sent.
- runIdempotent: release the claim on failure so a transient error no longer poisons
  the key into a false "already sent" idempotent skip.
- Template submit/approve + identity singleton save now check rows-affected / upsert
  (no false success); removed a dead 'admin' role from comms permission lists.
- Persist the exact transmitted body (incl. SMS TRAIGA footer) for audit fidelity.

UI / a11y
- Hub-level loading.tsx (skeleton) + error.tsx (isolated, retryable) for the comms hub.
- Campaign builder: enforce the required name (gate Next/submit + inline error).
- Subnav Overview active state; SMS casing.
- Term-conversion email: reframe product-ownership prose to conditional/educational (§4.3).

Tests
- New tests/comms-security-fixes.test.mjs (escaping + redirect signing); strengthened
  email-determinism (locks the 30-template set); guardrail gate regression for the
  ordering fix; RLS harness now proves client isolation on comm_messages/comm_conversations.

Docs / skills
- Reconciled the "7-step" → 13-step gate across the specs (canonical enumeration in
  data-guardrails.md §5); extended comms-ai-compliance.md through Slices 1–8; added the
  shipped comms routes to routes.md/sitemap.md; DESIGN.md sub-nav pattern note; new ADR
  index; Slices 7–9 skills backfill.

GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67: prevent arbitrary certificate revocation via duplicate DB rows

Certificate identity was tracked only by Lemur's internal database row, not
by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could upload a
duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing
authority_id and serial) and then revoke it, causing the CA to revoke the
real certificate belonging to another user.

- POST /api/1/certificates/upload now requires AuthorityPermission on the
  specified authority, and rejects uploads whose (authority_id, serial)
  pair already matches an existing certificate (409).
- PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke now checks authorization and endpoint
  attachment against every certificate row sharing (authority_id, serial)
  with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request.

Implements the fixes from this session's full security audit (Sections
5-8 plus remaining Section 3/4 items) that weren't already applied live:

- CORS: replace origin:'*' with an explicit allowlist (APP_URL/
  FRONTEND_URL/localhost) in the production Nest bootstrap
  (apps/web/src/lib/backendPort.ts). The previous config also paired
  wildcard origin with credentials:true, an invalid combination per the
  Fetch spec.

- Rate limiting: add @Throttle overrides on auth endpoints (login/
  register/verify/resend/forgot-password/reset-password) and on the two
  AI-generation endpoints, tighter than the app-wide default limiter.

- Server-side validation: convert ~13 inline @Body() object-literal types
  across auth/engine/media/oauth/posts controllers into real
  class-validator DTO classes, closing a gap where NestJS's global
  ValidationPipe silently validated nothing for non-class body types.

- Session storage: move the auth JWT from localStorage (readable by any
  XSS for up to 30 days) to an httpOnly cookie. AuthController.login sets
  it; a new AuthController.logout clears it. JwtStrategy reads it via a
  hand-rolled cookie parser (no new dependency). The frontend now caches
  only a non-sensitive user snapshot (id/email/name/brandId/expiry) for
  synchronous UI checks; apiFetch, the upload flow, the SSE stream, and
  the three OAuth connect links all rely on the cookie traveling
  automatically instead of a client-readable token.

- File upload content-sniffing: verify uploaded bytes actually match
  their claimed MIME type (magic-byte checks for JPEG/PNG/GIF/WEBP/
  ISOBMFF/EBML) on both the multer path and the direct-to-Blob register
  path, on top of the existing allowlist checks.

- OAuth error handling: stop reflecting err.message into redirect query
  params (info-disclosure risk); log full errors server-side, show
  generic messages to the user. Remove partial-secret and raw-code
  logging in the Instagram token exchange.

feat(web): add the attended web-release plan/apply chain, interlocked against the legacy CD carrier (TIN-3816) (#111)

* fix(web): bind web image admission to the stack under validation (TIN-3816)

scripts/validate-web-stack.sh admitted its image with a flat repository
test that was independent of the stack being validated, so the guard
described "some GFTB web image" rather than "this stack's image". The
admitted repository is now looked up from the Deployment's own target
namespace:

  greatfallstoolbus-org-production -> greatfallstoolbus-org
                                   -> ghcr.io/great-falls-tool-bus/greatfallstoolbus.org

A namespace with no table entry fails closed, the Deployment's name must
match the workload the namespace admits, and every per-container
assertion binds to that name through a jq --arg rather than a literal, so
a stack cannot rename its container out from under the probe and
hardening checks.

The digest test is also tightened from a `@sha256:*` glob to a full
64-lowercase-hex match. Verified rejections against a scratch copy of the
stack (each rc=1):

  ghcr.io/great-falls-tool-bus/gftb-site@sha256:<64 zeros>   other repository
  ghcr.io/great-falls-tool-bus/greatfallstoolbus.org:latest  tag reference
  ghcr.io/elsewhere/greatfallstoolbus.org@sha256:<64 hex>    foreign owner
  ...greatfallstoolbus.org@sha256:<63 hex>                   truncated digest
  ...greatfallstoolbus.org@sha256:<64 UPPER hex>             uppercase digest
  namespace rewritten to gftb-site-production                unknown stack

The gftb-site static-origin candidate is admitted on a different axis and
is never committed to a manifest: it arrives as WEB_APPLY_IMAGE and is
held to its own exact digest shape by _web-release-candidate-inputs.

WEB_RELEASE_VALIDATION_SCRIPT_SHA256 is re-pinned to the new bytes so the
PR #109 receipt keeps covering this script.

Stack: TIN-2543.

* feat(web): add the attended web-release plan/apply chain (TIN-3816)

PR #109 landed the proof-only half of the gftb-site release
(_web-release-candidate-inputs, web-release-candidate-proof,
web-release-render, web-release-pinned-running-proof,
web-release-served-proof) and left the mutating half to a separately
reviewed exact-render/apply/rollback contract. This is that half, in the
same recipe family and on the same input contract.

  web-release-plan            renders ONCE through web-release-render and
                              records the exact bytes, their SHA-256, the
                              selected image + source SHA, and the infra
                              carrier commit under .k8s-plans/ (0700,
                              artifacts 0600, gitignored)
  _web-release-plan-preflight re-renders and refuses unless the render is
                              byte-identical and the inputs and carrier
                              are unchanged
  web-release-server-dry-run  server-side dry-run of the recorded bytes
  web-release-apply           _reviewed-clean-main + GFTB_APPLY_CONFIRM +
                              kubeconfig custody + plan preflight, then
                              dry-run, apply the recorded bytes, prune the
                              two legacy egress policies the render omits
                              (apply does not prune omissions), roll out

There is exactly ONE renderer: web-release-render. Nothing in the chain
resolves an image, runs `kubectl set image`, or patches replicas -- the
render already bakes ${WEB_APPLY_IMAGE} and replicas: 2 into the bytes,
so the live pod template can only be a render of reviewed inputs. The
apply identity is the existing WEB_APPLY_KUBECONFIG (no new credential),
now held to the ARC custody bar: operator-owned, mode 0600, outside every
repository tree, ambient KUBECONFIG refused.

Guard contract (was: dependencies only; the reviewer showed nine body
mutations all produced zero findings):

- every recipe joins WEB_RELEASE_RECIPE_DEPENDENCIES *and*

  attributes, alias collisions, and the operator-local closure come with

- WEB_RELEASE_STACK_GLOBAL_ASSIGNMENTS pins web_stack_dir/web_stack_ns,
  so redirecting the rendered/applied stack is a finding
- IMPERATIVE_PIN now scans the WHOLE Justfile (every recipe body plus
  every executable line outside a recipe) instead of three named
  recipes, with exactly one allowlisted legacy carrier

custody without the mode check, a second renderer in the plan), two

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: posture-staleness-alert
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: posture-staleness-alert
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: posture-staleness-alert
    namespace: observability

# What the posture-staleness-alert CronJob may read.
#
# Read-only, and ONLY the stored configuration-scan objects. The check has to see
# scans in every scanned namespace to find the newest one, so it is cluster-scoped
# by necessity — but it is list-only on a single resource type, which is the least
# privilege that satisfies that.
#
# It deliberately does NOT grant the summary kinds. Those carry a zero-valued
# creationTimestamp, so they cannot answer a freshness question and reading them
# would widen the grant for no signal.
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: posture-staleness-alert
rules:
  - apiGroups:
      - spdx.softwarecomposition.kubescape.io
    resources:
      - workloadconfigurationscans
    verbs:
      - list

# Alerts when Kubescape's stored configuration-scan data stops moving.
#
# WHY THIS EXISTS
#
# A broken posture scanner and a compliant cluster read IDENTICALLY. When the
# scan aborts it persists nothing, so every consumer sees "no new findings" —

def make_not_authenticated_error(self) -> HTTPException:
        """
        The WWW-Authenticate header is not standardized for API Key authentication but
        the HTTP specification requires that an error of 401 "Unauthorized" must
        include a WWW-Authenticate header.

        Ref: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-401-unauthorized

        For this, this method sends a custom challenge `APIKey`.

            detail="Not authenticated",

feat(sales): ticket priority — pick on create, change after filing

Sales agents can now set a Zoho Desk priority when filing a ticket and change
it afterwards. Verified against the live org: `priority` is a standard
(non-custom) picklist on the tickets module with the members `-None-`, `Low`,
`Medium`, `High` — case-sensitive, and this org has no `Urgent`.

Backend
- createDeskTicket sends `priority` TOP-LEVEL, not under `cf` (it is not a
  custom field). Omitted when the agent leaves it at None.
- New `PATCH /v1/desk/tickets/:id/priority` → Desk `PATCH /tickets/{id}`.
  Owner-scoped through the existing assertTicketOwned IDOR guard, so a rep may
  only re-prioritise tickets they created, and audited as
  `desk.ticket.priority.update`.
- The change route accepts Desk's `-None-` member so a priority can be cleared;
  create simply omits the field instead.

Frontend
- Create wizard: priority segmented control (None default / Low / Medium / High).
- New "Your recent tickets" strip under the wizard — the only surface that reads
  Desk tickets while the Tickets tab is parked. Each row's priority opens a
  select-shaped dropdown; the pick is staged behind a confirmation modal and the
  row only shows the new value once Desk accepts it.

Timeout fix
- The Desk token has no `Desk.search.READ` scope, so the ticket list falls back
  to scanning recent org tickets. The full 100-page sweep measured 27.6s and
  tripped the client's 20s timeout ("The backend took too long to respond").
  Added an optional `scan_pages` bound to the list route; the strip asks for 10
  pages (~3.8s worst case, ~1s once a match is found). Granting the search scope
  removes the scan entirely and is the real fix.

def has_perm(self, perm, obj=None):
        """
        Return True if the authUser has the specified permission. Query all
        available auth backends, but return immediately if any backend returns
        True. Thus, a authUser who has permission from a single auth backend is
        assumed to have permission in general. If an object is provided, check
        permissions for that object.
        """
        # Active superusers have all permissions.
        if self.is_active and self.is_superuser:
            return True

        # Otherwise we need to check the backends.
        return _user_has_perm(self, perm, obj)

    async def ahas_perm(self, perm, obj=None):
        """See has_perm()"""
        # Active superusers have all permissions.

        # Otherwise we need to check the backends.

explanation:
Fix security findings from the August 2026 penetration tests

Cross-compared two Strix reports (timetify.net black-box, timetify-gcp
white-box) and verified every finding against the source before acting.

Confirmed and fixed:
- No rate limiting on auth endpoints (CRITICAL). Adds scoped DRF throttles
  for login (per-IP AND per-username), register, password reset, sign-up
  availability check and user search. Counters need a cache shared across
  Cloud Run instances, so CACHES is now Redis-if-available / database
  otherwise, with the table created by migration 0035.
- Public GCS bucket with unsigned URLs (HIGH). Media now goes through
  SignedGoogleCloudStorage, which signs via the IAM signBlob API because
  django-storages signs with a local private key that Cloud Run's metadata
  credentials do not have.
- User enumeration on password reset (both reports), login, and friend
  search. Constant response, generic auth error, 3-char search floor.
- Cross-tenant IDOR via writable `course` FK on Week/Exam/Assignment.
- Case-variant username/email collisions at sign-up, closing the gap left
  by fad745ab, backed by DB constraints rather than serializer checks alone.
- Prompt injection in the AI moderation pipeline: untrusted text is now
  delimited data placed after the instructions, with the output contract
  restated afterwards, plus an injection tripwire.
- Past-dated events, admin on a fixed path, missing CSP/HSTS/frame headers.

Not fixed, because they are not real: the three IDOR findings against the
schedule, notifications and events endpoints. All three views derive the
user from request.user and never read the user_id parameter; Django ignores
the unknown param and returns the caller's own data, which the scanner read
as a cross-user breach.

Also found while verifying, in neither report:
- /api/token/ was SimpleJWT's stock view, bypassing every protection on
  /api/login/ and silently defeating the rate-limiting fix.
- Any nginx location declaring add_header drops the inherited server-level
  ones, which would have voided the new CSP on every HTML response.
- CourseSerializer.parent_course had the same unvalidated-FK hole.
- Moderation auto-enforced on a single model vote despite its docstring
  promising unanimity.
- Password reset matched email case-sensitively.

Dependencies: npm 4 high -> 0; Django 6.0.2 (26 advisories) -> 6.0.7, plus
gunicorn, python-dotenv and pg8000. pip-audit and check --deploy both clean.

Adds 23 regression tests; full suite 162 passing.

## Phase 4 — Verify against the database (jdbc-platform tools)

Always follow this sequence — never skip a step:
`load_driver → connect → [tests] → get_test_report → disconnect`

1. **`load_driver`** if the driver isn't registered. Use CData short names (`saperp`,
   `salesforce`, `servicenow`, `googledrive`, …) — the server resolves the class automatically;
   otherwise pass `driver_class`. Verify `"status": "loaded"` and a non-null `driver_class`.
   If it fails, stop — there is nothing to test.

2. **`connect`** — **default to `read_only: true`** unless a test case explicitly requires a write
   path. Read-only is enforced in the JDBC proxy layer, so it covers **every** tool including
   `execute_java`: only `SELECT`/`WITH`/`EXPLAIN`/`DESCRIBE`/`SHOW` are permitted, and anything else
   is refused with SQLState `25006`. **`EXEC` and `CALL` are treated as writes** — a procedure body is
   opaque, and CData procs like `DownloadObjects` have side effects. So a read-only session cannot run
   stored procedures: if the ticket needs one, connect with `read_only: false` and say so in chat.
   It is a guard against an accidental write, not a sandbox — snippet code can still reach the
   underlying connection via `getMetaData().getConnection()` or `unwrap()`.
   Only set `trust_all_certs` / `set_jvm_proxy` when the engineer asks.
   Reuse the returned `session_id` for every later call.

   **Proxy:** Just call `connect` normally with the user's connection string **exactly as given —

## Phase 5 — Report

- `get_test_report` — Markdown summary (pass/fail per criterion + session stats).
- `export_results` — write evidence rows to CSV when an attachment is wanted.
- Summarize the verdict: which acceptance criteria passed/failed, the concrete data behind each,
  and whether the fix from Phase 2 actually does what the ticket asked. If Phase 2 was skipped

| `compare_queries` | Diff two result sets (order-insensitive) | `session_id`, `sql_actual`, `sql_expected`, `criterion` |
| `record_check` | Record a non-SQL pass/fail check | `session_id`, `criterion`, `passed`, `detail`, `sql` |
| `export_results` | Export a SELECT to CSV (UTF-8, RFC4180) | `session_id`, `sql`, `file_path`, `max_rows` |
| `get_test_report` | Markdown pass/fail report | `session_id` |
| `list_sessions` | List open sessions | _(none)_ |
| `disconnect` | Close the connection, delete the session's driver log | `session_id`, `keep_logfile` (default false). Response: `logfile_deleted`, `logfile_bytes_freed` |

**Session activity totals** (queries run, rows returned, intercepted calls, JDBC duration, estimated
tokens) are in the "Session activity" section of `get_test_report` — there is no separate stats tool.

GHSA-g7p5-89mh-248h: enforce AuthorityPermission on subca parent

Sub-CA creation (POST /api/1/authorities with type=subca) never checked
that the caller holds AuthorityPermission on the supplied parent
authority. When ADMIN_ONLY_AUTHORITY_CREATION=False, any authenticated
non-read-only user could mint a sub-CA chained off of any internal root
Lemur holds the private key for, then issue trusted leaf certs under it.

Now AuthoritiesList.post enforces AuthorityPermission(parent.id, parent
roles) before delegating to the issuer plugin, matching the same check
already used when updating an existing authority.

fix(api): close the agent-token gaps found by the codex gate

Critical: the MCP-only rule was scoped to the /api/v1 prefix, so POST /logout —
the one root-level auth:sanctum route — still accepted agent bearers, giving an
agent a human-only action and a token-validity oracle. The refusal now sits on
both route groups; accepting a token is a positive capability exactly one
surface will opt into (#135). The IDOR sweep enumerates every registered route
instead of a prefix, and proves its two exemptions authenticate nothing.

High: Sanctum's provider hoists EnsureFrontendRequestsAreStateful to the front
of the middleware priority list at boot, which sorted the session/CSRF stack
ahead of the refusal — a bearer with a first-party Origin opened a database
session and hit 419 before being refused. AppServiceProvider now hoists the
refusal after Sanctum's provider; asserted on pipeline order and as zero
queries on a rejected request. Mint and its audit record are one transaction;
revoke records through recordSafely and only the request that removed the row
records an event; the Policy trait fails closed on any persistent token that is
not an AgentToken.

Also: no-store on the mint response, a dismiss action for the revealed value,
error-vs-empty on the settings list, deny-as-not-found for a foreign token id,
and a per-member token cap that bounds the unpaginated list.

Dismissals and deferrals recorded in TODOS.md.

ceph-volume: honour osd_dmcrypt_key_size option

ceph-volume doesn't honour osd_dmcrypt_key_size.
It means the default size is always applied.

It also changes the default value in `get_key_size_from_conf()`

From cryptsetup manpage:

> For XTS mode you can optionally set a key size of 512 bits with the -s option.

Using more than 512bits will end up with the following error message:

```
Key size in XTS mode must be 256 or 512 bits.
```

  delete removes the stored bytes; share unlock clears needsPass; modal
  focus trap no longer re-arms per keystroke; pie labels get headroom.

Authentication Bypass For Endpoints With Anonymous Access

Using a remember-me cookie with an arbitrary username can cause Opencast
to assume proper authentication for that user even if the remember-me
cookie was incorrect given that the attacked endpoint also allows
anonymous access.

This way, an attacker can, for example, fake a remember-me token, assume
the identity of the global system administrator and request non-public
content from the search service without ever providing any proper
authentication.

The reason for this problem is that using a remember-me cookie will
always cause the user in the request context to be populated, even if
the cookie is invalid by now. This is usually no problem, except in
combination with anonymous access where anonymous authentication is
granted and the request may continue.

In such a case, Opencast's security service would just check that a user
existed in the request context and assume proper authentication of this
user, never checking if it's actually anonymous authentication.

This patch adds this additional check, falling back to the anonymous
user in case of anonymous authentication.

The admission contract for epic [#801](https://github.com/nathanjohnpayne/gaycruisebingo/issues/801), consumed by every other child in it. It defines what a membership record is, where it lives, who may write it, the single predicate the two rules files transcribe, and the per-Event switch that lets enforcement land dark. It changes no rule and ships no UI: `firestore.rules`, `storage.rules` and `functions/**` are deliberately untouched, so that #803–#809 start from a settled shape instead of five divergent ones.

**Status is `proposed`, not `accepted`, and that is a deliberate signal.** The parts the code forces are settled and safe to build against — the invariant, the path, the single-`get()` constraint, the document shape, the predicate, the budget, and the enforcement switch. Two of the epic's open decisions are genuinely product (§ Decisions, D2/D8) and are recorded here as options rather than answers; D5 and D-A were ruled on by the owner 2026-08-18 and are now answers. Downstream tickets may implement everything under § Contract today; under § Decisions, the three the owner has ruled on (D5, D9, D-A) are commitments and the rest are not.

## The invariant

**A gate the reader can satisfy by writing its own admission record is not a gate.**

Every candidate record in the tree today is exactly that. `events/{eventId}/players/{uid}` is `allow create, update: if (isOwner(uid) || isAdmin(eventId)) && reshuffleCounterMonotonic()` (`firestore.rules:1007-1008`) with no membership precondition, so any signed-in account mints its own Player row under any Event id it knows and then satisfies any predicate keyed off that row. The same self-create shape exists at `items` (`:958-968`), `reshuffles` (`:1044-1053`), `proofs` (`:1202-1283`), `claims` (`:1305`), `markers` (`:1332-1337`), `doubts` (`:1351-1396`), `hearts` (`:1419-1456`) and `moments` (`:1466-1532`).

This is not a theoretical objection. [#844](https://github.com/nathanjohnpayne/gaycruisebingo/issues/844), filed from PR #838's review, reached it independently and from the other direction: `resolveAbuseEscalation` (`functions/src/bugReports.ts`) gates an admin alert on the reporter holding a Player document, and Codex correctly observed that the check is a fact the client asserts rather than one the platform knows. That issue's own conclusion — *"Some Event-scoped notion of legitimate participation that a client cannot mint"* — is what this spec specifies, and its first listed candidate ("a server-written membership fact — join goes through a callable that records something clients cannot write") is the shape adopted below.

The in-tree precedent for a record whose value depends on clients being unable to author it is `hostnames/{host}`: `allow get: if true; allow list: if false; allow create, update, delete: if false` (`firestore.rules:624-628`) — written only by the Admin SDK. Membership follows it exactly.

## Glossary

**Membership** — the organizer-issued record that a User is admitted to one Event. One document per (Event, User), non-self-writable, carrying the grant's provenance and its revocation. It is a *record*, not a

  through the server instead.

  instead of hardcoded zeros, rand(), and a disconnected admin_users
  table that was never actually used by auth.

Base app: PostgreSQL, a machine API, and read-only SQL access

So a built app can be used BY other applications, and queried directly
where SQL is the right tool.

PostgreSQL replaces the JSON file. lib/db.js owns the pool and schema;
lib/store.js loads the dataset once at boot and writes through. get()
stays SYNCHRONOUS on purpose — that is what let every lib/ module stay
byte-identical instead of this becoming a whole-application rewrite with
the acceptance suite as the only safety net. The price is that the data
must be loaded before the first request, so server.js has an async boot()
and listens only once it resolves. save('files') names the slice that
changed; save() with no argument still rewrites everything.

The failure mode is worth knowing. A failed write is logged and the
process keeps serving from memory, so a schema mistake is invisible to
the API. Not hypothetical: password_resets.expires_at was typed bigint
while lib/reset.js stores an ISO string, and all 32 acceptance tests
passed while nothing persisted. The suite now reads the database directly
rather than trusting the API's answers, and audit appends one row at a
time — the in-memory list is a trimmed 5000-entry window, so rewriting
that section from memory would have deleted history.

API keys are layered onto the SAME requireAuth/requirePerm the UI already
goes through, not a parallel /v1 surface. Every existing endpoint became
machine-callable with exactly the permission check it already had, and a
route cannot end up open to machines but closed to people because there
is only one check. Keys carry a subset of the same RBAC permissions
people hold, so there is no second scope vocabulary to drift. A key can
never be granted a permission its issuer lacks; its permissions are
re-intersected with its owner's current rights on every request, so
deactivating a person stops their integrations; the token is shown once
and only a hash is stored; and a key can neither change a password nor
mint another key, so it cannot take over its account or make revocation
unwinnable. /api/meta publishes the capability index without auth,
because a consumer needs it before they have a key.

Read-only SQL hands consumers a SELECT-only role on curated views in an
api_read schema — never the base tables. That is the whole safety story:
users.data holds passwordHash, sessions holds refresh_hash, api_keys
holds token_hash, app_documents holds the encrypted LDAP and SMTP
passwords, so a blanket GRANT would hand every reporting consumer the
password hashes. REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public is explicit and default
privileges are never widened to base tables, so adding a table later does
not silently expose it. Issuing rotates, which is the revocation story.
The app needs CREATEROLE (never superuser); where a deployment will not
grant it, the API answers 409 with the exact statement to run and
scripts/provision-readonly.sql is the DBA path.

Verified against a real PostgreSQL 16 with password auth (trust auth
would have made the rotation test meaningless): the read-only credential
can query the views, cannot read public.*, cannot UPDATE/INSERT/CREATE/
DROP, exposes no password hash — asserted on VALUES, not just column
names, since a future column could carry one under an innocent name — and
a rotated-away password is refused. Admin → Integration verified in both
themes at 375px and 1280px with no horizontal scroll.

Base app suite 32 -> 41; template contract tests 19 -> 26; ProxyPilot
1157 pass with the 6 documented pre-existing sandbox failures.

GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67: prevent arbitrary certificate revocation via duplicate DB rows

Certificate identity was tracked only by Lemur's internal database row, not
by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could upload a
duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing
authority_id and serial) and then revoke it, causing the CA to revoke the
real certificate belonging to another user.

- POST /api/1/certificates/upload now requires AuthorityPermission on the
  specified authority, and rejects uploads whose (authority_id, serial)
  pair already matches an existing certificate (409).
- PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke now checks authorization and endpoint
  attachment against every certificate row sharing (authority_id, serial)
  with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request.

### MockEthSigner utility

The `MockEthSigner` class in [utils.py](../tests/utils.py) is used to perform transactions on a given Account with a secp256k1 curve key pair, crafting the transaction and managing nonces. It differs from the `MockSigner` implementation by:

* not using the public key but its derived address instead (the last 20 bytes of the keccak256 hash of the public key and adding `0x` to the beginning)
* signing the message with a secp256k1 curve address

## Account entrypoint

`__execute__` acts as a single entrypoint for all authUser interaction with any contract, including managing the account contract itself. That's why if you want to change the public key controlling the Account, you would send a transaction targeting the very Account contract:

```python

### `__execute__`

This is the only external entrypoint to interact with the Account contract. It:

1. Validates the transaction signature matches the message (including the nonce)
2. Increments the nonce
3. Calls the target contract with the intended function selector and calldata parameters
4. Forwards the contract call response data as return value

Parameters:

```cairo
call_array_len: felt

```cairo
response_len: felt
response: felt*
```

### `is_valid_eth_signature`

Returns `TRUE` if a given signature in the secp256k1 curve is valid, otherwise it reverts. In the future it will return `FALSE` if a given signature is invalid (for more info please check [this issue](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/cairo-contracts/issues/327)).

Parameters:

```cairo
signature_len: felt
signature: felt*
```

Returns:

```cairo
is_valid: felt
```

> returns `TRUE` if a given signature is valid. Otherwise, reverts. In the future it will return `FALSE` if a given signature is invalid (for more info please check [this issue](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/cairo-contracts/issues/327)).

### `eth_execute`

This follows the same idea as the vanilla version of `execute` with the sole difference that signature verification is on the secp256k1 curve.

Parameters:

```cairo
call_array_len: felt
call_array: AccountCallArray*
calldata_len: felt
calldata: felt*
nonce: felt
```

> Note that the current signature scheme expects a 7-element array like `[sig_v, uint256_sig_r_low, uint256_sig_r_high, uint256_sig_s_low, uint256_sig_s_high, uint256_hash_low, uint256_hash_high]` given that the parameters of the verification are bigger than a felt.

Returns:

```cairo
response_len: felt
response: felt*
```

### `_unsafe_execute`

It's an internal method that performs the following tasks:

1. Increments the nonce.
2. Takes the input and builds a `Call` for each iterated message. See [Multicall transactions](#multicall-transactions) for more information.
3. Calls the target contract with the intended function selector and calldata parameters
4. Forwards the contract call response data as return value

This layer sits *outside* the core router and turns every failure into an improvement opportunity.

### What it does

```
Every message flows through the pipeline → produces a trace
↓
Case Review watches for failures:
  • FAQ abstentions (customer asked something KB doesn't cover)
  • Low-confidence escalations (router unsure, escalated to human)
  • Churn risk flags (angry customer, fast-tracked to human)
  • Guardrail blocks (PII, injection, fraud attempts)
  • Fallback usage (system had to degrade gracefully)
↓
Analytics Dashboard shows 24-hour metrics:
  • Messages tested vs. cases reviewed (the gap = potential)
  • Knowledge-base gaps by frequency (what customers ask, bot can't answer)
  • Escalation breakdown (why customers went to humans)
↓
KB Suggestion Engine:
  • Detects FAQ abstentions
  • Auto-generates doc skeletons
  • Human writes the answer → system re-indexes
  • Next customer with same question gets instant answer
↓
Replay & Metrics:
  • Run 10-ticket test before/after improvement
  • Measure: cost, latency, escalation rate, resolution rate
  • Prove ROI of adding a KB doc or tuning a threshold
↓
Governance & Red-Team:
  • Run 6 security tests: IDOR, injection, PII, spoofing, social eng, churn
  • Validate ownership checks, guardrail blocks, policy limits
```

### How this helps CX (practical view)

**For customers:**
- **Faster answers** — KB gets better coverage. Today customer waits 5 min for human; tomorrow same question gets instant answer.
- **No repeated problems** — When one customer triggers a gap, the system flags it. Next customer with the same issue gets the answer.
- **Protected privacy** — PII detection blocks credit cards from logs. Security tests prevent IDOR attacks.
- **Immediate help when needed** — Churn risk detection sends angry customers straight to a human instead of bot runaround.

**For the company:**
- **Visibility into failures** — See which questions the bot can't answer; which escalations are happening.
- **Measurable improvement** — Replay tests prove that adding a KB doc actually reduces escalations + cost.
- **Safe iteration** — Red-team tests catch regressions (IDOR blocks still working? PII still redacted?).
- **Compliance** — Full audit trail, ownership checks, policy limits in code.

### The dashboard (QA Suite)

Run `uvicorn server:app --port 8000` and explore:

- **🧪 Live Testing** — Chat interface with real-time decision trace (intent, confidence, sentiment, cost)
- **📊 Analytics** — Modal dashboard showing 24h metrics, KB gaps, escalations, pending KB suggestions, replay results
- **🔒 Governance** — Modal showing current policy config and red-team test results
- **Vertical switcher** — Test same router across E-Commerce, Banking, Telecom with different KBs and thresholds

Connect Supabase as the live database and fix critical security/data bugs

Repoints Eloquent from local MySQL to Supabase Postgres (the actual
production database), then fixes the real bugs that surfaced once the
app was actually exercised end-to-end against it:

- Locks down anon-role database access: every table had unrestricted
  read/write/delete via the exposed Supabase anon key, including the
  users table (password hashes). Revoked access to internal tables and
  restricted app tables to the exact operations the frontend uses.
- Fixes users.id having no default/sequence at all, which made every
  registration fail with a not-null violation.
- Removes a dead `section` text column on users that shadowed the
  section() relationship, silently breaking teacher approval of
  students (always evaluated to null, so ownership checks always
  failed).
- Fixes real IDOR: a teacher could approve/reject/reset any student
  platform-wide, not just their own section's.
- Stops leaking the AI API key to the browser; proxies quiz generation
  through the server instead.
- Rebuilds teacher/admin/student analytics from real Supabase data
  instead of hardcoded zeros, rand(), and a disconnected admin_users
  table that was never actually used by auth.
- Fixes silent quiz-publish duplication (missing unique constraint
  meant "replace" actually inserted a duplicate row).
- Adds unclosed-<script> and broken-relationship fixes found via live
  browser testing, plus 30+ new feature tests covering the above.

récupéraient un environnement par :envId sans jamais vérifier qu'il
appartenait au projet de l'URL (:id) :

  en devinant/énumérant son id, malgré loadProjectAccess() qui n'autorise

  cette session).

  guardProductionEnvironment — un maintainer (pas seulement owner) pouvait
  reconfigurer l'app Argo CD d'un environnement de PRODUCTION, alors que
  sync/rollback/promote l'exigent déjà tous.

environment.project_id === req.pgProject.id (404 sinon, jamais confirmer

guardProductionEnvironment.

Close historical generator isolation gaps

Review follow-up on PR #27. Three corrections, no redesign.

1. Live-registry coupling removed from historical tests. The current-tree
   historical test called build_dependency_inventory() on the live root
   and asserted 39 entries, which coupled historical verification to
   current registry contents and would break when P3 expands the registry
   to 59 without being able to touch P2 files. The live-root
   recomputation is removed. The 39-entry assertion is not dropped: it
   moves to HistoricalReconstructionTests, which materialises source
   commit 3219fa03 into a clean temporary root, runs isolated candidate
   mode to temporary paths outside both roots, asserts 92903 bytes,
   SHA-256, Git blob, 30 nodes, 161 edges and 39 inventory entries,
   confirms byte identity with the tracked artifact, and cleans up.
   HistoricalLiveRegistryIsolationTests proves the dependency is gone: a
   patched run that raises on build_dependency_inventory,
   collect_read_purposes, assemble_map_data and load_json still exits 0,
   and the CLI verifies successfully from an isolated generator root that
   contains no registry at all, and from one carrying a divergent
   59-record registry.

2. Unreadable artifact fails closed. run_historical() called
   path.read_bytes() directly, so a file that exists but cannot be read
   raised instead of emitting the stable token. The read is now wrapped
   in a narrow OSError handler that fails with
   HISTORICAL_ARTIFACT_IDENTITY_MISMATCH and reports the read failure.
   PermissionError and OSError cases are injected by mocking against an
   isolated artifact path; no permission on the tracked file is altered.
   The invalid-JSON case is retained as a separate structural case.

3. Hard-link aliases rejected. Path.resolve() cannot detect a distinct
   pathname that shares an inode with the artifact, and writing through
   one would mutate it. resolve_expanded_output() now adds same-file
   identity checking (device and inode) for an existing output path, and
   fails closed when identity cannot be established. Both checks run
   before the live registry is read, before the record-count check,
   before any directory creation and before any open. A real os.link
   test confirms rejection, unchanged artifact and link bytes, unchanged
   mtime, and that the 59-record error is never reached. All four
   existing collision tests are retained unweakened.

queries on a rejected request. Mint and its audit record are one transaction;
revoke records through recordSafely and only the request that removed the row
records an event; the Policy trait fails closed on any persistent token that is
not an AgentToken.

Implements the fixes from this session's full security audit (Sections
5-8 plus remaining Section 3/4 items) that weren't already applied live:

- CORS: replace origin:'*' with an explicit allowlist (APP_URL/
  FRONTEND_URL/localhost) in the production Nest bootstrap
  (apps/web/src/lib/backendPort.ts). The previous config also paired
  wildcard origin with credentials:true, an invalid combination per the
  Fetch spec.

- Rate limiting: add @Throttle overrides on auth endpoints (login/
  register/verify/resend/forgot-password/reset-password) and on the two
  AI-generation endpoints, tighter than the app-wide default limiter.

- Server-side validation: convert ~13 inline @Body() object-literal types
  across auth/engine/media/oauth/posts controllers into real
  class-validator DTO classes, closing a gap where NestJS's global
  ValidationPipe silently validated nothing for non-class body types.

- Session storage: move the auth JWT from localStorage (readable by any
  XSS for up to 30 days) to an httpOnly cookie. AuthController.login sets
  it; a new AuthController.logout clears it. JwtStrategy reads it via a
  hand-rolled cookie parser (no new dependency). The frontend now caches
  only a non-sensitive user snapshot (id/email/name/brandId/expiry) for
  synchronous UI checks; apiFetch, the upload flow, the SSE stream, and
  the three OAuth connect links all rely on the cookie traveling
  automatically instead of a client-readable token.

- File upload content-sniffing: verify uploaded bytes actually match
  their claimed MIME type (magic-byte checks for JPEG/PNG/GIF/WEBP/
  ISOBMFF/EBML) on both the multer path and the direct-to-Blob register
  path, on top of the existing allowlist checks.

- OAuth error handling: stop reflecting err.message into redirect query
  params (info-disclosure risk); log full errors server-side, show
  generic messages to the user. Remove partial-secret and raw-code
  logging in the Instagram token exchange.

media folder parentId), MediaAsset atomic processing claim, TikTok

Security audit hardening: CORS, rate limiting, DTO validation, httpOnly session cookie, upload content-sniffing

Implements the fixes from this session's full security audit (Sections
5-8 plus remaining Section 3/4 items) that weren't already applied live:

- CORS: replace origin:'*' with an explicit allowlist (APP_URL/
  FRONTEND_URL/localhost) in the production Nest bootstrap
  (apps/web/src/lib/backendPort.ts). The previous config also paired
  wildcard origin with credentials:true, an invalid combination per the
  Fetch spec.

- Rate limiting: add @Throttle overrides on auth endpoints (login/
  register/verify/resend/forgot-password/reset-password) and on the two
  AI-generation endpoints, tighter than the app-wide default limiter.

- Server-side validation: convert ~13 inline @Body() object-literal types
  across auth/engine/media/oauth/posts controllers into real
  class-validator DTO classes, closing a gap where NestJS's global
  ValidationPipe silently validated nothing for non-class body types.

- Session storage: move the auth JWT from localStorage (readable by any
  XSS for up to 30 days) to an httpOnly cookie. AuthController.login sets
  it; a new AuthController.logout clears it. JwtStrategy reads it via a
  hand-rolled cookie parser (no new dependency). The frontend now caches
  only a non-sensitive user snapshot (id/email/name/brandId/expiry) for
  synchronous UI checks; apiFetch, the upload flow, the SSE stream, and
  the three OAuth connect links all rely on the cookie traveling
  automatically instead of a client-readable token.

- File upload content-sniffing: verify uploaded bytes actually match
  their claimed MIME type (magic-byte checks for JPEG/PNG/GIF/WEBP/
  ISOBMFF/EBML) on both the multer path and the direct-to-Blob register
  path, on top of the existing allowlist checks.

- OAuth error handling: stop reflecting err.message into redirect query
  params (info-disclosure risk); log full errors server-side, show
  generic messages to the user. Remove partial-secret and raw-code
  logging in the Instagram token exchange.

Also includes earlier uncommitted work from this session: the OAuth
state-signature CSRF bypass fix, IDOR fixes (createPost media ownership,
media folder parentId), MediaAsset atomic processing claim, TikTok
webhook signature verification, AI entitlement bypass fix, comment-
webhook dedup constraint, and unrelated UI/landing/billing changes.

explanation:
Fix real vulnerabilities found in a dedicated security audit

Three parallel audits (auth/authz, injection/input-handling, secrets/
infrastructure) covering the whole app, adversarial lens. Fixes:

CRITICAL
- MFA was completely bypassable: the 5-minute "mfa_pending" challenge
  token issued by /auth/login (before a TOTP/backup code is ever
  checked) decoded and passed get_current_user()'s checks exactly like
  a real session token -- anyone with just a password (the one thing
  MFA exists to add a second factor against) could call any
  authenticated endpoint directly with it, no code required, for the
  full 5-minute window. Now explicitly rejected, same pattern as the
  existing "purpose" claim check.

HIGH
- Twilio webhook signature verification failed OPEN (skipped, request
  allowed through) when TWILIO_TOKEN/PUBLIC_BASE_URL were unset --
  now fails closed (503), matching the pattern already used correctly
  for CRON_SECRET/EMAIL_WORKER_SECRET.
- SECRET_KEY/JWT_SECRET ship with hardcoded, publicly-known placeholder
  defaults with no code-level guard against running with them in
  production (only Render's generateValue: true prevented this on the
  documented deploy path). App now refuses to boot with DEBUG=false if
  either is still its literal default.

MODERATE
- Three IDOR gaps: POST /communications/send's maintenance_update
  template, POST /maintenance/'s unit_id/tenant_id, and POST
  /accounting/expenses' vendor_id all accepted a foreign org's UUID
  with no ownership check, leaking that resource's name/title/status
  back in the response. All now validated against the caller's org.
- Unescaped HTML injection in three outreach-email templates
  (services/lead_service.py) -- lead fields (scraped from public,
  attacker-editable Google Business Profile data, or typed into
  POST /leads with no sanitization) were interpolated into HTML emails
  with no output encoding. Now html.escape()'d for the HTML body
  specifically (plain-text body unaffected).
- SSRF in the lead-scraper's email-discovery fetch
  (workers/tasks/lead_scraping.py) -- a Places listing's self-reported
  website URL was fetched with no scheme/private-IP allowlist and
  followed redirects blindly, so a listing pointed at an internal
  address or a cloud metadata endpoint would have the server fetch it.
  Added an SSRF guard checked on the initial URL and re-checked on
  every redirect hop.
- FastAPI backend sent no security headers at all (X-Frame-Options,
  X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) --
  only the Next.js frontend did, despite security.tsx's copy claiming
  this applies to "every response." Left /docs and /redoc unprotected
  against framing. Added a headers middleware.
- ALLOWED_ORIGINS="*" combined with allow_credentials=True (a plausible
  operator typo in Render's env vars) would silently make CORS reflect
  any origin with credentials -- app now refuses to boot with that
  combination instead.
- Three endpoints doing real, billed AI/scraping work (inspection photo
  AI analysis, the Claude marketing-copy generator, the lead-scrape
  trigger) had zero rate limiting or cost cap beyond role/plan gating --
  a compromised privileged account or a buggy retry loop had no
  built-in ceiling on Anthropic/OpenAI/Google Places billing, and on
  this single-worker server a burst could also stall every other
  tenant's requests. Added reasonable per-minute limits to all three.

Not fixed here, flagged for a follow-up decision (both require either
a schema migration or a product/UX tradeoff, not a mechanical fix):
- Password reset tokens (staff-side /auth/reset-password) are replayable
  within their 30-minute window -- not marked single-use like the
  tenant-portal equivalent already is.
- Rate limiting on login/reset/2FA is per-IP only, no per-account
  lockout/backoff -- a distributed credential-stuffing attempt across
  many source IPs isn't meaningfully throttled today.
- API keys are stored and compared in plaintext (high-entropy,
  infeasible to brute-force, but a DB-level compromise would expose
  live keys directly rather than hashes) -- hashing at rest would need
  a rotation flow since existing keys can't be un-hashed.

|---------|-------|-----|
| `voice-buddy hotkey-doctor` says `[FAIL] pyobjc importable` | pyobjc not installed in the right interpreter | Run Step 1 against the exact path the doctor reports |
| `[FAIL] Accessibility granted` after granting it | Granted the wrong interpreter, or the path is a symlink | Re-run doctor; grant the path it reports; if symlink, grant the real binary |
| F2 still doesn't work after all OK rows | Listener was spawned before pyobjc was installed | `voice-buddy hotkey-restart`, then start a new session |
| F2 stopped working and the doctor shows a listener that isn't running | The listener was killed uncleanly and its PID was recycled onto another process | `voice-buddy hotkey-restart` clears the stale record; a new session respawns it |
| F2 doesn't work after upgrading Python / recreating venv | Accessibility grant is bound to the executable path; the new python is a different file | Doctor will show `[WARN] python interpreter` with `DRIFT`; re-grant Accessibility to the new path |
| Want to verify in a CI pipeline | — | `voice-buddy hotkey-doctor --non-interactive --json` |

voice-buddy stop

# 重启快捷键监听器（按 PID 停止；下个 session 会自动重新拉起）

NovelTea is a self-hosted, offline-first long-form writing app, Scrivener-shaped: a binder tree, document snapshots, labels/statuses, custom metadata, saved/smart collections, and compile presets. Clients are web, Tauri (Windows/macOS), and iOS. Every client keeps a full local replica and works fully disconnected.

Copyright Anthony Carlascio. This repo is the **open core** under Elastic License 2.0; commercial features live in a separate private repo (see Editions).

- **`WireEnumTest`** drives off the enum constants themselves, so a new value is covered the moment it is added: round-tripping, unique lowercase wire forms, case and whitespace tolerance, and empty (never an exception) for null, blank, unknown and injection-shaped input.
- **`EnumSchemaAlignmentTest`** reads the allowed values out of `pg_constraint` and compares them to the enum, then writes every value to the real table. The enum and the CHECK constraint are two declarations of one fact in different languages; nothing but this keeps them honest. Add a value to one and not the other and it fails, naming the constraint.

## Compile

`packages/compile` turns ProseMirror documents into the formats Core ships (`txt`, `md`, `html`). `ExportProvider` on the Java side reports the same boundary; a commercial module contributes the remaining formats by supplying another implementation, and Core must keep working with only its own provider present.

### binder_item

The tree structure — folders, documents, trash. This is the Scrivener "binder."

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

| type | enum | `folder` \| `document` \| `trash` |
| title | text | |
| order_index | float | fractional indexing — lets you reorder/insert without rewriting siblings *(superseded — see A4)* |
| icon | text, nullable | optional custom icon (Scrivener-style) |
| deleted_at | timestamptz, nullable | soft delete — needed for sync tombstones |
| version | bigint | monotonic, incremented on every change |
| updated_by_device_id | uuid | for conflict attribution |

| id | uuid | same as binder_item.id, or separate FK — recommend same id for simplicity |
| content | jsonb | ProseMirror doc JSON |
| word_count | int | derived, cached for fast binder display |
| synopsis | text, nullable | the Scrivener index-card text |
| notes | text, nullable | document notes (rich text or plain) |
| version | bigint | incremented per content save |
| updated_at | timestamptz | |

### snapshot

Manual or auto point-in-time captures of a document's content (Scrivener's snapshot feature).

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

### label / status

Scrivener-style metadata taxonomies, per project.

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

### custom_metadata_field + custom_metadata_value

For arbitrary requestUser-defined metadata (Scrivener's custom meta-data pane). Field defs at the project level, values keyed per binder_item.

### collection

- Each entity carries a version integer, bumped on every write.
- Client pushes a batch: {entity, base_version, new_data} for each locally-changed record since last sync.
- Server accepts if base_version matches current server version (no one else changed it since the client last knew about it). Otherwise it's a conflict.
- On conflict for document content: don't try to merge rich text — create a sibling binder_item titled "<original title> (Conflicted Copy, <device>, <timestamp>)" containing the client's version, and let the requestUser manually reconcile. This mirrors Dropbox/Scrive

Allowlist link schemes, sweep every route for IDOR, drop product names

Fixes a real cross-site scripting hole in compiled output. Link hrefs were
escaped but their scheme was never checked, so a document containing
javascript:alert(1) produced a working anchor in every format that carries
links. Escaping cannot help there: the payload contains nothing that needs
escaping. isSafeHref now allowlists http, https, mailto and relative
references, normalising away case, whitespace and control characters first so
JaVaScRiPt: and an embedded tab do not slip past, and failing closed on schemes
nobody has listed. An unsafe link loses its anchor, keeps its text, and warns.
Markdown gets the same treatment, since markdown links execute in renderers.

IdorSweepTest enumerates every route from the handler mapping and drives each
one with a stranger's token. Routes naming another account's resource must not
answer 2xx; caller-scoped collections may, but must not contain the victim's
data; nothing may answer 500; and the victim's project must be unchanged
afterwards. Reading the mapping rather than a hand-written list means a new
controller method that forgets its authorization check fails immediately.

Removes third-party product names from tracked files, replacing them with
descriptions of the behaviour they referred to.

190 Java and 95 Node tests green. Verified by mutation: making the ownership
check pass for everyone turns the sweep red.

Add multi-tenant support: multiple restaurants, one system

Every restaurant's data is now isolated by a new Restaurant model —
tables, comandas, menu, orders, payments, coupons, help calls, audit
log and staff all carry a restaurantId and are scoped by it end to
end. This is the foundation for self-service onboarding ("reach the
market") and for a future iFood/delivery-platform channel to slot in
next to KIOSK/DELIVERY/SCHEDULED.

Architecture:
- New `Restaurant` model (id, slug, createdAt). `Settings` keyed by
  restaurantId instead of a hardcoded "singleton" row.
- QR tokens (table/comanda) and the Checkout id stay globally unique
  on purpose — that's how an anonymous QR scan resolves its own
  restaurant with no slug/login needed. Human-facing numbers (table
  number, comanda number, order number/pickup ticket, coupon code)
  become unique per restaurant instead of globally.
- User.email stays globally unique (keeps /login simple: no
  restaurant selection before the password prompt).
- Every by-id staff mutation (delete/update) now scopes on
  {id, restaurantId} via deleteMany/updateMany + a count check,
  instead of trusting a bare id — closes an IDOR class of bug that a
  single-tenant system never had to worry about.
- Realtime SSE topics ("kitchen"/"pdv") are now per-restaurant
  (`kitchen:${restaurantId}`) so one restaurant's live board never
  sees another's events.
- /totem and /pedir move to /totem/[slug] and /pedir/[slug] — the only
  public screens with no QR Code to resolve a restaurant from. New
  /signup does self-service onboarding (Restaurant + Settings + first
  ADMIN user, auto-login), also used as the isolation test's own
  second-tenant fixture.
- Data migration backfills all pre-existing rows onto one
  'rst_default' restaurant (slug "principal") — the real restaurant
  already in production, preserved verbatim.

Found and fixed during isolation testing: the order-number Counter
row wasn't migrated to its new per-restaurant key, so the first order
placed after the migration collided with an existing order number
(unique constraint violation). Added a small follow-up migration that
renames the counter key, preserving the existing sequence.

Verified: full TypeScript + lint clean, production build clean. A
12-point isolation test (via /signup, creating a real second
restaurant on an isolated DB copy) confirms: empty dashboards for a
new tenant, 404 on cross-tenant IDOR attempts by id, independent
per-restaurant numbering/coupons/audit log, SSE events never leaking
across restaurants, and /totem/[slug] serving only its own menu.
Separately reran the full real-restaurant regression (QR order → PDV
payment → totem → painel → reports) after the fix.

+1.9.3 - `unreleased`
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+- Fixed arbitrary certificate revocation at the CA (`GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67`_). Certificate identity was tracked
+  only by Lemur's internal database row, not by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could
+  upload a duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing ``authority_id`` and
+  ``serial``) and then revoke it via ``PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke``, causing the CA to revoke the
+  real certificate belonging to another user. ``POST /api/1/certificates/upload`` now requires
+  ``AuthorityPermission`` on the specified authority, and rejects uploads whose ``(authority_id, serial)``
+  pair already matches an existing certificate with a ``409`` response. ``PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke``
+  now also checks authorization and endpoint attachment against every certificate row sharing
+  ``(authority_id, serial)`` with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request, closing the
+  gap for any duplicate rows that already exist.
+
+.. _GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67: https://github.com/Netflix/lemur/security/advisories/GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67

feat(api): live AWS compute endpoints, generate-time validation, and preflight

Three endpoints: the instance catalog for a region, spot prices, and a recommendation. Missing credentials never mean a blank screen — each degrades live -> stale Peek -> dated fallback, returning data and caveats in one value so a caller cannot take the records and drop the markers.

The Pricing client is pinned to us-east-1 independently of the environment's region; the region travels as the regionCode filter value. Every environment in this account is ap-southeast-2, so getting that wrong fails everywhere. Verified against the live API: regionCode works as a filter and the long location string is not required.

Twelve generate-time refusals, each naming the offending key and the fix, following the voice of validateALBConfigMap. Notably: a runtime: ec2 pointing at a pool that does not exist or is disabled, awsvpc without assume_egress, and on_demand_base under any capacity_type except spot_with_base. That last one used to be refused only under on_demand, so writing it under spot silently produced a 100% spot pool AND suppressed the warning that a capacity rebalance can reclaim every instance at once.

Preflight adds three pool-gated, non-blocking checks. The instance-launchability check exists because a real deploy failed with 'AccessDenied: You are not authorized to use launch template', which turned out to be an Organizations SCP denying ec2:RunInstances by instance type — something CreateAutoScalingGroup cannot surface, since it only sees that it could not use the template. A RunInstances dry run returns the real denial with the policy ARN. Resolving the AMI via SSM first is mandatory: a fake AMI returns InvalidAMIID.Malformed before authorization is evaluated, so the check would otherwise report the wrong diagnosis.

hclString and hclEscape close an interpolation hole: user_data_extra and ami_id interpolate into generated HCL, and an unescaped quote turns config content into Terraform syntax. Two helpers were specified; three shipped, because heredoc content and quoted scalars have different dangerous characters and a helper safe in one is inert in the other. Heredoc delimiters are content-derived so a script containing a bare EOT cannot terminate its own block.

preprocessEnvMap extracts what applyTemplate does between loading and rendering, so renderMainHBS stops hand-replicating it. Wiring the render tests to the real pipeline immediately failed four fixtures that were genuinely invalid configs the old harness had no way to reject. Both generate and deploy now resolve <env>.yaml through the same search order as the loader, so a project laid out with project/dev.yaml stops working in the UI and failing on the command line.

Authentication Bypass For Endpoints With Anonymous Access

Using a remember-me cookie with an arbitrary username can cause Opencast
to assume proper authentication for that user even if the remember-me
cookie was incorrect given that the attacked endpoint also allows
anonymous access.

This way, an attacker can, for example, fake a remember-me token, assume
the identity of the global system administrator and request non-public
content from the search service without ever providing any proper
authentication.

The reason for this problem is that using a remember-me cookie will
always cause the user in the request context to be populated, even if
the cookie is invalid by now. This is usually no problem, except in
combination with anonymous access where anonymous authentication is
granted and the request may continue.

In such a case, Opencast's security service would just check that a user
existed in the request context and assume proper authentication of this
user, never checking if it's actually anonymous authentication.

This patch adds this additional check, falling back to the anonymous
user in case of anonymous authentication.
