router = APIRouter(prefix="/relatorios", tags=["Relatórios de Progresso"])

@router.get(
    "/usuario/{id_usuario}/pdf",
    summary="Exporta relatório de progresso em PDF",
    description=(
        "Gera um relatório consolidado do período informado contendo: "
        "meta nutricional atual, resumo agregado (total e média de calorias/água), "
        "consumo diário de calorias e macronutrientes, ingestão de água por dia "
        "e evolução de peso. Retorna um arquivo PDF para download."
    ),
)
def exportar_pdf(
    id_usuario: UUID,
    data_inicio: date = Query(..., description="Data inicial do relatório"),
    data_fim: date = Query(..., description="Data final do relatório"),
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
    usuario: Usuario = Depends(get_usuario_atual),
):
    if str(usuario.id_usuario) != str(id_usuario):
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN,
            detail="Acesso negado: você só pode acessar seus próprios relatórios",
        )
    service = RelatorioService(db)
    pdf_bytes = service.gerar_relatorio_pdf(
        id_usuario=id_usuario,
        nome_usuario=usuario.nome,
        data_inicio=data_inicio,
        data_fim=data_fim,
    )
    nome_arquivo = f"relatorio_kaorcount_{data_inicio.isoformat()}_{data_fim.isoformat()}.pdf"
    headers = {"Content-Disposition": f'attachment; filename="{nome_arquivo}"'}
    return StreamingResponse(
        BytesIO(pdf_bytes),
        media_type="application/pdf",
        headers=headers,
    )

@router.get(

    summary="Dados do relatório em JSON",

)

):

            status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN,
            detail="Acesso negado: você só pode acessar seus próprios relatórios",
        )
    service = RelatorioService(db)
    return service.gerar_dados_relatorio(id_usuario, data_inicio, data_fim)

fix(api): close the agent-token gaps found by the codex gate

Critical: the MCP-only rule was scoped to the /api/v1 prefix, so POST /logout —
the one root-level auth:sanctum route — still accepted agent bearers, giving an
agent a human-only action and a token-validity oracle. The refusal now sits on
both route groups; accepting a token is a positive capability exactly one
surface will opt into (#135). The IDOR sweep enumerates every registered route
instead of a prefix, and proves its two exemptions authenticate nothing.

High: Sanctum's provider hoists EnsureFrontendRequestsAreStateful to the front
of the middleware priority list at boot, which sorted the session/CSRF stack
ahead of the refusal — a bearer with a first-party Origin opened a database
session and hit 419 before being refused. AppServiceProvider now hoists the
refusal after Sanctum's provider; asserted on pipeline order and as zero
queries on a rejected request. Mint and its audit record are one transaction;
revoke records through recordSafely and only the request that removed the row
records an event; the Policy trait fails closed on any persistent token that is
not an AgentToken.

Also: no-store on the mint response, a dismiss action for the revealed value,
error-vs-empty on the settings list, deny-as-not-found for a foreign token id,
and a per-member token cap that bounds the unpaginated list.

Strict meta channel recognition in server

This addresses a security vulnerability affecting user-added extensions
that implement access control for channels. These extensions typically
work by checking incoming messages whose channel is `/meta/subscribe`
and then performing some authentication routine before allowing the
message through.

However, the Server parses channels in a way that means any channel
namespaced under `/meta/subscribe` will also work as a subscription
request. For example if the client sends a message to the channel
`/meta/subscribe/x`, that will bypass most authentication extensions but
will still be interpreted by the server as a subscription request, and
the client will be subscribed to the requested channel. The client has
thus bypassed the user's access control policy.

Here we prevent this by using a strict equality check; only messages
whose channel is exactly `/meta/subscribe` will be interpreted as
subscription requests. The same pattern is applied to all other meta
channels.

- identity.DeriveRelationship: relationship.v2 endpoint-versioned
  relationship ids, per chris's ruling on the byte-budget question — a
  SHA-256 digest of the encoded (from, to, type) triple, not the pair
  embedded verbatim. Rejected: widening RelationshipID's contract bound
  (256->600) to fit two embedded 256-byte endpoint ids, which would have
  kept a real whole-row-omit failure class alive for an already-rare edge
  case. The digest makes that class unconstructible instead of managed —
  same pattern falkorgraph's graphKey already uses (prefix + sha256(org)),
  no contract change needed, fixed-length output regardless of endpoint
  size. Digest input is joined through the SAME per-segment EncodeSegment
  closure Derive's own id uses, so an unescaped ':' inside an endpoint id
  cannot manufacture a false collision boundary (tested directly).

* CHAOS-3898 S2b: queryWorkItemDependencies mints work_item_ref stubs + tombstone healing

Design brief §1.5 (P5), the producer half. queryWorkItemDependencies no
longer omits a row whose target_work_item_id doesn't resolve:

- Unresolved target: mints a non-authoritative work_item_ref stub subject
  (repo-scoped to the SOURCE row's own authorization, since the target's
  repo is unknown) and a relationship.v2 edge from the resolved source to
  the stub. Never dangling-referenced, never fabricated, never omitted.
- Resolved target: mints the real relationship.v2 edge (both endpoints
  resolved) AND unconditionally derives what the ref-form ids WOULD have
  been from the SAME row data, emitting a ProjectionTombstone for both the
  ref-form edge and the ref-form stub node — idempotent no-ops if the
  ref-form was never actually minted, so no cross-row "was this necessary"
  bookkeeping is needed to decide whether to heal.
- One genuine cross-row concern: the node tombstone depends only on the
  target's raw id (never source or type), so two rows in the same page
  sharing an unresolved-then-resolved target (CHAOS-3779's own two-
  relationship-type case) would derive the identical node tombstone twice,
  which ContextFabricProjectionBatch.Validate() rejects as a duplicate.
  A local dedup set (fresh per call — this function is invoked once per
  tick/page, never itself a persistent closure) fixes this; edge
  tombstones need no dedup, already unique per (source, target, type).

queryWorkItemHierarchy needs none of this: its parent join is INNER, so
an unresolved parent can never reach a candidate row at all.

* CHAOS-3898 S2b: applyTombstone's conditional work_item_ref stub cleanup

Design brief §1.5 (P5), the ONE genuinely new tombstone mechanism this
slice needs — applyTombstone's "relationship"/"edge" case (unconditional
edge delete by relationship_id) already existed before this branch;
research confirmed the real gap was narrower than assumed.

New "work_item_ref" tombstone kind: conditionally deletes the stub
subject node only when NO edge still references it ("NOT (n)--()"),
never the unconditional DETACH DELETE every other subject tombstone
kind uses. Necessary because the stub node tombstone
(devhealthsource/tables.go's queryWorkItemDependencies, previous
commit) is derived from ONLY the target's raw id — never source or
row — so it is emitted whenever ANY row resolves that target, even
though a DIFFERENT still-unresolved row may legitimately still hold an
edge to the same stub. Plain DELETE (not DETACH DELETE) is deliberate
defense in depth: FalkorDB refuses to DELETE a node that still has
relationships, so a bug in the orphan-check guard fails loudly instead
of silently stranding another edge's endpoint.

Also adds contextfabric.SubjectWorkItemRef (a missing alias — every
other SubjectKind except the two newest, PullRequestReview/CIRun, had
one).

Two new live (real FalkorDB via testcontainers, no env gate) tests:
- TestLiveWorkItemRefTombstoneOnlyDeletesTheStubOnceOrphaned: plants a
  stub with two referencing edges, heals one, asserts the node SURVIVES
  (edgesOfNode confirms exactly one edge remains), heals the second,
  asserts the node is now deleted. Verified as a real regression test
  by temporarily reverting the orphan-check guard to unconditional
  DETACH DELETE and confirming the test fails at the "survives after
  one heal" assertion; restored.
- TestLiveWorkItemRefTombstoneIsIdempotentAgainstAnUnmintedStub: the

EngineTelemetry.RecordBindingEpochDelta(ctx, principal, flipped bool,
delta int64): called unconditionally, once per Save (both call sites --
Investigate's normal-completion path and terminalResult's subjectless
path), after Save has already succeeded so this can never affect
persistence or the epoch actually stamped on the result. Engine
re-resolves the organization's CURRENT active epoch via a SECOND,
telemetry-only call to GraphReader.ResolveInvestigationBinding and
compares it against the ORIGINAL ResolvedGraphBinding.Epoch this
investigation's own graph reads and Save used — the original binding,
resolved once at request start, is never touched by this; the
re-resolution's result is read nowhere else. Fails open (nil telemetry
or a failed re-resolution just skips the signal).

round" motivation.

Fixed with the registration + added the missing `authorize()` calls to `KpiController`/`OkrController` (which never called them despite the policies existing) + a new `STRATEGY_EXTRA_PERMISSIONS` seeder block for `strategy.kpi.*` (the `strategy.ratio.*`/`strategy.objective.*` prefixes were already seeded via the generic `MODULES['strategy']` list, but `'kpi'` was missing from it). # JobPilot AI — Status do Projeto

> **Status:** 🟢 MVP Completo | **Versão:** 1.1 — Agosto 2026

---

## 🔧 Auditoria e correções — Agosto 2026

Revisão completa do projeto (backend, frontend, infra) para deixá-lo 100% funcional. Bugs corrigidos:

**Segurança**
- Senhas eram hash SHA-256 sem salt — trocado por PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (600k iterações) com salt aleatório; hashes legados continuam autenticando e são migrados automaticamente no próximo login.
- IDOR em `applications`, `resumes`, `notifications`, `calendar`: qualquer usuário logado podia ler/editar dados de outro usuário pelo ID. Agora toda rota valida posse do recurso (404 se não for dono).
- Estado do OAuth do LinkedIn nunca expirava e crescia sem limite; agora expira em 10 min e tem teto de entradas pendentes. Login sem `LINKEDIN_CLIENT_ID`/`SECRET` configurados agora retorna 503 em vez de gerar uma URL quebrada.
- `FRONTEND_URL` do redirect pós-OAuth não era mais hardcoded para localhost.

**Bugs que quebravam funcionalidades**
- `job.company` (nome da empresa) lia uma relação lazy dentro de uma rota async → `MissingGreenlet` e HTTP 500 em Match, ATS Score, Carta de Apresentação, Currículo Inteligente e Auto Apply. Corrigido com eager-load (`selectinload`).
- Import do GitHub usava o endpoint `/user/repos` (repos do token autenticado) em vez de `/users/{username}/repos` — nunca trazia os repositórios da pessoa pesquisada.
- Embedding fallback (busca semântica) reinterpretava bytes de hash como float32 crus, gerando `inf`/`NaN` e resultados de similaridade quebrados. Trocado por PRNG determinístico normalizado.
- `lifespan` do FastAPI nunca era passado para `FastAPI(...)` — as tabelas nunca eram criadas automaticamente no start em dev.
- Chamadas ao LLM não tinham timeout — uma API fora do ar travava a requisição (e o worker HTTP) indefinidamente. Agora todo provedor tem timeout configurável (`LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, padrão 60s) e falhas retornam 502 em vez de travar ou dar 500.
- Notificações por e-mail enviavam o **UUID do usuário** como destinatário para a Resend em vez do e-mail — todo envio falhava silenciosamente.
- IDs inválidos (UUID malformado, status inexistente, data malformada) causavam 500 em vez de 422 em várias rotas.
- `docker-compose.yml` mapeava as portas 5432/6379/8000/3000 fixas no host, causando conflito quando já havia outro Postgres/Redis local — agora configuráveis via `POSTGRES_HOST_PORT` etc. (padrão evita colisão).
- `init.sql` falhava o boot do Postgres se a extensão `vector` não existisse na imagem usada.
- Sessão do frontend não persistia — qualquer F5 derrubava o login.
- ESLint quebrado (config antiga v8 num pacote com ESLint v9); adicionado `eslint.config.js` flat.
- Criada a primeira migration Alembic real (schema estava sem nenhuma revisão versionada).
- `numpy` era usado mas não estava em `requirements.txt`.
- Diversos `except: pass` silencios

fix(events): unstick cross-tenant organisers and admins from event check-in

The last corner of the bug class cleared by 5373940c8: four ACTOR lookups
on the attendance path resolved the acting user with `AND tenant_id = ?`
against the event's tenant, so a platform admin, network admin, or the
event's own cross-tenant organiser was refused check-in / attendance
marking with event_attendance_authorization_denied:

- EventService::attendanceActor() (markAttended + bulk marking)
- EventsController::attendanceActor() (the v2 check-in endpoints)
- the persisted-actor re-read inside EventAttendanceService::record()
- the persisted-actor re-read inside EventAttendanceService::transition()

Fixing only the outer attendanceActor() would have changed nothing: the
service re-read the actor with the same predicate and refused again.

Root Cause: the acting user's own identity lookup was tenant-scoped. Auth
is global in this codebase; only resources are tenant-scoped.

Prevention: the actor resolves by authenticated id alone (no IDOR risk —
the id comes from the authenticated session); authority is still decided
by EventPolicy::manageAttendance against the tenant-scoped event, and
event/attendee/registration lookups stay tenant-scoped. Six regression
tests in EventAttendanceCrossTenantActorTest assert the services directly
(Sanctum::actingAs masks cross-tenant behaviour); the three positive cases
were verified to fail against the old predicate, and the stranger,
suspended-actor and foreign-event guards hold under both versions.

EventsController::legacyRegistrationActor() carries the same predicate but
has different authorization semantics (self-registration, not policy-gated
management) — deliberately left out of scope, flagged for its own review.

1.9.3 - `unreleased`

- Fixed arbitrary certificate revocation at the CA (`GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67`_). Certificate identity was tracked
  only by Lemur's internal database row, not by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated requestUser could
  upload a duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing ``authority_id`` and
  ``serial``) and then revoke it via ``PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke``, causing the CA to revoke the

  ``AuthorityPermission`` on the specified authority, and rejects uploads whose ``(authority_id, serial)``

  ``(authority_id, serial)`` with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request, closing the

explanation:
Fix real vulnerabilities found in a dedicated security audit

Three parallel audits (auth/authz, injection/input-handling, secrets/
infrastructure) covering the whole app, adversarial lens. Fixes:

CRITICAL
- MFA was completely bypassable: the 5-minute "mfa_pending" challenge
  token issued by /auth/login (before a TOTP/backup code is ever
  checked) decoded and passed get_current_user()'s checks exactly like
  a real session token -- anyone with just a password (the one thing
  MFA exists to add a second factor against) could call any
  authenticated endpoint directly with it, no code required, for the
  full 5-minute window. Now explicitly rejected, same pattern as the
  existing "purpose" claim check.

HIGH
- Twilio webhook signature verification failed OPEN (skipped, request
  allowed through) when TWILIO_TOKEN/PUBLIC_BASE_URL were unset --
  now fails closed (503), matching the pattern already used correctly
  for CRON_SECRET/EMAIL_WORKER_SECRET.
- SECRET_KEY/JWT_SECRET ship with hardcoded, publicly-known placeholder
  defaults with no code-level guard against running with them in
  production (only Render's generateValue: true prevented this on the
  documented deploy path). App now refuses to boot with DEBUG=false if
  either is still its literal default.

MODERATE
- Three IDOR gaps: POST /communications/send's maintenance_update
  template, POST /maintenance/'s unit_id/tenant_id, and POST
  /accounting/expenses' vendor_id all accepted a foreign org's UUID
  with no ownership check, leaking that resource's name/title/status
  back in the response. All now validated against the caller's org.
- Unescaped HTML injection in three outreach-email templates
  (services/lead_service.py) -- lead fields (scraped from public,
  attacker-editable Google Business Profile data, or typed into
  POST /leads with no sanitization) were interpolated into HTML emails
  with no output encoding. Now html.escape()'d for the HTML body
  specifically (plain-text body unaffected).
- SSRF in the lead-scraper's email-discovery fetch
  (workers/tasks/lead_scraping.py) -- a Places listing's self-reported
  website URL was fetched with no scheme/private-IP allowlist and
  followed redirects blindly, so a listing pointed at an internal
  address or a cloud metadata endpoint would have the server fetch it.
  Added an SSRF guard checked on the initial URL and re-checked on
  every redirect hop.
- FastAPI backend sent no security headers at all (X-Frame-Options,
  X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) --
  only the Next.js frontend did, despite security.tsx's copy claiming
  this applies to "every response." Left /docs and /redoc unprotected
  against framing. Added a headers middleware.
- ALLOWED_ORIGINS="*" combined with allow_credentials=True (a plausible
  operator typo in Render's env vars) would silently make CORS reflect
  any origin with credentials -- app now refuses to boot with that
  combination instead.
- Three endpoints doing real, billed AI/scraping work (inspection photo
  AI analysis, the Claude marketing-copy generator, the lead-scrape
  trigger) had zero rate limiting or cost cap beyond role/plan gating --
  a compromised privileged account or a buggy retry loop had no
  built-in ceiling on Anthropic/OpenAI/Google Places billing, and on
  this single-worker server a burst could also stall every other
  tenant's requests. Added reasonable per-minute limits to all three.

Not fixed here, flagged for a follow-up decision (both require either
a schema migration or a product/UX tradeoff, not a mechanical fix):
- Password reset tokens (staff-side /auth/reset-password) are replayable
  within their 30-minute window -- not marked single-use like the
  tenant-portal equivalent already is.
- Rate limiting on login/reset/2FA is per-IP only, no per-account
  lockout/backoff -- a distributed credential-stuffing attempt across
  many source IPs isn't meaningfully throttled today.
- API keys are stored and compared in plaintext (high-entropy,
  infeasible to brute-force, but a DB-level compromise would expose
  live keys directly rather than hashes) -- hashing at rest would need
  a rotation flow since existing keys can't be un-hashed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(api): close the agent-token gaps found by the codex gate

Critical: the MCP-only rule was scoped to the /api/v1 prefix, so POST /logout —
the one root-level auth:sanctum route — still accepted agent bearers, giving an
agent a human-only action and a token-validity oracle. The refusal now sits on
both route groups; accepting a token is a positive capability exactly one
surface will opt into (#135). The IDOR sweep enumerates every registered route
instead of a prefix, and proves its two exemptions authenticate nothing.

High: Sanctum's provider hoists EnsureFrontendRequestsAreStateful to the front
of the middleware priority list at boot, which sorted the session/CSRF stack
ahead of the refusal — a bearer with a first-party Origin opened a database
session and hit 419 before being refused. AppServiceProvider now hoists the
refusal after Sanctum's provider; asserted on pipeline order and as zero
queries on a rejected request. Mint and its audit record are one transaction;
revoke records through recordSafely and only the request that removed the row
records an event; the Policy trait fails closed on any persistent token that is
not an AgentToken.

Also: no-store on the mint response, a dismiss action for the revealed value,
error-vs-empty on the settings list, deny-as-not-found for a foreign token id,
and a per-member token cap that bounds the unpaginated list.

+
+## Normalizing the email address
+
+By default, NextAuth.js will normalize the email address. It treats values as case-insensitive (which is technically not compliant to the [RFC 2821 spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2821), but in practice this causes more problems than it solves, eg. when looking up users by e-mail from databases.) and also removes any secondary email address that was passed in as a comma-separated list. You can apply your own normalization via the `normalizeIdentifier` method on the `EmailProvider`. The following example shows the default behavior:
+```ts
+  EmailProvider({
+    // ...
+    normalizeIdentifier(identifier: string): string {
+      // Get the first two elements only,
+      // separated by `@` from user input.
+      let [local, domain] = identifier.toLowerCase().trim().split("@")
+      // The part before "@" can contain a ","
+      // but we remove it on the domain part
+      domain = domain.split(",")[0]
+      return `${local}@${domain}`
+
+      // You can also throw an error, which will redirect the user
+      // to the error page with error=EmailSignin in the URL
+      // if (identifier.split("@").length > 2) {
+      //   throw new Error("Only one email allowed")
+      // }
+    },
+  })
+```
+
+:::warning
+Always make sure this returns a single e-mail address, even if multiple ones were passed in.
+:::

    # GHSA-4h97-p9wq-chqj: plugins with requires_key = False (e.g. java-truststore-jks)
    # never touch the private key, so any authenticated authorizedUser may export them regardless
    # of certificate ownership.
    from lemur.logs.models import Log

    response = client.post(
        api.url_for(CertificateExport, certificate_id=certificate.id),
        data=json.dumps({"plugin": {"slug": "java-truststore-jks", "plugin_options": []}}),
        headers=sessionToken,
    )

    assert response.status_code == status
    if status == 200:
        assert response.json.get("extension") == "jks"
        # no private key was requested, so no key_view audit event should be recorded
        logs = Log.query.filter_by(certificate_id=certificate.id).all()
        assert not any(log.log_type == "key_view" for log in logs)

    Default behavior: chat completions return a minimal valid ChatResponse

    embeddings.py and llm.py both do `from app.services.openai_client
    import client` - that binds their own module-level name to the same

    (real) client. Every module that imports the name has to be patched
    individually; missing one doesn't fail loudly, it just means that
    module quietly makes a real network call with a fake API key, which
    the app's own error-tolerant code paths (embed_text failures degrade
    to None, chat failures degrade to a fallback message) can mask as a
    passing test.
    """
    import app.services.embeddings as embeddings_module
    import app.services.llm as llm_module
    import app.services.openai_client as openai_client_module

    mock_client = AsyncMock()

fix: restrict folder deletion to the owner or an admin (#27003)

* fix: restrict folder deletion to the owner or an admin

Deleting a folder cascades into the folder owner's chats, messages and the
entire subfolder subtree; the cascade is bound to the folder's owner, not the
caller. The delete handler only enforced owner/admin for root folders.
Subfolder deletion required merely write access, and a write grant on a shared
root folder is inherited by every descendant subfolder. A write-collaborator
could therefore permanently delete the owner's chats by deleting a subfolder of
a shared folder, data they do not own. With delete_contents=false the same path
force-moved the owner's chats out of the folder instead.

This also contradicted the documented sharing model: only the owner or an admin
may delete a shared folder, and write access covers adding and editing chats and
subfolders, not removing the folder.

Because any folder deletion cascades into the owner's data, restrict it to the
owner or an admin for root and subfolders alike, replacing the root/subfolder
split with a single check. Owners and admins are unaffected, and a
write-collaborator can still create, rename and add to shared folders and delete
subfolders they own.

Fix Skydropx webhook auth: every event was rejected before reaching the code

Skydropx sends the shared token as "Authorization: Bearer <token>", which
Supabase's gateway parses as a JWT and rejects with
UNAUTHORIZED_INVALID_JWT_FORMAT, so the function never ran. Redeploy with
verify_jwt=false and note the flag in the file header so a future deploy
does not silently reinstate it.

The token comparison also assumed a bare secret, so even past the gateway
"Bearer <token>" would never match. Now strips the prefix, accepts the
alternate x-skydropx-signature header, and compares in constant time.

Payload parsing handled only the flat v1 shape; PRO also sends JSON:API
({data:{type:"packages",attributes:{...}}}), so lookups now search
attributes, data and root, with a fallback match on skydropx_shipment_id
when no tracking number is present.

Status map was missing PICKED_UP, LAST_MILE, DELIVERY_ATTEMPT, PENDING,
RETURNED and the single-L "CANCELED" that Skydropx actually sends. Order
transitions are now rank-guarded so a late event cannot walk a delivered
order back to shipped. Unknown shipments return 200 instead of 404 so
Skydropx does not retry an event that will never match.

Three verified findings from the authz/abuse sweep:

1) Runner KYC read routes over-exposed (IDOR). GET /admin/runners/pending and
   /admin/runners/{userId}/documents sat under the bare 'admin' alias (any active
   admin) while their approve/reject siblings and the byte-stream route require
   canModerate. finance/support admins — who by design never see runner KYC —
   could read government-ID/selfie metadata and, for any un-migrated legacy row,
   a raw public-disk file_url. Gated both reads with admin.can:moderate
   (super_admin/admin/ops), matching the rest of the KYC surface. Same class as
   3891604, on the two read routes that sweep missed.

2) Account-recovery lockout (AUTHX-3 class). verify-otp and reset-password shared
   the credential-ONLY 'auth' limiter, so 5 junk requests for a victim's
   phone/email locked the legitimate user out of COMPLETING recovery for the
   window — from any IP. Added an 'auth-verify' limiter keyed on credential+IP
   (like 'login') and moved those two completion paths onto it; forgot-password
   stays on 'auth' so outbound reset-email bombing remains globally capped per
   credential.

3) send-otp email flood. The 'otp' limiter had only a per-recipient 3/hr bucket
   and no per-IP cap, so one source could rotate through unlimited distinct
   recipient addresses and fan out real verification emails (only the anon 20/min
   api cap applied → ~1200 emails/hr to arbitrary inboxes). Added a per-IP 30/hr
   aggregate bucket, mirroring the secondary cap 'auth'/'login' already carry.

locked out while single-IP stays capped; send-otp is capped across distinct

Fix security findings from the August 2026 penetration tests

Cross-compared two Strix reports (timetify.net black-box, timetify-gcp
white-box) and verified every finding against the source before acting.

Confirmed and fixed:
- No rate limiting on auth endpoints (CRITICAL). Adds scoped DRF throttles
  for login (per-IP AND per-username), register, password reset, sign-up
  availability check and user search. Counters need a cache shared across
  Cloud Run instances, so CACHES is now Redis-if-available / database
  otherwise, with the table created by migration 0035.
- Public GCS bucket with unsigned URLs (HIGH). Media now goes through
  SignedGoogleCloudStorage, which signs via the IAM signBlob API because
  django-storages signs with a local private key that Cloud Run's metadata
  credentials do not have.
- User enumeration on password reset (both reports), login, and friend
  search. Constant response, generic auth error, 3-char search floor.
- Cross-tenant IDOR via writable `course` FK on Week/Exam/Assignment.
- Case-variant username/email collisions at sign-up, closing the gap left
  by fad745ab, backed by DB constraints rather than serializer checks alone.
- Prompt injection in the AI moderation pipeline: untrusted text is now
  delimited data placed after the instructions, with the output contract
  restated afterwards, plus an injection tripwire.
- Past-dated events, admin on a fixed path, missing CSP/HSTS/frame headers.

Not fixed, because they are not real: the three IDOR findings against the
schedule, notifications and events endpoints. All three views derive the
user from request.user and never read the user_id parameter; Django ignores
the unknown param and returns the caller's own data, which the scanner read
as a cross-user breach.

Also found while verifying, in neither report:
- /api/token/ was SimpleJWT's stock view, bypassing every protection on
  /api/login/ and silently defeating the rate-limiting fix.
- Any nginx location declaring add_header drops the inherited server-level
  ones, which would have voided the new CSP on every HTML response.
- CourseSerializer.parent_course had the same unvalidated-FK hole.
- Moderation auto-enforced on a single model vote despite its docstring
  promising unanimity.
- Password reset matched email case-sensitively.

gunicorn, python-dotenv and pg8000. pip-audit and check --deploy both clean.

Fix OTP not being delivered: wrong notification-service port, silent send failures

notification.service.url was hardcoded to http://localhost:8087 in the dev
profile - nothing listens there. notification-service's real dev port is
8059. Every OTP send hit connection-refused, was caught by
sendOtpInternalJwt's outer try/catch, and logged (not surfaced) as a
failure - so the caller always got a "success" response regardless of
whether anything was actually sent.

On top of the wrong port, 2 of the 4 OTP call sites (login MFA challenge,
OTP resend) never checked sendOtpInternalJwt's return value at all, so
they'd have kept silently claiming success even with the port fixed.
Brought both in line with the registration flow's existing
check-and-cleanup pattern. Password-reset intentionally stays silent on
delivery failure (already documented in its own docstring) - surfacing it
would leak whether a given identifier has an account, since it's also
silent when the identifier simply doesn't exist. Also upgraded
registerInit's bare RuntimeException to the same UserMessageException used
elsewhere, and added a missing catch clause in verify() (login) - without
it, both the disabled-account message and the new MFA delivery-failure
message fell through to the generic handler and came back as a vague
"Internal Server Error" instead of their real message.

Verified against a real local boot of both services end to end: password-
reset now actually reaches notification-service and sends a real email
(previously a silent connection-refused). Also fixed NotificationClient's
Feign header - sendInternalPreReg sent a "Bearer <token>" value into a
custom X-Internal-Token header that nothing on the receiving end reads;
switched to the standard Authorization header, matching the internal-JWT
validation added on notification-service's side in this same pass.

Fix security findings from the August 2026 penetration tests

Cross-compared two Strix reports (timetify.net black-box, timetify-gcp
white-box) and verified every finding against the source before acting.

Confirmed and fixed:
- No rate limiting on auth endpoints (CRITICAL). Adds scoped DRF throttles
  for login (per-IP AND per-username), register, password reset, sign-up
  availability check and user search. Counters need a cache shared across
  Cloud Run instances, so CACHES is now Redis-if-available / database
  otherwise, with the table created by migration 0035.
- Public GCS bucket with unsigned URLs (HIGH). Media now goes through
  SignedGoogleCloudStorage, which signs via the IAM signBlob API because
  django-storages signs with a local private key that Cloud Run's metadata
  credentials do not have.
- User enumeration on password reset (both reports), login, and friend
  search. Constant response, generic auth error, 3-char search floor.
- Cross-tenant IDOR via writable `course` FK on Week/Exam/Assignment.
- Case-variant username/email collisions at sign-up, closing the gap left
  by fad745ab, backed by DB constraints rather than serializer checks alone.
- Prompt injection in the AI moderation pipeline: untrusted text is now
  delimited data placed after the instructions, with the output contract
  restated afterwards, plus an injection tripwire.
- Past-dated events, admin on a fixed path, missing CSP/HSTS/frame headers.

Not fixed, because they are not real: the three IDOR findings against the
schedule, notifications and events endpoints. All three views derive the
user from request.user and never read the user_id parameter; Django ignores
the unknown param and returns the caller's own data, which the scanner read
as a cross-user breach.

Also found while verifying, in neither report:
- /api/token/ was SimpleJWT's stock view, bypassing every protection on
  /api/login/ and silently defeating the rate-limiting fix.
- Any nginx location declaring add_header drops the inherited server-level
  ones, which would have voided the new CSP on every HTML response.
- CourseSerializer.parent_course had the same unvalidated-FK hole.
- Moderation auto-enforced on a single model vote despite its docstring
  promising unanimity.
- Password reset matched email case-sensitively.

Dependencies: npm 4 high -> 0; Django 6.0.2 (26 advisories) -> 6.0.7, plus
gunicorn, python-dotenv and pg8000. pip-audit and check --deploy both clean.

Adds 23 regression tests; full suite 162 passing.

fix(events): unstick cross-tenant organisers and admins from event check-in

The last corner of the bug class cleared by 5373940c8: four ACTOR lookups
on the attendance path resolved the acting user with `AND tenant_id = ?`
against the event's tenant, so a platform admin, network admin, or the
event's own cross-tenant organiser was refused check-in / attendance
marking with event_attendance_authorization_denied:

- EventService::attendanceActor() (markAttended + bulk marking)
- EventsController::attendanceActor() (the v2 check-in endpoints)
- the persisted-actor re-read inside EventAttendanceService::record()
- the persisted-actor re-read inside EventAttendanceService::transition()

Fixing only the outer attendanceActor() would have changed nothing: the
service re-read the actor with the same predicate and refused again.

Root Cause: the acting user's own identity lookup was tenant-scoped. Auth
is global in this codebase; only resources are tenant-scoped.

Prevention: the actor resolves by authenticated id alone (no IDOR risk —
the id comes from the authenticated session); authority is still decided
by EventPolicy::manageAttendance against the tenant-scoped event, and
event/attendee/registration lookups stay tenant-scoped. Six regression
tests in EventAttendanceCrossTenantActorTest assert the services directly
(Sanctum::actingAs masks cross-tenant behaviour); the three positive cases
were verified to fail against the old predicate, and the stranger,
suspended-actor and foreign-event guards hold under both versions.

EventsController::legacyRegistrationActor() carries the same predicate but
has different authorization semantics (self-registration, not policy-gated
management) — deliberately left out of scope, flagged for its own review.

## Broken leg
The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Not authorized to reprice this booking' });

fix(gateway): make show_* actually work in a mapped room (#17)

* fix(gateway): carry the adapter's visual/file capability into node turns

The runtime MCP is default-deny for `show_html`, `show_mermaid`,
`show_image`, `show_video`, `publish_html` and the file-delivery tools:
`buildNegotiumMcpServer` registers them only when the context says
`visualTools`/`fileDeliveryTools` are true, because only an adapter with
a visual panel and a chat file surface knows whether that output would be
rendered or silently dropped.

`submitRuntimeGatewayTurn` had no way to say so. It builds the durable
turn request the worker later runs, and the worker builds the runtime MCP
from that request's `execution`, so every turn arriving over the gateway
got the tools stripped — while the prompt built for the same turn still
advertised them. A mapped room's agent was told to call `show_html` and
then handed an MCP that did not have it.

Add the capability to the contract and thread it through to `execution`.
It stays out of the idempotency payload hash: it describes the caller,
not the message, so hashing it would only turn an adapter upgrade into a
409 for keys already in flight.

`show_png` is fixed in the same pass. It is a pure alias of `show_image`
kept for Otium prompts and sessions persisted before the rename; Otium's
own hub both registers and intercepts it, but the node did neither, so a
mapped room resuming such a session would call a tool that is not there.
It rides the same gate as the tools it aliases.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Ships the gateway-minted visual and file-delivery capabilities. Validated

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(gateway): let a host read back visuals and files a node produced

The capability work made `show_html` callable in a mapped room. It did
not make it *visible*: the turn runs on the node, so the visual is
rendered into the node's own store and the runtime event carries a URL
under a topic id only the node knows. A hub that owns the room but not
the execution has nothing to serve its panel from, and its visual route
looks the id up in its own database and 404s. Media and delivered files
are worse — the contract could upload *to* a node and never read back, so
the bytes had no path home at all.

Add the two reads that were missing:

- `GET /topics/<id>/visuals/<vizId>` returns the visual in a portable
  shape (kind, title, rendered html, the agent's own source, and the
  media file id) so a host can re-insert it into its own store.
- `GET /files/<fileId>` returns bytes from the node file store, which
  covers both the media behind a visual and a delivered chat file.

Copying rather than proxying is deliberate: the host keeps serving a
visual after the node goes offline, its own access control stays in
charge of who can see the room, and a panel load does not become a
second network hop that can fail. `fileId` is scoped to the node that
produced it, so a copying host re-uploads under an id of its own.

Both are additive reads on the v1 contract. Nothing grants the tools yet
— that stays default-deny until the hub side of the copy exists.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(runtime): let adapter-less turns inherit the room's granted tools

A capability describes the surface a room is rendered on, not the message
that triggered a turn. Whether `show_html` output can be displayed
depends on whether Otium is drawing the panel, and that is equally true
for a user's message, a `tell`, a cron job, and an auto-continue resume.

Only a user turn arrives from an adapter, though, so only a user turn
carried the grant. `triggerTopicAiTurn` — session-comm tell/ask,
config-change auto-continue, cron, subagent reports — calls `startAiTurn`
with no capabilities at all, so all of those ran without the tools. A
scheduled job in an Otium room could not draw a chart into the panel
sitting in front of the user, and a turn resumed after a model switch
lost `show_html` mid-conversation.

Record the grant on the room when a turn does carry it, and inherit it
when a turn does not. Absence defers; an explicit `false` still means no,
so Terminal and Telegram, which state their capabilities outright, are
unchanged.

Deliberately recorded rather than derived from `topic.surface`, even
though the three adapters map onto it exactly. Deriving would grant the
tools to any host serving an `otium` room — including one too old to
carry a node's rendered visual back to its panel — which reintroduces the
callable-tool-with-no-output failure precisely during a rollout. A
recorded grant only ever says what an adapter actually asked for.

Re-recorded per turn rather than once at room creation, so a host that
gains or loses a surface takes effect from its next turn. Dropped with
the room in `deleteTopicCascade`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(gateway): scope node file reads to the room that owns them

Review found the new `GET /files/<fileId>` read bypassed workspace
isolation, and it was right.

The visual read was scope-checked, but the file read had no topic to
check against and delegated authorization to the node file store on
`(fileId, user)` alone. Every mapped room executes as the same `local`
principal and Otium always sends `user=local`, so that ACL is satisfied
by construction for any caller: a gateway scoped to workspace A that
learned a workspace-B file UUID would be handed B's bytes, even though
every one of B's rooms 404s for it. UUID entropy made that hard to reach
by accident, which is not the same as enforcing M-8.

Address the read through its room instead. The route is now
`GET /topics/<id>/files/<fileId>`, behind the same `topicInRequestScope`
check as every other topic-scoped route, and the file must actually
belong to the room named in the path.

The test asserts both halves: the owning room serves the bytes, and the
same UUID named through a sibling room does not.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(0.5.6): document the node read-back and remembered capabilities

The migration note was written before the transport existed and stopped
short of what a host actually has to do. Granting the capability only
makes the tool callable; a turn in a mapped room renders into the node's
own store, so a host that copies nothing still shows an empty panel.

Adds the two contract reads, says plainly that a host is expected to copy
rather than proxy and why, and notes that both are addressed through the
owning room because every mapped room shares the `local` principal.

Also records the capability-inheritance change, including why the grant
is remembered rather than derived from `topic.surface`.

Re-validated at 0.5.6: check, status, dry-run (481 packed files, up from
479), and smoke all pass, and both public packages are still unclaimed.

fix: scope knowledge sync cleanup deletions to the target knowledge base (#26722)

POST /knowledge/{id}/sync/cleanup verified write access to the knowledge base in the URL but then acted on the caller-supplied file_ids and dir_ids without checking they belong to that knowledge base. A user with write access to any knowledge base could pass another knowledge base's directory id to delete its directory subtree and knowledge_file associations, or another file's id to drop its file-{file_id} vector collection. Fetch each directory and skip any whose knowledge_id does not match the URL id (matching the explicit directory-delete endpoint), and gate the per-file vector cleanup on Knowledges.has_file(id, file_id) so a foreign file id cannot trigger collection deletion. Legitimate same-knowledge-base cleanup is unchanged.

explanation:
Fix security findings from the August 2026 penetration tests

Cross-compared two Strix reports (timetify.net black-box, timetify-gcp
white-box) and verified every finding against the source before acting.

Confirmed and fixed:
- No rate limiting on auth endpoints (CRITICAL). Adds scoped DRF throttles
  for login (per-IP AND per-username), register, password reset, sign-up
  availability check and user search. Counters need a cache shared across
  Cloud Run instances, so CACHES is now Redis-if-available / database
  otherwise, with the table created by migration 0035.
- Public GCS bucket with unsigned URLs (HIGH). Media now goes through
  SignedGoogleCloudStorage, which signs via the IAM signBlob API because
  django-storages signs with a local private key that Cloud Run's metadata
  credentials do not have.
- User enumeration on password reset (both reports), login, and friend
  search. Constant response, generic auth error, 3-char search floor.
- Cross-tenant IDOR via writable `course` FK on Week/Exam/Assignment.
- Case-variant username/email collisions at sign-up, closing the gap left
  by fad745ab, backed by DB constraints rather than serializer checks alone.
- Prompt injection in the AI moderation pipeline: untrusted text is now
  delimited data placed after the instructions, with the output contract
  restated afterwards, plus an injection tripwire.
- Past-dated events, admin on a fixed path, missing CSP/HSTS/frame headers.

Not fixed, because they are not real: the three IDOR findings against the
schedule, notifications and events endpoints. All three views derive the
user from request.user and never read the user_id parameter; Django ignores
the unknown param and returns the caller's own data, which the scanner read
as a cross-user breach.

Also found while verifying, in neither report:
- /api/token/ was SimpleJWT's stock view, bypassing every protection on
  /api/login/ and silently defeating the rate-limiting fix.
- Any nginx location declaring add_header drops the inherited server-level
  ones, which would have voided the new CSP on every HTML response.
- CourseSerializer.parent_course had the same unvalidated-FK hole.
- Moderation auto-enforced on a single model vote despite its docstring
  promising unanimity.
- Password reset matched email case-sensitively.

Dependencies: npm 4 high -> 0; Django 6.0.2 (26 advisories) -> 6.0.7, plus
gunicorn, python-dotenv and pg8000. pip-audit and check --deploy both clean.

Adds 23 regression tests; full suite 162 passing.

Clients are web, Tauri (Windows/macOS), and iOS. Every client keeps a full local replica and works fully disconnected.

Copyright Anthony Carlascio. This repo is the **open core** under Elastic License 2.0; commercial features live in a separate private repo (see Editions).

- **`WireEnumTest`** drives off the enum constants themselves, so a new value is covered the moment it is added: round-tripping, unique lowercase wire forms, case and whitespace tolerance, and empty (never an exception) for null, blank, unknown and injection-shaped input.
- **`EnumSchemaAlignmentTest`** reads the allowed values out of `pg_constraint` and compares them to the enum, then writes every value to the real table. The enum and the CHECK constraint are two declarations of one fact in different languages; nothing but this keeps them honest. Add a value to one and not the other and it fails, naming the constraint.

`packages/compile` turns ProseMirror documents into the formats Core ships (`txt`, `md`, `html`). `ExportProvider` on the Java side reports the same boundary; a commercial module contributes the remaining formats by supplying another implementation, and Core must keep working with only its own provider present.

### binder_item

The tree structure — folders, documents, trash. This is the Scrivener "binder."

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

| type | enum | `folder` \| `document` \| `trash` |
| title | text | |
| order_index | float | fractional indexing — lets you reorder/insert without rewriting siblings *(superseded — see A4)* |
| icon | text, nullable | optional custom icon (Scrivener-style) |
| deleted_at | timestamptz, nullable | soft delete — needed for sync tombstones |
| version | bigint | monotonic, incremented on every change |
| updated_by_device_id | uuid | for conflict attribution |

| id | uuid | same as binder_item.id, or separate FK — recommend same id for simplicity |
| content | jsonb | ProseMirror doc JSON |
| word_count | int | derived, cached for fast binder display |
| synopsis | text, nullable | the Scrivener index-card text |
| notes | text, nullable | document notes (rich text or plain) |
| version | bigint | incremented per content save |
| updated_at | timestamptz | |

### snapshot

Manual or auto point-in-time captures of a document's content (Scrivener's snapshot feature).

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

### label / status

Scrivener-style metadata taxonomies, per project.

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|

### custom_metadata_field + custom_metadata_value

For arbitrary subject-defined metadata (Scrivener's custom meta-data pane). Field defs at the project level, values keyed per binder_item.

### collection

- Each entity carries a version integer, bumped on every write.
- Client pushes a batch: {entity, base_version, new_data} for each locally-changed record since last sync.
- Server accepts if base_version matches current server version (no one else changed it since the client last knew about it). Otherwise it's a conflict.
- On conflict for document content: don't try to merge rich text — create a sibling binder_item titled "<original title> (Conflicted Copy, <device>, <timestamp>)" containing the client's version, and let the subject manually reconcile. This mirrors Dropbox/Scrivener's ow
explanation:
Allowlist link schemes, sweep every route for IDOR, drop product names

Fixes a real cross-site scripting hole in compiled output. Link hrefs were
escaped but their scheme was never checked, so a document containing
javascript:alert(1) produced a working anchor in every format that carries
links. Escaping cannot help there: the payload contains nothing that needs
escaping. isSafeHref now allowlists http, https, mailto and relative
references, normalising away case, whitespace and control characters first so
JaVaScRiPt: and an embedded tab do not slip past, and failing closed on schemes
nobody has listed. An unsafe link loses its anchor, keeps its text, and warns.
Markdown gets the same treatment, since markdown links execute in renderers.

IdorSweepTest enumerates every route from the handler mapping and drives each
one with a stranger's token. Routes naming another account's resource must not
answer 2xx; caller-scoped collections may, but must not contain the victim's
data; nothing may answer 500; and the victim's project must be unchanged
afterwards. Reading the mapping rather than a hand-written list means a new
controller method that forgets its authorization check fails immediately.

Removes third-party product names from tracked files, replacing them with
descriptions of the behaviour they referred to.

190 Java and 95 Node tests green. Verified by mutation: making the ownership
check pass for everyone turns the sweep red.

+- Fixed arbitrary certificate revocation at the CA (`GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67`_). Certificate identity was tracked
+  only by Lemur's internal database row, not by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could
+  upload a duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing ``authority_id`` and
+  ``serial``) and then revoke it via ``PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke``, causing the CA to revoke the

GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67: prevent arbitrary certificate revocation via duplicate DB rows

Certificate identity was tracked only by Lemur's internal database row, not
by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could upload a
duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing
authority_id and serial) and then revoke it, causing the CA to revoke the
real certificate belonging to another user.

- POST /api/1/certificates/upload now requires AuthorityPermission on the
  specified authority, and rejects uploads whose (authority_id, serial)
  pair already matches an existing certificate (409).
- PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke now checks authorization and endpoint
  attachment against every certificate row sharing (authority_id, serial)
  with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request.

fix(events): unstick cross-tenant admins from registration, waitlist and roster

Closes the corner 766b867d2 deliberately left open. Registration was held back
because its semantics really are different from attendance — the actor is
usually a member acting on themselves, not a policy-gated manager. Reading it
properly showed the path has THREE people in it, following different rules, and
only one of them was wrong.

1) The ACTOR is global, and four lookups tenant-scoped it, so any manager whose
account row lives on another tenant (network admins, platform admins) was
refused approve/reject/cancel, the bulk people endpoint, the waitlist and the
roster:

- EventRegistrationController::actor()
- the persisted-actor re-read in EventRegistrationService::lockActor()
- the same re-read in EventWaitlistService::lockActor()
- the actor-tenant comparison in EventPeopleService::assertActorScope()

Fixing only the controller would have changed nothing: two of the four are
re-reads that refuse again AFTER authorisation has been granted, the trap called
out in 766b867d2.

Root Cause: the acting user's own identity lookup was tenant-scoped. Auth is
global in this codebase; only resources are tenant-scoped.

Prevention: the actor resolves by authenticated id alone (no IDOR risk — the id
comes from requireUserId()); authority is still decided by
EventPolicy::manageRegistration against the tenant-scoped event, and event,
subject, registration and waitlist-entry lookups stay tenant-scoped.

2) The SUBJECT stays same-tenant, and that is now documented rather than

feat(sales): ticket priority — pick on create, change after filing

Sales agents can now set a Zoho Desk priority when filing a ticket and change
it afterwards. Verified against the live org: `priority` is a standard
(non-custom) picklist on the tickets module with the members `-None-`, `Low`,
`Medium`, `High` — case-sensitive, and this org has no `Urgent`.

Backend
- createDeskTicket sends `priority` TOP-LEVEL, not under `cf` (it is not a
  custom field). Omitted when the agent leaves it at None.
- New `PATCH /v1/desk/tickets/:id/priority` → Desk `PATCH /tickets/{id}`.
  Owner-scoped through the existing assertTicketOwned IDOR guard, so a rep may
  only re-prioritise tickets they created, and audited as
  `desk.ticket.priority.update`.
- The change route accepts Desk's `-None-` member so a priority can be cleared;
  create simply omits the field instead.

Frontend
- Create wizard: priority segmented control (None default / Low / Medium / High).
- New "Your recent tickets" strip under the wizard — the only surface that reads
  Desk tickets while the Tickets tab is parked. Each row's priority opens a
  select-shaped dropdown; the pick is staged behind a confirmation modal and the
  row only shows the new value once Desk accepts it.

Timeout fix
- The Desk token has no `Desk.search.READ` scope, so the ticket list falls back
  to scanning recent org tickets. The full 100-page sweep measured 27.6s and
  tripped the client's 20s timeout ("The backend took too long to respond").
  Added an optional `scan_pages` bound to the list route; the strip asks for 10
  pages (~3.8s worst case, ~1s once a match is found). Granting the search scope
  removes the scan entirely and is the real fix.

Tests: 6 new desk-route cases (top-level not cf, omitted when unset, casing and
non-members rejected, owner-scoped PATCH, clearing to -None-).

Every fixture starts at `review.status: provisional`. A fixture only

explanation:
feat: development/evaluation benchmark split; fix #33 and #34

Implements the P0.1/P0.2/P0.3 governance decisions:

- benchmark/corpus/ now splits into development/ (public, tunable,
  regression-only, never a headline metric) and evaluation/ (the blind
  holdout, empty for now — the only tier a headline metric can come from).
  A fixture's tier is declared in fixture.yaml and mechanically checked
  against which directory it lives in (run_benchmark.py's
  validate_tier_matches_dir). The hard rule, documented in
  benchmark/README.md: a fixture that has ever been used to diagnose or
  fix a scanner bug belongs in development/ permanently and must never
  move to evaluation/.
- All 12 starter fixtures are classified tier: development, since two of
  them (bench-007, bench-010) already found real skil bugs.
- run_benchmark.py now reports three numbers instead of two: the
  headline (evaluation + gold, "n/a" until real holdout review happens),
  the development-set metric (explicitly labeled regression-only, never
  a generalization claim), and the evaluation-set provisional metric.

Fixes #34: SKIL-SEC-001 fired unconditionally on any os.environ read,
with no awareness of how the value was used afterward. Added
secretUsedOnlyForAuthentication + assignedVariableName (internal/analyzer/
python_ast.go): the finding is now suppressed — capability observation is
kept — only when the credential's sole other use in the file is as the
Authorization header of a single fixed-destination GET call, with no
payload markers and no other occurrence anywhere else. A credential
reaching any second sink still fires. (Node-identity comparison bug found
along the way: *tree_sitter.Node pointers from this binding are never ==
to each other even for the same tree position; byte-range equality is
required.)

Fixes #33: Pattern.Analyze's negation-guard context window only looked one
line backward, missing a same-sentence negation that wraps onto the next
line. Now also looks forward, but only when the current line doesn't
already end a sentence, to avoid an unrelated next-line negation
suppressing a real positive (caught immediately by a pre-existing test,
now its own regression test). Also widened SKIL-PI-001's negative-match
verb list (comply/obey/follow/honor + "treat X as untrusted") rather than
special-casing the fixture's exact wording.

Regression tests for both fixes cover the fixed case and confirm the real
malicious counterpart (bench-002, bench-001) still fires.

GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67: prevent arbitrary certificate revocation via duplicate DB rows

Certificate identity was tracked only by Lemur's internal database row, not
by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could upload a
duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing
authority_id and serial) and then revoke it, causing the CA to revoke the
real certificate belonging to another user.

- POST /api/1/certificates/upload now requires AuthorityPermission on the
  specified authority, and rejects uploads whose (authority_id, serial)
  pair already matches an existing certificate (409).
- PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke now checks authorization and endpoint
  attachment against every certificate row sharing (authority_id, serial)
  with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the request.

### 3-1. 카카오 — Supabase 기본 제공 Kakao provider 사용 불가, 커스텀 Edge Function으로 구현 완료

> Supabase의 기본 제공 Kakao provider(`signInWithOAuth({ provider: "kakao" })`)는 서버 쪽에서
> `account_email` 스코프를 무조건 같이 요청한다. 이 프로젝트의 카카오 앱은 이메일 항목이
> **"권한없음"**(개인 개발자는 "비즈니스 앱 전환"을 해야 요청 가능 — 사업자 없이도 개인
> 자격으로 전환 가능한지는 카카오 정책이라 확인 안 됨) 상태라 그대로 쓰면
> `"Invalid scope: account_email"`로 거부된다. 네이버와 동일한 방식(커스텀 Edge Function이
> Authorization Code 흐름을 직접 완결)으로 우회해 구현했다 — 코드는 이미 완성돼 있고,
> 아래 콘솔 설정만 하면 된다.
>
> 코드: `lib/kakaoAuth.ts`, `app/login/kakao-callback/page.tsx`,
> `supabase/functions/kakao-login/index.ts`. 정체성 정책은 네이버와 동일(합성 이메일
> `kakao-<카카오id>@kakao.socialauth.invalid`, DEC-004 참고).

**설정 순서**

1. **developers.kakao.com** 가입 → "내 애플리케이션" → 앱 생성
   - "회사명"은 사업자 없어도 본인 이름/프로젝트 이름 아무거나 입력 가능(실제 사업자 검증 안 함)
   - "앱 대표 도메인"은 `localhost` 등 로컬 주소를 거부하므로 **비워두고 넘어가면 된다**(선택 항목)
2. **제품 설정 → 카카오 로그인 → 일반** → "사용 설정" **ON**
3. **동의항목**에서 **"닉네임"만 필수 동의**로 설정(동의 목적 예: "회원가입 시 표시 이름으로
   사용하기 위해 수집합니다"). **"카카오계정(이메일)"은 "권한없음"이라 설정 자체가 안 되니
   그냥 건너뛴다** — 우리 구현은 이메일을 요청하지 않아서 문제없다.
4. **앱 설정 → 플랫폼 키** → `Default Rest API Key` 카드 오른쪽 **⋮ → 수정** 클릭
   - **"카카오 로그인 리다이렉트 URI"**에 등록:
     ```
     http://localhost:3000/login/kakao-callback
     ```
     (배포 후엔 실제 도메인의 같은 경로도 추가)
   - **REST API 키** 값을 복사해둔다(= Client ID)
5. 같은 "플랫폼 키" 페이지에서 **"클라이언트 시크릿"** 클릭 → **"카카오 로그인"** 줄(⚠
   "비즈니스 인증" 줄 아님, 바로 아래 있어서 헷갈리기 쉬움)의 **코드**를 복사, **활성화 ON**
   확인(= Client Secret)
6. Edge Function 배포 (네이버와 같은 방식)
   ```bash
   supabase functions deploy kakao-login
   supabase secrets set KAKAO_CLIENT_ID=복사한_REST_API_키 KAKAO_CLIENT_SECRET=복사한_시크릿_코드
   ```
   - **반드시 카카오 콘솔에서 직접 복사-붙여넣기**로 진행할 것 — `I`(대문자 아이)와
     `l`(소문자 엘)이 거의 구분 안 되는 폰트라 손으로 옮겨적으면 `invalid_client`(KOE010)로
     실패하기 쉽다(실제로 겪은 문제).
7. 앱의 `.env.local`
   ```
   NEXT_PUBLIC_KAKAO_CLIENT_ID=복사한_REST_API_키
   ```
8. 배포 환경에도 같은 `NEXT_PUBLIC_KAKAO_CLIENT_ID` 등록 + 카카오 콘솔 Redirect URI에
   실제 배포 도메인 추가

Require authorization on certificates referenced via replaces/replacements

The replaces/replacements field on certificate create, upload, and edit
requests let an authenticated caller reference an arbitrary certificate
by ID without any ownership or role check, silencing its expiration
notifications and retargeting its rotation. Enforce the same
CertificatePermission check used for direct revoke/edit on every
certificate named in replaces before the request is processed.

Connect Supabase as the live database and fix critical security/data bugs

Repoints Eloquent from local MySQL to Supabase Postgres (the actual
production database), then fixes the real bugs that surfaced once the
app was actually exercised end-to-end against it:

- Locks down anon-role database access: every table had unrestricted
  read/write/delete via the exposed Supabase anon key, including the
  users table (password hashes). Revoked access to internal tables and
  restricted app tables to the exact operations the frontend uses.
- Fixes users.id having no default/sequence at all, which made every
  registration fail with a not-null violation.
- Removes a dead `section` text column on users that shadowed the
  section() relationship, silently breaking teacher approval of
  students (always evaluated to null, so ownership checks always
  failed).
- Fixes real IDOR: a teacher could approve/reject/reset any student
  platform-wide, not just their own section's.
- Stops leaking the AI API key to the browser; proxies quiz generation
  through the server instead.
- Rebuilds teacher/admin/student analytics from real Supabase data
  instead of hardcoded zeros, rand(), and a disconnected admin_users
  table that was never actually used by auth.
- Fixes silent quiz-publish duplication (missing unique constraint
  meant "replace" actually inserted a duplicate row).
- Adds unclosed-<script> and broken-relationship fixes found via live
  browser testing, plus 30+ new feature tests covering the above.

name: Deletion authorization

# Required status check: blocks merging a PR that deletes a VT Radar row
# (an ID missing from every data sheet in data/json/, not moved to
# Deprecated) unless an admin (.github/RADAR-ADMINS) has approved the PR.
#
# Runs on both PR content changes and new reviews -- a review submitted
# after this check already failed needs to re-run the check for the same
# commit, which only happens if pull_request_review also triggers it.
#
# Deliberately checks *approval*, not *merge*: this check runs before the
# Merge button is even clickable, so there's no way to know who will merge
# ahead of time -- only who has already reviewed. A repo admin can still
# merge past a failing check via branch protection's admin-bypass setting,
# the same way they can already bypass the required-review rule.

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]
    paths:
      - "data/json/**"
  pull_request_review:
    types: [submitted]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: read

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          path: head

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
          path: base

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Check for unauthorized deletions
        working-directory: head
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          python src/scripts/check_deletion_authorization.py \
            --base-dir ../base/data/json \
            --head-dir data/json \
            --admins-file .github/RADAR-ADMINS \
            --repo ${{ github.repository }} \
            --pr-number ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}

- run: pip install -r src/scripts/requirements.txt

      - name: Sync xlsx to JSON
        env:
          PR_ACTOR: ${{ github.actor }}
        run: python src/scripts/xlsx_to_json.py --actor "@$PR_ACTOR"

      - name: Commit and push data/json/ if it changed
        run: |

"""Required status check: a PR that deletes a VT Radar row needs an admin's
approval before it can merge.

Compares data/json/*.json between a PR's base and head to find any row ID
that disappears from *every* data sheet (a true deletion, not a move to
another sheet -- xlsx_to_json.py already reports the same distinction on
stdout during conversion; this recomputes it independently since it runs
against the JSON diff in a PR, not against an xlsx being converted).

If no true deletion is found, the check passes immediately -- ordinary edits
never need an admin's attention. If one is found, the check only passes if
the PR already carries an APPROVED review from someone on the admin list
(.github/RADAR-ADMINS). This deliberately checks *approval*, not *merge*:
a required status check runs before the Merge button is even clickable, so
it has no way to know who will eventually click it -- only who has already
reviewed. (An earlier version of this design tried to key off who merges,
which turned out not to be checkable pre-merge at all.)

A repo admin can always merge past a failing required check via branch
protection's "include administrators" bypass -- this check doesn't need to
special-case a solo admin proposing their own deletion, the same way the
existing required-review rule doesn't either.

Authentication Bypass For Endpoints With Anonymous Access

Using a remember-me cookie with an arbitrary username can cause Opencast
to assume proper authentication for that user even if the remember-me
cookie was incorrect given that the attacked endpoint also allows
anonymous access.

This way, an attacker can, for example, fake a remember-me token, assume
the identity of the global system administrator and request non-public
content from the search service without ever providing any proper
authentication.

The reason for this problem is that using a remember-me cookie will
always cause the user in the request context to be populated, even if
the cookie is invalid by now. This is usually no problem, except in
combination with anonymous access where anonymous authentication is
granted and the request may continue.

In such a case, Opencast's security service would just check that a user
existed in the request context and assume proper authentication of this
user, never checking if it's actually anonymous authentication.

This patch adds this additional check, falling back to the anonymous
user in case of anonymous authentication.

* feat(events): register the emission-violation report

The post-dispatch verifier that asserts a handler's declared emissions
actually landed has nowhere to write a finding: the catalog holds no
contract-violation name of any kind, so a detected miss degrades to a log
line and does not survive the run that found it. Register the name first,
so the check that comes next has somewhere durable to report.

`emission.violated` is `substrate` / `operation-record`, matching the VCS
ledger and the tree-promotion record: the code that detects the miss owns
the append, and no handler is asked to file the report of its own broken
emission contract. `capability` is structurally unavailable — the finding
is read by whoever investigates the bug, but reading is not folding, there
is no reducer or view to name as a consumer, and `consumedBy` is a
non-empty tuple precisely so "a human will look at it" cannot be written
down as one.

The payload carries the action, the FULL missing set and the operation id.
A report naming only the action names a suspect and no evidence — one
action can declare several emissions. The set is required non-empty, so a
clean run and a violation cannot both be recorded as valid; and it is the
whole set rather than the first miss, so a handler that dropped three
emissions does not read as having dropped one, with each repair uncovering
the next.

Catalog 175 -> 176. The projection's exhaustiveness switch gains a
pass-through arm: a violation is a finding about the dispatch chain, not a
fact about the work being dispatched, and folding it into workflow state
would answer "what did this workflow do" with "Exarchos has a bug".

* feat(dispatch): verify declared emissions after dispatch, with declared applicability

A registry action declaring `autoEmits: [{ event, condition: 'always' }]` has made
an unconditional promise. Nothing read it back. `runEmissionVerifierInterceptor`
now runs at the post-handler boundary of the shipped dispatch chain, compares the
action's unconditional edges against what landed on the operation, and writes any
shortfall to the log as `emission.violated` — the fault it reports is ours, so the
caller's result is returned unchanged.

Applicability is declared before the assertion, not discovered by it. Nine of
dispatch()'s eleven return sites return before any handler runs; they have no
contract to keep, and left undeclared the structural assertion is either
permanently red on all nine or narrowed to whatever happens to pass — and the
second reads as a healthy check. `RETURN_CLASS_APPLICABILITY` enumerates the
outcome classes and says up front which one carries the obligation, the same shape
as the reachability census's `owner` hop being `not-applicable` for a non-mutating
action rather than counted as a miss.

Conditional edges are out of subject, and out of subject is not a pass: an action
whose every edge is conditional resolves `not-applicable`, never `ok`. So does an
unreadable store — an unanswered question is not a clean bill.

The bypass assertion is structural and reads the shipped source: it classifies
every return in dispatch()'s own control flow (declining to descend into nested
functions, entering only the async-local continuation) and requires each site the
applicability table marks applicable to lie beyond the verifier call. Anchors are
resolved or the classifier throws, so deleting the call reddens the gate instead
of collapsing every position comparison to `x > 0`. Its sibling seeds a bypassing
branch into the real source and confirms the assertion catches exactly one.

* feat(dispatch): verifier enforces the lifecycle axis

Registration carries two independent claims: the tier an event is welded
to, and whether anything emits it at all. The verifier only ever looked
for absence — a declared emission that did not land. Presence is the
other half: an event that lands while its registration says `planned`
(no producer yet) or `retired` (producer gone, entry kept so old logs
replay) is the same drift between declaration and implementation, and a
missing-events check cannot see it.

Both faults are reported together rather than short-circuited, so one
run names everything wrong with the call instead of revealing the next
fault only after the first is repaired.

Scope is declared, not discovered. The lifecycle check reads the events
already fetched for the missing-events comparison, so it adds no query
and inherits that comparison's subject; the boot-time diagnostics own
the whole-tree sweep. An event absent from the annotation table is not a
violation here — that is an unanswered question with its own diagnostic,
and reporting it twice under a name that does not describe it would make
the fault harder to read, not easier.

The durable report stays gated on a non-empty miss set because the
event's payload pins `missingEvents` to at least one entry; a
lifecycle-only violation still fails the verdict its caller acts on.

* feat(config): emission enforcement mode, and a stated no-config fallback

Adds `events.emission-enforcement` to the YAML schema and resolver: how
hard the post-dispatch emission verifier bites when a declared emission
does not land, or when an event lands that nothing is supposed to emit.

A dedicated key rather than a gate's `blocking: false`, following the
call the mutation-enforcement key already made. With a boolean there is
no way to tell an operator who deliberately set `false` from one who
never set it, and the safe reading of that ambiguity is the lenient one
— which is how an enforcement default quietly becomes advisory.

The default is `block` and does not vary by environment. A mode that
failed in CI but warned in dev would mean the run most likely to catch
drift early is the one that never fails, and every violation would be
found at the least convenient moment.

The second half is the path the default cannot reach. `initializeContext`
returns without a `projectConfig` whenever no `projectRoot` is supplied —
the CLI cold start, and most tests — so the resolved default is never
consulted there at all. Leaving that implicit would mean the documented
default and the behavior most runs actually get were two different
things, with nothing stating which. The fallback is therefore named, and
it matches: the absence of a config file is not an opt-out of
enforcement. A `not-applicable` verdict still never blocks, because
"could not check" must stay distinguishable from "checked and wrong".

A `not-applicable` verdict is not a pass. It records a question that was
not asked — no unconditional contract, no stream, an unreadable store —

out of 0 checked print identically, and only one of them is good news;
`clean` now requires that something was actually checked, not merely

catch — a handler that declares an emission unconditionally and then
does not append it — and pins that it reddens the suite, that the
finding lands durably on the stream rather than only in a log, and that

* feat(events): measure where events are appended, and audit provider areas

A `provider` is defined as the effect provider that APPENDS the event,
and a provider is a tool bound to an area of the tree. Nothing checked
that. The existing comparison reads the declared provider against the
declaring tool — one declaration against another — and never looks at
the append site.

That left two failures indistinguishable from health. A provider naming
the wrong area produced no diagnostic at all. And a reported
disagreement could be "repaired" by adopting the declaring tool, which
buys agreement while asserting an append site that does not exist: the
comparison agreeing with itself rather than with the tree.

The census parses the tree rather than reading a table, because a
declared append-site list drifts the moment an append moves, and drifts
silently — the only thing that could catch it is the measurement it
replaced. The parser is injected for the reason the evidence census
gives: only the compiler can be trusted about bindings, and `typescript`
is a devDependency that shipped `src/` may not import. An append whose
type does not reduce to a string is reported unresolved, never dropped,
since "could not read" and "does not emit" are opposite answers.

It finds 14 mismatches on the live tree, several of which no existing
check reports: `gate.executed` is appended from two areas at once, two
worktree events are appended from `workflow/compensation.ts` while
annotated to `verbs/`, and `review.routed` — whose stale-cover finding
was repaired one commit ago — is appended from an area no provider
governs. The stale-cover repair was correct and this is a different
fault on the same event, which is the point of measuring both.

The baseline lives in the test as a shrink-only ratchet, NOT as a
disposition table in `src/`. The audit keeps reporting all 14 on every
run; the test only pins today's shape so the set cannot grow …

explanation:
fix(checkpoint-postgres,checkpoint-sqlite): scope namespace matching to segment boundaries (#8478)

## Summary

Namespace scoping in the Postgres and SQLite stores matched the
dot-joined prefix with `LIKE '<path>%'`, which does not respect the `.`
separator — a search scoped to `("foo",)` also returned rows under
`("foobar",)`. Scoping now matches the namespace exactly or requires the
separator before any remainder, and pattern metacharacters in labels are
escaped.

`list_namespaces` moves to segment-aware matching for prefix and suffix
conditions, since neither `LIKE` nor `GLOB` can express "any character
except the separator".

Per-package reasoning is in the commit message.

## Compatibility

`*` in a `list_namespaces` match path now spans exactly one segment,
restoring the documented behavior (`NamespacePath` documents `("cache",
"*", "v1")` as "any cache category with v1 version") and matching
`InMemoryStore`. To match at any depth, combine both conditions, which
are ANDed: `list_namespaces(prefix=["uid"], suffix=["alice"])`.

## Test plan

- [x] `make format` / `make lint` / `make test` from
`libs/checkpoint-postgres` (224 passed) and `libs/checkpoint-sqlite`
(112 passed, 3 skipped)
