fix: close the anchor-guard composition gaps (by Wren)

Round-8 review blockers from Lumen on #514. All four were composition
failures: each guard was individually correct and defeated by what ran
after it.

1. A supplied canonical UUID was being invalidated by slug ambiguity.
   Discovery exists to gate the SLUG fallback, not to veto an identity we
   already hold — with a UUID in hand every tier below is UUID-scoped and a
   duplicate slug cannot reach them. Ambiguity now refuses only when there
   is no canonical id.

2. Both anchor helpers could accept a row carrying sb_id=OTHER through the
   absent+slug fallback. A row that CARRIES an identity must match it
   canonically, always; only a null-sb row may use the slug, and only on a
   positive `absent`.

3. The findByUserAndAgent UUID option was never passed and was missing from
   ISessionRepository, so canonical A still reused sibling B. Both fixed.
   Ambiguous unthreaded work now skips general reuse entirely rather than
   falling back to the slug — it is not refused, since unthreaded work does
   not lease a studio, but it must not be silently attached to another
   identity's session either.

4. A failed explicit-studio authorization returned an ordinary `refused`
   tier, which is only inspected at the create boundary — while alias,
   threadKey, default-session and general reuse all run BEFORE it. A
   matching fallback therefore satisfied a request whose explicit anchor had
   just been rejected. Invalid explicit anchors are now fatal at the point of
   rejection, as is the ambiguity refusal, which the reuse rungs could
   otherwise slug-match past.

Tests: the guard regressions are rewritten to the pattern review asked for —
guard PLUS a plausible later fallback, rather than a guard with every later
rung mocked absent. Each now seeds alias/threadKey/general reuse with a
session the ladder would happily return, so the test fails if the guard
leaks instead of merely proving nothing was available.

150 session-service (was 145) + 8 routing-hold + 8 sender-context; full API
2409; typecheck at the known five-error baseline.

Mutation-checked: making the explicit-anchor refusal non-fatal, admitting an
sb_id-bearing row through the slug fallback, or letting ambiguity veto a
supplied UUID each turn exactly one test red.

The positive-case test is worth noting: its first version asserted only "does
not throw" and failed against the ORDINARY no-route refusal, which is correct
behaviour. It now supplies a UUID-scoped route-pattern studio and asserts the
session is created against it, so success distinguishes "reached the
UUID-scoped tiers" from "was not refused for some other reason".

Security audit hardening: CORS, rate limiting, DTO validation, httpOnly session cookie, upload content-sniffing

Implements the fixes from this session's full security audit (Sections
5-8 plus remaining Section 3/4 items) that weren't already applied live:

- CORS: replace origin:'*' with an explicit allowlist (APP_URL/
  FRONTEND_URL/localhost) in the production Nest bootstrap
  (apps/web/src/lib/backendPort.ts). The previous config also paired
  wildcard origin with credentials:true, an invalid combination per the
  Fetch spec.

- Rate limiting: add @Throttle overrides on auth endpoints (login/
  register/verify/resend/forgot-password/reset-password) and on the two
  AI-generation endpoints, tighter than the app-wide default limiter.

- Server-side validation: convert ~13 inline @Body() object-literal types
  across auth/engine/media/oauth/posts controllers into real
  class-validator DTO classes, closing a gap where NestJS's global
  ValidationPipe silently validated nothing for non-class body types.

- Session storage: move the auth JWT from localStorage (readable by any
  XSS for up to 30 days) to an httpOnly cookie. AuthController.login sets
  it; a new AuthController.logout clears it. JwtStrategy reads it via a
  hand-rolled cookie parser (no new dependency). The frontend now caches
  only a non-sensitive user snapshot (id/email/name/brandId/expiry) for
  synchronous UI checks; apiFetch, the upload flow, the SSE stream, and
  the three OAuth connect links all rely on the cookie traveling
  automatically instead of a client-readable token.

- File upload content-sniffing: verify uploaded bytes actually match
  their claimed MIME type (magic-byte checks for JPEG/PNG/GIF/WEBP/
  ISOBMFF/EBML) on both the multer path and the direct-to-Blob register
  path, on top of the existing allowlist checks.

- OAuth error handling: stop reflecting err.message into redirect query
  params (info-disclosure risk); log full errors server-side, show
  generic messages to the user. Remove partial-secret and raw-code
  logging in the Instagram token exchange.

Also includes earlier uncommitted work from this session: the OAuth
state-signature CSRF bypass fix, IDOR fixes (createPost media ownership,

* fix: bound process incarnation probes

Three synchronous probes — `sysctl` and `ps` on darwin, `wmic` on win32 —
passed no timeout, so a wedged child held the Node main thread with no
reachable abort. Nothing could interrupt it: every deadline mechanism here is
asynchronous and none of them preempt a synchronous `execFileSync`.

What this fixes and what it does not. A wedged probe now returns instead of
hanging forever. It does not make any caller's deadline enforceable —
`waitForAbsence` runs its whole synchronous sweep before computing a remaining
budget, and that sweep probes every recorded root rather than stopping at the
first failure — so worst-case observation latency is this bound times two
subprocesses times the root cap. Making deadlines hold there needs a
deadline-aware asynchronous probe, which is a larger change.

Safe because a timeout can only turn a would-be-successful observation into a
throw, and every call site's existing `catch` answers `null`. It cannot
fabricate a token, so no equality-gated authorization newly passes.

Deliberately not claimed: that `null` is uniformly "could not observe" to
every consumer. `probeCoordinator` collapses "no record" and "unobservable
process" into one `null` and `handoff-runner` reads that as no live
coordinator, so a transient timeout can now drop a live incumbent from
routing. Nor is every signal equality-gated — `observeContainment` authorizes
a group signal from an ESRCH-absent leader plus a live group. Both predate
this change; both are newly reachable through a transient condition, and both
are recorded rather than papered over.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: let a coordinator probe say it could not observe the pid

`probeCoordinator` answered `record | null`, and `null` meant two different
things: no discovery record at all, and a record whose pid this reader could
not observe. Its own comment said "nothing downstream may treat it as proof"
while the return type left no way to obey — `readLiveCoordinatorHealth` read
both as no incumbent and routed a contender to the current backend, and
`readVerifiedIncumbentFromDiscovery` read both as no verified incumbent.

#324 moved incarnation comparison to the signalling sites and gave liveness
three values for the same reason; this reader kept two. The instruction now
lives in the type: `live`, `absent`, `unobservable`. Only decisive absence
short-circuits. `unobservable` carries its record, because that record holds
the `bootToken` a contender needs to ask an incumbent to stand down, and
discarding it over an unanswered probe is what turns "could not observe" into
a false "nobody is there".

Observed with `observeProcessLiveness` rather than `probeProcessIncarnation`.
Liveness is the whole question here and the one this reader can answer alone —
it is a single `kill(pid, 0)`, where the incarnation probe forks two
subprocesses on darwin to build a token this function then discarded. That
also removes this path's exposure to the probe timeout added alongside it,
which is what made a false absence reachable from a transient condition rather
than only from an unsupported platform.

* fix: cache a standing fact again — the previous predicate asked the wrong question

The commit before this stopped caching a fabricated project source, which was
right, but keyed the decision on whether git had "answered at all" — the error
carrying a numeric `status`. Verified against Node: a non-zero exit carries
`status: 128`, a missing binary carries `code: 'ENOENT'` with `status: null`,
and a timeout carries `code: 'ETIMEDOUT'` with `status: null`. So the predicate
grouped a missing git binary with a wedged mount, and on any machine without git
nothing was ever cached — every provider operation and every KB tool call
re-spawned git, for the life of the daemon.

The question that decides caching is not "did the command answer" but "could
the answer differ next time". Only the timeout could: it describes one moment.
No repository, no remote, and no git binary are standing facts about the
environment and are cached like any other answer.

Pinned by tests, because this behaviour had none — which is why it could be
reversed silently while every gate stayed green. Three failure shapes, each
asserting whether the fallback is remembered, with the ENOENT case naming the
regression it exists to catch.

    """
    The permissions system provides a way to assign permissions to specific
    users and groups of users.

    The permission system is used by the Django admin site, but may also be
    useful in your own code. The Django admin site uses permissions as follows:

        - The "add" permission limits the user's ability to view the "add" form
          and add an object.
        - The "change" permission limits a user's ability to view the change
          list, view the "change" form and change an object.
        - The "delete" permission limits the ability to delete an object.
        - The "view" permission limits the ability to view an object.

    Permissions are set globally per type of object, not per specific object
    instance. It is possible to say "Mary may change news stories," but it's
    not currently possible to say "Mary may change news stories, but only the
    ones she created herself" or "Mary may only change news stories that have a
    certain status or publication date."

    The permissions listed above are automatically created for each model.

Scheduled/pending notifications is currently not supported due to the lack of a scheduler API.

To respond to notification after the application is terminated, your application should be registered as DBus activatable (see [DBusApplicationLaunching](https://wiki.gnome.org/HowDoI/DBusApplicationLaunching) for more information), and register action before activating the application. This is difficult to do in a plugin because plugins instantiate during application activation, so `getNotificationAppLaunchDetails` can't be implemented without changing the main user application.

## 📷 Screenshots

Before proceeding, please make sure you are using the latest version of the plugin. The reason for this is that since version 3.0.1+4, the amount of setup needed has been reduced. Previously, applications needed changes done to the `AndroidManifest.xml` file and there was a bit more setup needed for release builds. If for some reason, your application still needs to use an older version of the plugin then make use of the release tags to refer back to older versions of readme.

### Requesting permissions on Android 13 or higher

From Android 13 (API level 33) onwards, apps now have the ability to display a prompt where users can decide if they want to grant an app permission to show notifications. For further reading on this matter read https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/ui/notifiers/notification-permission. To support this applications need target their application to Android 13 or higher and the compile SDK version needs to be at least 33 (Android 13). For example, to target Android 13, update your app's `build.gradle` file to have a `targetSdkVersion` of `33`. Applications can then call the following code to request the permission where the `requestPermission` method is associated with the `AndroidFlutterLocalNotificationsPlugin` class (i.e. the Android implementation of the plugin)

Note that when a full-screen intent notification actually occurs (as opposed to a heads-up notification that the system may decide should occur), the plugin will act as though the user has tapped on a notification so handle those the same way (e.g. `onSelectNotification` callback) to display the appropriate page for your application.

fix(api): gate runner-KYC reads + close auth-recovery lockout & OTP email-flood

Three verified findings from the authz/abuse sweep:

1) Runner KYC read routes over-exposed (IDOR). GET /admin/runners/pending and
   /admin/runners/{userId}/documents sat under the bare 'admin' alias (any active
   admin) while their approve/reject siblings and the byte-stream route require
   canModerate. finance/support admins — who by design never see runner KYC —
   could read government-ID/selfie metadata and, for any un-migrated legacy row,
   a raw public-disk file_url. Gated both reads with admin.can:moderate
   (super_admin/admin/ops), matching the rest of the KYC surface. Same class as
   3891604, on the two read routes that sweep missed.

2) Account-recovery lockout (AUTHX-3 class). verify-otp and reset-password shared
   the credential-ONLY 'auth' limiter, so 5 junk requests for a victim's
   phone/email locked the legitimate user out of COMPLETING recovery for the
   window — from any IP. Added an 'auth-verify' limiter keyed on credential+IP
   (like 'login') and moved those two completion paths onto it; forgot-password
   stays on 'auth' so outbound reset-email bombing remains globally capped per
   credential.

3) send-otp email flood. The 'otp' limiter had only a per-recipient 3/hr bucket
   and no per-IP cap, so one source could rotate through unlimited distinct
   recipient addresses and fan out real verification emails (only the anon 20/min
   api cap applied → ~1200 emails/hr to arbitrary inboxes). Added a per-IP 30/hr
   aggregate bucket, mirroring the secondary cap 'auth'/'login' already carry.

Tests: finance/support 403 & ops 200 on the KYC reads; cross-IP recovery is not
locked out while single-IP stays capped; send-otp is capped across distinct
recipients per IP. 665 pass on SQLite and MySQL 8.

fix(reprice): P1 — split !userId (401) from ownership check (403) on POST /:requestId/reprice (#1913)

## Broken leg
The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Not authorized to reprice this booking' });
    }

Unauth callers ate a wasted bookingRequests SELECT before hitting a
MISLEADING 403 that suggested a permissions problem, not a
credentials problem. The audit agent classified this as "risky-cosmetic"
because it's a 403→401 client-behavior change; on inspection the reprice
client is always an authenticated logged-in customer, so a 401 only fires
for callers that shouldn't be reaching the endpoint at all.

## Fix (server-only, split into two clean checks)
1. Explicit 401 at the door — before the DB fetch — with an honest
   'Authentication required' message.
2. Ownership check no longer needs the !userId branch — reads cleanly
   as "owner OR verified admin".

Both branches unchanged behaviorally for legitimate callers.

## Test
server/tests/reprice-401-hygiene.regression.test.ts — 3 pins:
  ✓ returns 401 explicitly when there is no userId
  ✓ 401 guard sits BEFORE the first db.select() (no wasted round-trip)
  ✓ ownership check no longer folds !userId into the 403 branch

    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  3 passed (3)

## Dependency
None. Completes the auth-slippage sweep on booking-requests.ts —
prior sweep PRs #1904 (confirm), #1911 (7 POSTs), #1912 (GET). This
covers the last remaining router-mounted handler with the same shape.

## Risk
Very low. 401 replaces 403 for anon callers only (a case that already
denied). Legitimate customer + admin repricing unchanged.

## Do not merge
Per standing CEO directive.

## Phase 4 — Verify against the database (jdbc-platform tools)

Always follow this sequence — never skip a step:
`load_driver → connect → [tests] → get_usage_stats → disconnect`

1. **`load_driver`** if the driver isn't registered. Use CData short names (`saperp`,
   `salesforce`, `servicenow`, `googledrive`, …) — the server resolves the class automatically;
   otherwise pass `driver_class`. Verify `"status": "loaded"` and a non-null `driver_class`.
   If it fails, stop — there is nothing to test.

2. **`connect`** — **default to `read_only: true`** unless a test case explicitly requires a write
   path. Read-only blocks `execute_update` and write `execute_prepared`, protecting shared and
   production data. Only set `trust_all_certs` / `set_jvm_proxy` when the engineer asks.
   Reuse the returned `session_id` for every later call.

   **Proxy:** Just call `connect` normally with the user's connection string **exactly as given —

## Phase 5 — Report

- `get_test_report` — Markdown summary (pass/fail per criterion + session stats).
- `get_usage_stats` — include `total_queries`, `total_intercepted_calls`, `estimated_tokens_used`.
- `export_results` — write evidence rows to CSV when an attachment is wanted.
- Summarize the verdict: which acceptance criteria passed/failed, the concrete data behind each,
  and whether the fix from Phase 2 actually does what the ticket asked. If Phase 2 was skipped

| `compare_queries` | Diff two result sets (order-insensitive) | `session_id`, `sql_actual`, `sql_expected`, `criterion` |
| `record_check` | Record a non-SQL pass/fail check | `session_id`, `criterion`, `passed`, `detail`, `sql` |
| `export_results` | Export a SELECT to CSV (UTF-8, RFC4180) | `session_id`, `sql`, `file_path`, `max_rows` |
| `get_usage_stats` | Cumulative session stats | `session_id` |
| `get_test_report` | Markdown pass/fail report | `session_id` |
| `list_sessions` | List open sessions | _(none)_ |
| `disconnect` | Close the connection, delete the session's driver log | `session_id`, `keep_logfile` (default false). Response: `logfile_deleted`, `logfile_bytes_freed` |

---

## CData-specific knowledge

This project's `.claude/settings.json` allowlists every read/list/search tool on Jira
(`atlassian`), Azure DevOps (`azure-devops`), and `jdbc-platform` (`execute_query`,
`execute_prepared`, `get_metadata`, `compare_queries`, `assert_query`, `record_check`,
`export_results`, `list_sessions`, `get_usage_stats`, `get_test_report`), plus read-only shell
commands and the read-only `find-linked-prs.ps1` PR-discovery helper. Use these without asking —
just narrate what you're reading as you go through Phases 1–4. Two different write boundaries apply:
- **Database side** (`execute_update`, `load_driver`, `connect`/`disconnect`) — needed for testing;

### Session discipline

1. `load_driver` → `connect` → tests → `get_usage_stats` → `get_test_report` → `disconnect`. Always.
2. **SELECT-only runs connect with `read_only: true`.** Any CUD/batch/proc-with-side-effects run
   needs `read_only: false` — say so explicitly before connecting, and confirm with the engineer
   if the target is shared or production-like data.

- Compare.evaluate fell back to lexicographic comparison whenever either side
  was not numeric, and String.valueOf(null) is "null". A NULL column therefore
  satisfied ">= 100", because "null" sorts after "100". Null now fails every
  ordering comparator and participates only in eq/ne.
- The same function coerced both sides through BigDecimal, so "007" equalled
  "7" and "01234" equalled "1234" — silently passing assertions on zero-padded
  ids, zip codes and order numbers. Numeric comparison now requires an actual
  number on one side; two strings compare exactly. assert_query reports which
  rule decided the verdict, so a recorded check can be audited.
- Timestamps were formatted with no fractional-seconds field, so .123456789
  serialized as plain seconds. Millisecond-precision values compared equal to
  each other and to whole seconds, making that class of ticket untestable.
  Seconds are still always present (the PR #1 fix); fractions are appended only
  when non-zero.
- Types.FLOAT read through getFloat(). JDBC maps FLOAT to double — only REAL is
  single-precision — so every SQL FLOAT column was rounded to ~7 digits before
  any assertion saw it (1234567.891234567 -> 1234567.875).

Safety:

- read_only was enforced by only two of the eight tools that execute SQL. Two
  paths wrote freely: execute_query routes EXEC through Statement.execute(),
  and execute_java hands snippet code a live Connection. The guard now lives in
  the JDBC proxy layer, the only placement that can cover snippet code, and
  refuses anything not plainly a read with SQLState 25006. EXEC/CALL count as
  writes, since a procedure body is opaque. Documented as a guard, not a
  sandbox: getMetaData().getConnection() and unwrap() still escape it.
- The capture addon logged Authorization/Cookie verbatim, leaving live bearer
  tokens in the system temp directory (73 across two logs on this machine).
  They are now replaced by length + truncated SHA-256, which still identifies
  a token or a refresh. Bodies are capped (JDBC_MCP_MITM_MAX_BODY, 64 KB):
  uncapped bodies are what grew a single entry to 435 KB.
- export_results silently truncated whatever was at file_path; it now refuses
  without overwrite=true, and streams rows instead of materializing the whole
  result set, which was the documented path for "full exports".
- set_jvm_proxy set process-global proxy properties permanently, rerouting
  every later connection in the server. Now reference-counted and restored on
  disconnect or idle eviction.

Missing traces:

- executeBatch/addBatch were never intercepted, so the batch checklist ran with
  an empty intercepted_calls. Batch calls now report batch_size and summed row
  counts, with the first parameter set for prepared batches.
- prepareCall returned an unwrapped CallableStatement: no trace, and no
  ProxyResultSet, so the query deadline from PR #12 did not cover procedures.
- Failures returned a bare {"error": …} with no trace — precisely the calls
  being investigated, while the pass criteria are written in terms of
  intercepted_calls[*].error. compare_queries never returned traces at all and
  its second beginCall() wiped the first query's log.
- execute_java swapped the global System.out and restored it in a finally. A
  snippet outliving its timeout is only interrupted, so its next println landed
  on the real stdout — the JSON-RPC channel — and could break the session.
  Capture is now bound to the thread, not to a time window, and capped.

Also: get_metadata called getColumns once per table (an N+1 the checklists warn
about) and returned an uncapped bare array that could exhaust the caller's
context; it now makes one call, caps results, and reports counts. setNull was
traced as the type code 12 rather than null. Text truncation compared char
length against a byte budget. The connect probe's request appears in the capture
with no matching intercepted_call, so probe_sql is now reported.

Removed get_usage_stats: all five of its fields are already in the "Session
activity" section of get_test_report, and estimated tokens are on every
response's _meta.

fix(reprice): P1 — split !userId (401) from ownership check (403) on POST /:requestId/reprice (#1913)

## Broken leg
The reprice IDOR fix folded !userId into the ownership 403 branch:

    if (!userId || (br.ownerId !== userId && !isSuperAdminVerified(...))) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Not authorized to reprice this booking' });
    }

Unauth callers ate a wasted bookingRequests SELECT before hitting a
MISLEADING 403 that suggested a permissions problem, not a
credentials problem. The audit agent classified this as "risky-cosmetic"
because it's a 403→401 client-behavior change; on inspection the reprice
client is always an authenticated logged-in customer, so a 401 only fires
for callers that shouldn't be reaching the endpoint at all.

## Fix (server-only, split into two clean checks)
1. Explicit 401 at the door — before the DB fetch — with an honest
   'Authentication required' message.
2. Ownership check no longer needs the !userId branch — reads cleanly
   as "owner OR verified admin".

Both branches unchanged behaviorally for legitimate callers.

## Test
server/tests/reprice-401-hygiene.regression.test.ts — 3 pins:
  ✓ returns 401 explicitly when there is no userId
  ✓ 401 guard sits BEFORE the first db.select() (no wasted round-trip)
  ✓ ownership check no longer folds !userId into the 403 branch

    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  3 passed (3)

## Dependency
None. Completes the auth-slippage sweep on booking-requests.ts —
prior sweep PRs #1904 (confirm), #1911 (7 POSTs), #1912 (GET). This
covers the last remaining router-mounted handler with the same shape.

## Risk
Very low. 401 replaces 403 for anon callers only (a case that already
denied). Legitimate customer + admin repricing unchanged.

Per standing CEO directive.

feat(sales): ticket priority — pick on create, change after filing

Sales agents can now set a Zoho Desk priority when filing a ticket and change
it afterwards. Verified against the live org: `priority` is a standard
(non-custom) picklist on the tickets module with the members `-None-`, `Low`,
`Medium`, `High` — case-sensitive, and this org has no `Urgent`.

Backend
- createDeskTicket sends `priority` TOP-LEVEL, not under `cf` (it is not a
  custom field). Omitted when the agent leaves it at None.
- New `PATCH /v1/desk/tickets/:id/priority` → Desk `PATCH /tickets/{id}`.
  Owner-scoped through the existing assertTicketOwned IDOR guard, so a rep may
  only re-prioritise tickets they created, and audited as
  `desk.ticket.priority.update`.
- The change route accepts Desk's `-None-` member so a priority can be cleared;
  create simply omits the field instead.

Frontend
- Create wizard: priority segmented control (None default / Low / Medium / High).
- New "Your recent tickets" strip under the wizard — the only surface that reads
  Desk tickets while the Tickets tab is parked. Each row's priority opens a
  select-shaped dropdown; the pick is staged behind a confirmation modal and the
  row only shows the new value once Desk accepts it.

Timeout fix
- The Desk token has no `Desk.search.READ` scope, so the ticket list falls back
  to scanning recent org tickets. The full 100-page sweep measured 27.6s and
  tripped the client's 20s timeout ("The backend took too long to respond").
  Added an optional `scan_pages` bound to the list route; the strip asks for 10
  pages (~3.8s worst case, ~1s once a match is found). Granting the search scope
  removes the scan entirely and is the real fix.

Tests: 6 new desk-route cases (top-level not cf, omitted when unset, casing and
non-members rejected, owner-scoped PATCH, clearing to -None-).

feat(confidentiality): SL-030 egress redaction — restricted topic snapshots redacted at projection (FR-163, AC-114) (#295)

* feat(topics): Topic.IsRestricted + Restrict/Declassify (FR-163, DEC-063)

Domain increment of SL-030. A plain bool, not a level enum - C-AUTHZ-04 names
exactly one classification. Exposed to the shared kernel through a new
IConfidentialResource contract as a DECLARED PRIMITIVE, the same reason
AffectsAllStreams is one (ADR-0001/ADR-0021): a Confidentiality enum would live in
Topics.Domain and referencing it from the shared kernel inverts the dependency.

Restrict/Declassify are DELIBERATELY exempt from EnsureMutable. Every other field
setter refuses once a topic is Decided/Closed/Converted; inheriting that would
make an archived sensitive topic PERMANENTLY undeclassifiable, which is exactly
when a declassification request arrives. Classification is metadata ABOUT the
record, not a change TO the decided record, so the immutability EnsureMutable
protects (AC-034) is not what is at stake.

Both are idempotent by state: a second Restrict raises nothing, because it is not
a classification event and emitting one would put a change in the audit trail
that never happened.

Migration adds a bit column defaulting to false, so every existing row is
unrestricted and no backfill is needed. Unlike Streams/Systems/Tags (JSON columns)
this is queryable - which is what lets the visibility predicate compose in SQL.

* feat(topics): the read-side visibility predicate (FR-163, C-AUTHZ-04)

The READ half of the control. It has to be a query predicate rather than an
authorization requirement because no topic read path calls IAuthorizationService
at all - reads are a bare RequireAuthorization() group plus an empty AllowedRoles,
which GuestSurfaceMiddleware's own header records as the reason it had to exist.

ITopicVisibility resolves the caller's reach ONCE per request (scoped) and is
applied at:
- GetBacklog, which is one line covering FIVE product surfaces - backlog, kanban,
  agenda pool, role dashboards and reports all read through it. Applied before
  every filter and long before paging, so a Restricted topic is never counted into
  a total the caller may not see.
- GetTopicDetail, the IDOR path. It carried NO authorization before this - empty
  AllowedRoles, no EnsureAsync - so filtering the list while leaving it open would
  have hidden a topic from the backlog and handed it to anyone with the key. It
  returns null, which the endpoint renders as 404 NOT 403: a 403 confirms the
  topic exists, which is the fact being protected.
- TopicSearchProvider, composed BEFORE .Take. After it the control would shrink
  pages instead of filtering them - a search asking for 5 hits returning 3.

The predicate is SQL-translatable: IsRestricted is a plain bit column (unlike
streams/systems/tags, which are JSON and filter in memory) and the grant set is a
materialised array so Contains becomes an IN clause.

Existing suites get a permissive stub with a comment saying why: they assert
backlog filtering, detail mapping and search-engine behaviour, and a restrictive
scope would silently change what each of them measures.

⚠ Nothing here yet PROVES the narrowing - every stub is permissive and the suite
is green either way. The tests that force the refusal come next.

When an edge/join re-projects a field through its own AQL::FIELDS,
authorizeTargetFields() (the T6 guard) re-applies the target model's
Field::REQUIRES so a masked field cannot be re-exposed through the
relation. That inheritance was absolute — a relation could never declare
that, in its own context, another permission suffices.

Field::SELF_REQUIRES lifts exactly that, and only that: a field refused
by the target model is kept when it declares SELF_REQUIRES and the
authorizer grants at least one of its subjects (logical OR). It is read
only by authorizeTargetFields(); first-level model reads never pass
through that helper, so the T6 guard stays intact everywhere else.

Affirmative grant only: the subjects are normalized to a non-empty list
of strings before the check, so an empty/malformed SELF_REQUIRES cannot
borrow isAuthorized()'s "no subject -> allowed" fail-open and silently
re-open the hole T6 closes. Backward compatible: with no SELF_REQUIRES
the behaviour is byte-for-byte the former gate; fail-open unchanged.

Tests: 5 new AuthorizeTargetFieldsTest cases. FR/EN wiki
edges-joins-projection.md gains an "Overriding the target gate for this
relation" section. CHANGELOG updated.

fix: Do not run sensible-pager as root if using sudo/pkexec

The apport-cli supports view a crash. These features invoke the default
pager, which is likely to be less, other functions may apply.

It can be used to break out from restricted environments by spawning an
interactive system shell. If the binary is allowed to run as superuser
by sudo, it does not drop the elevated privileges and may be used to
access the file system, escalate or maintain privileged access.

apport-cli should normally not be called with sudo or pkexec. In case it
is called via sudo or pkexec execute `sensible-pager` as the original
user to avoid privilege elevation.

Proof of concept:

```
$ sudo apport-cli -c /var/crash/xxx.crash
[...]
Please choose (S/E/V/K/I/C): v
!id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
!done  (press RETURN)
```

1.9.3 - `unreleased`
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
- Fixed arbitrary certificate revocation at the CA (`GHSA-pxmc-2ffp-8j67`_). Certificate identity was tracked
  only by Lemur's internal database row, not by the actual CA-side certificate. Any authenticated user could
  upload a duplicate record for a certificate they didn't own (matching an existing ``authority_id`` and
  ``serial``) and then revoke it via ``PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke``, causing the CA to revoke the
  real certificate belonging to another user. ``POST /api/1/certificates/upload`` now requires
  ``AuthorityPermission`` on the specified authority, and rejects uploads whose ``(authority_id, serial)``
  pair already matches an existing certificate with a ``409`` response. ``PUT /api/1/certificates/<id>/revoke``
  now also checks authorization and endpoint attachment against every certificate row sharing
  ``(authority_id, serial)`` with the one being revoked, not just the row named in the clientRequest, closing the
  gap for any duplicate rows that already exist.

`adr-2026-08-13` chose versioned typed finding identities (rubric + concernKind + anchor
references, hashed) but deliberately left each rubric's reference schema to be "carefully
designed." In practice that design happened incrementally in BUILD: successive
`build_review` laps of feature #1611 found each not-yet-canonical anchor field, and the
remediation planner authored a new reference grammar per lap — plan-task id grammar,
tautology test selectors (`rem-rootcause-7`), and finally a line-coordinate rootCause
hunk locus `path@oldStart,oldCount:newStart,newCount` (`rem-rootcause-9/10`, commit
`d8fa79150`) — 21 appended tasks against an 18-task plan, with no operator checkpoint
(intake #1695). The operator rejected and reverted the line-coordinate locus.

Forces:

- **Identity must survive wording drift** (the #1611 defect) — references, never prose.
- **Identity must survive rebases.** The sibling feature
  `rubric-cache-identity-is-sha-anchored-so-a-rebase-` (plan 2026-08-15) already ruled
  the same way for the rubric cache: content-only identity, because SHA- and
  coordinate-anchored identity breaks on every rebase that leaves content unchanged.
  Line-coordinate loci re-import exactly that fragility into finding identity: a clean
  rebase renumbers hunks, drifting every open finding's id and detaching accepted
  dispositions — recreating #1611 through the mechanism built to fix it.
- **The schema must be closed class-level.** A field-by-field schema invites the
  observed failure: each unspecified field becomes a future finding and an unapproved
  grammar. The vocabulary ADR (`adr-2026-08-16`) already established the pattern:
  closed, corpus-validated sets, bound by an integrity check.
- **Dispositions suppress findings**, so identity must not over-match: an identity that
  survives a *content* change would let an accepted disposition silently swallow a
  materially different defect at the same location.

## Options Considered

### Option A: Enumerated per-field canonical grammars (status-quo trajectory)

Each anchor field gets a bespoke validated string grammar (path refs, task-id grammar,
test-selector strings, coordinate loci), added as rubrics discover them.

- **Pros:** Fully mechanical; each grammar is precise; incremental delivery.
- **Cons:** The schema is open-ended by construction — the lap-by-lap enumeration and
  unapproved grammar authoring already observed; coordinate-bearing grammars are
  rebase-fragile; every new grammar is an identity-semantics change that invalidates
  existing dispositions.

### Option B: Content-anchored references (closed three-kind schema)

Every anchor reference is exactly one of three canonical kinds, uniform across rubrics;
no other reference kind may be introduced without superseding this ADR.

- **Pros:** Class-level and closed — no future field can demand a new grammar without an
  operator-approved supersession; rebase-stable (content survives a clean rebase;
  coordinates do not); content change ⇒ new identity, which is the correct fail-closed
  narrowness for dispositions; symmetric with the cache's approved content-only identity.
- **Cons:** Content hashes are opaque in reports (mitigated: the canonical payload
  retains the human-readable display string alongside the hash); a conflict-resolved
  rebase that edits hunk

Hash token before storing it in Swift

Swauth uses token value as object name. Object names are logged in proxy
and object servers. Anybody with access to proxy/object server logs can
see token values. Attacker can use this token to access user's data in
Swift store. Instead of token, hashed token (with HASH_PATH_PREFIX and
HASH_PATH_SUFFIX) is used as object name now.

fix: require message authorship for standard-channel message edit and delete (#27197)

The channel message update and delete handlers enforced authorship only on group and dm channels. On standard channels the else branch accepted any caller holding write access on the channel, so a member who could post could also edit or delete messages authored by other members. Because the update form binds content, data and meta, and the model layer never touches message.user_id, an edited message kept the original author's attribution, so another member's message could be rewritten under their name.

Write access on a channel is the capability to post, not a moderation capability, and the frontend gates the edit and delete controls on authorship (message.user_id === user.id, or admin) for every channel type. The group and dm branch already encodes this with an explicit authorship check. Apply the same rule to the standard branch: the caller must hold write access on the channel and be the message author, unless they are an admin. Pinning is unchanged, since it is exposed to every member by design.

Fix issues found auditing the codebase, and add CI (#4)

* Fix issues found auditing the codebase

Native core (native/sslocal-ffi):

* `sslocal_last_error` handed out a pointer into the mutex-guarded
  `LAST_ERROR` slot and released the lock before returning, so a
  concurrent `set_last_error` — the core's own tasks record errors —
  could free the buffer while the caller was reading it. The message is
  moved into a slot of its own first; the pointer now stays valid until
  the next `sslocal_last_error` call.
* `sslocal_start_tun_fd` dups the tun descriptor. The tun device closes
  the fd it was given when the runtime is torn down (in the background),
  while `VpnConnection.destroy()` closes the app's; sharing one number
  risked the second close landing on an unrelated descriptor.
* The plugin forwarder's accept loop `continue`d on every error, turning
  a dead listener into a CPU-burning spin. Per-connection failures now
  retry after a back-off, anything else stops the loop.
* `cargo clippy` failed to compile (`not_unsafe_ptr_arg_deref` on
  `sslocal_set_stat_address`); C-string arguments go through one shared
  helper. `cargo fmt` is clean again.
* Unit tests that touch the process-wide state serialize on a lock
  instead of racing each other.
* `net_helper` prints usage instead of panicking on a missing argument.

App (entry/src/main/ets):

* Updating an existing subscription always failed: `SubscriptionStore`
  returned `JSON.parse` output cast to `Subscription`, so `ensureId()`
  was missing and `upsert` threw. Added `fromJson`, mirroring
  `ProfileStore`.
* `JsonStore.remove` called the async `fs.unlink`, whose rejection
  escaped the surrounding try as an unhandled rejection — which
  `TrafficStatsStore.clear` triggers on every VPN start.
* The VPN ability retained every flow-stat connection forever. The core
  opens a new one per 500 ms sample, so the list grew by two entries a
  second for the life of the tunnel; connections are dropped on close.
* Editing a subscription-owned profile dropped its `subscriptionId`, so
  the next subscription update re-added it as a duplicate.
* `Index` never cleared its stats poll timer, which outlived the page.
* `Profile.parseUrl` let a malformed percent escape throw out of the
  parser; in a subscription body one bad entry took the rest with it.
* Store failures in click handlers, a rejected VPN stop, and a
  permission-gated `updateVpnAuthorizedState` no longer surface as
  unhandled rejections.
* The stat endpoint builds a fresh server per port attempt and closes
  the ones that failed to bind.

Scripts:

* `run-tun-e2e-docker.sh` and `build-ohos.sh` expanded empty arrays
  under `set -u`, which aborts on the bash 3.2 that macOS ships — the
  host those scripts exist for. The docker runner also reports a
  missing iproute2 instead of failing with `ip: command not found`.
* `test-e2e-host.sh` numbered its first step 1/2 of 3.
* The on-device e2e's marker URL is a documented constant, not an
  address buried mid-test.

Verified: 30 unit + 2 e2e Rust tests, the OHOS cross-compile check, the
tun packet-routing e2e in Docker, 15 ArkTS unit tests, and both the
default and ohosTest HAP builds.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add CI: run the core tests and all three e2e steps on every push

This repository had no CI at all, and both README.md and AGENTS.md pointed
at a `.github/workflows/harmony.yml` in the parent repo that does not
exist. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` now runs, on every push and pull
request: rustfmt, clippy (`-D warnings`), the Rust unit tests, the SOCKS5
and simple-obfs plugin e2e tunnels, the OpenHarmony cross-compile check,
and the tun packet-routing e2e.

The tun e2e is the notable one — it drives real IP packets through the
tun stack and, until now, could only be run from a privileged container
by hand. A GitHub Linux runner has /dev/net/tun and passwordless sudo, so
`test-e2e-host.sh` now escalates itself instead of requiring the whole
script to run as root, and reports precisely why it skips when it cannot.
The workflow asserts /dev/net/tun exists so a runner change surfaces as a
failure rather than a silent skip.

The Rust crate path-depends on the shared shadowsocks-rust checkout that
lives *outside* this repository, so the workflow clones it to the sibling
path the Cargo manifest expects, at the same v1.23.4 the Android app's
submodule pins.

Also fixed, found while validating the above on Linux:

* `recover_tun_name` cast `c_char` to `u8` unconditionally. `c_char` is
  signed on x86_64 but unsigned on aarch64, so on aarch64-linux the cast
  is a no-op and clippy's `unnecessary_cast` fires — invisible from macOS,
  where that function is not even compiled.
* `run-tun-e2e-docker.sh` always built an x86_64 helper. On an Apple
  Silicon host — the whole reason that script exists — the container ran
  it under qemu emulation, which segfaulted roughly one run in twelve.
  It now builds for the host architecture; 8/8 clean runs after.
* README listed SIP003 plugins as "not ported"; they have been supported
  since 0e264fa.

The ArkTS tests and the HAP build stay out of CI: they need the DevEco
command-line tools, which are not publicly downloadable.

Verified by replaying the whole workflow in a Linux container — clone
step, fmt, clippy, and all three test-e2e-host.sh steps including the tun
e2e as a non-root user via sudo — end to end, exit 0.

> same roots on cluster (pod) daemons — is proposed below.
>
> Before this design an agent's workspace was exactly one repository.
> Additional repositories existed only as an authorization allowlist

> consequences: a GitHub review of an authorized-but-secondary repository had no
> trusted checkout and degraded to a "revision-only" empty directory, and an
> ordinary session could not read the secondary repositories at all except
> through the network. On self-hosted daemons that is no longer the case; on
> cluster (pod) daemons it still is, which is what phase 7 addresses.
>
> This design turns the allowlist into **workspace roots**: one primary root

On a cluster daemon the workspace lives on the sandbox pod's volume, mounted at
the root the pod reports (`/agent` today), and the daemon process runs on
another machine. Every `node:fs` call in `workspace-manager.ts` therefore
inspects the daemon's own disk, which is why the session-worktree path is
refused there (`refuseSessionIsolationInCluster`, a migration guard from the
cwd-coordinates fix, not a design choice) and why phases 3–5 skip `sandboxMode`.
Nothing about the pod forbids any of it: the pod's ACP runtime already takes a
per-session `cwd`, `git worktree` is in the exec allowlist, the volume survives
suspend/resume, and git credentials in the pod are routed by URL through the
tunnelled helper — a secondary repository authenticates today.

What is missing is one seam, the filesystem twin of `GitRunner`:

| Op                                                  | Used for                                                | Local         | Sandbox                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

the shim's fd-anchored descent, which is stronger than the daemon's lexical
checks; the daemon keeps only path composition in the pod's coordinates
(`<mount>/worktrees/<sid>`, `<mount>/repos/<owner>/<repo>/{checkout,worktrees/<sid>}`).
The exec allowlist gains `symbolic-ref`, `branch`, `show-ref`, `ls-remote` and
`show`, which the worktree and secondary-root paths already use locally.

With the seam in place the worktree, secondary-root, retirement and review-cwd
code stops touching `node:fs` directly and runs unchanged on both drivers;
`refuseSessionIsolationInCluster` and the `sandboxMode` short-circuits go away.
Two PRs: the seam plus session worktrees on the pod (which also gives pool
agents an exact same-repository review checkout for the first time), then
secondary roots and cross-repository review on the pod. `gh` inside the pod
stays a separate item: the runtime image ships no `gh` and the wrapper is a file
on the daemon's PATH.

feat(daemon): secondary workspace roots and cross-repository review on the sandbox volume (#1236)

* feat(daemon): secondary workspace roots and cross-repository review on the sandbox volume

Phase 7 part 2 of `docs/designs/multi-repository-workspaces.md`. #1225 put the
`WorkspaceFs` seam and the primary root's session worktrees on the pod volume;
this puts the secondary roots there too, so a cluster agent gets the same
`additionalDirectories` and the same exact cross-repository review checkout a
self-hosted one has had since phase 3.

Every secondary-root path now takes its filesystem from `fsFor(agentId)` and its
paths from the placement's mount: `secondaryRootsAt(agent, mount)` composes
`<mount>/repos/<owner>/<repo>/{checkout,worktrees}` the way `primaryRootAt`
composes the primary's, materialization stages a clone and publishes it by
rename through the seam, `.materialization.json` and the `.session-cwd-<id>.json`
attestation are read and written through it, `.gitmodules` is read from the
checkout that carries it, the subtree scan behind the ready-roots snapshot and
the retirement sweep goes through `readdir`, and `prepareClusterWorkspace` runs
the same secondary preparation and session-isolation handling — review of a
secondary root included — that `prepareWorkspace` runs locally. The
`sandboxMode ⇒ skip` short-circuits are gone, including the one that made a
review of a secondary root on a pool agent fall back to revision-only.

Because a pod cannot be stat-ed synchronously, the hand-out and GC entry points
that answered from `existsSync` are now async: `readySecondaryRoots`,
`sessionAdditionalRoots`, `additionalWorkspaceDirectories`,
`sessionWorktreeRoots`/`hasSessionWorktreeRoots`, `retiredSecondaryRoots`, and
`submoduleReposOf`. The ripple is mechanical — the runtime-session callbacks
(`workspaceDirectories`, `metaContext`, `resumeSystemContext`) and the session
manager's memoized standing context become promises.

`sweepRetiredWorkspaceRoots` runs its listing and its removal under
`withAgentVolume`, like the session-worktree removal already does, and skips a
sandboxed agent whose channel is not already bound rather than waking a
suspended pod for a GC pass. The admission fence and the idle re-check are
unchanged.

What a reviewer should check:

- No `node:fs` is left on any path a sandboxed agent reaches. What remains is
  daemon-side bookkeeping (the workspace materialization/conversion markers),
  activation and prefetch (local-only by construction), and the local branch of
  a mount-aware split.
- The delete-licensing discipline #1225 established: where an emptiness proof
  licenses a delete, it is one `rmdir` rather than a `readdir` followed by a
  recursive remove — publishing a staged clone over a leftover, and reclaiming a
  retired checkout that has no `.git`. The subtree removal that Git's own
  status/rev-list checks license stays an `rmTree`, under the admission fence.
- The review cwd swap: the reviewed root's exact worktree is the cwd, the
  primary and remaining roots ride along at their default branches, and the
  attestation is written last so a restart resolves the same directory.
- Local behaviour is byte-identical. The two self-hosted tests that pinned the
  old cluster short-circuits are gone; the rest of `workspace-secondary-roots`
  only gained `await`.

Not here: `gh` inside the pod (the image ships none, and the wrapper is a file
on the daemon's PATH), and the console's own workspace browsing, which still
answers with no root for a secondary repository on a cluster agent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): judge a session's roots under the volume, and never read an unanswerable one as empty

Two lifecycle regressions the review caught in the cluster secondary-root path.

`cleanupSessionWorktree` asked `hasSessionWorktreeRoots` before binding the
agent's volume. That predicate now reads the filesystem holding the roots, and a
suspended sandbox has none bound — so this daemon's own disk answered, and for a
from-scratch agent (no primary root) it answered "none" even when the pod volume
carried the session's secondary worktrees. Retention then reported
`not_applicable` and deleted the session row without the dirty/unique-commit
rules ever running against them. The prefilter is now `mayOwnSessionWorktrees`,
a spec-only question (`git-repo` primary, or any authorized additional
repository), and the real predicate moved inside the same `withAgentVolume` hold
as the removal.

`secondarySubtreesUnder` translated every workspace-filesystem failure into an
empty tree. An empty answer there licenses resuming a cross-repository session in
the primary checkout and licenses judging only the primary worktree, so a dropped
shim channel must abort the operation instead. Absence still reads as absence —
`stat` reporting `missing` or a non-directory — but a `stat`/`readdir` that
raises now propagates. The synchronous twin keeps its forgiving behaviour: its
one caller computes a sandbox boundary, where an unreadable directory means one
less carve-back rather than one less safety check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(daemon): keep a scratch agent in retention scope while a retired root survives

A retired secondary root keeps its worktrees after its authorization row
disappears (decision 12), so the spec-only prefilter answered `false` for a
from-scratch agent whose last row was removed — and retention purged the session
metadata without the dirty/unique-commit rules ever running against the worktree
in that retired root. The prefilter now also asks whether a `repos` subtree is
there at all: a cheap listing locally, and "maybe" on a pod, where only the
volume can say and the bound predicate inside the fence decides.

from config import AGENT_MODEL

from src.logging_utils import Trace

_SYSTEM = (
    "You are a factual FAQ assistant. Answer the customer's question using ONLY "
    "the provided knowledge-base context. If the context does not contain the "
    "answer, reply exactly: 'INSUFFICIENT_CONTEXT'. Never use outside knowledge. "
    "Cite the source filename(s) you used in square brackets at the end."
)

_store: rag.VectorStore | None = None

def _get_store() -> rag.VectorStore:
    global _store
    if _store is None:
        _store = rag.VectorStore.load()
    return _store

def handle(message: str, trace: Trace) -> str:
    hits = _get_store().search(message, k=3)
    relevant = [h for h in hits if h.score >= rag.RELEVANCE_FLOOR]

    if not relevant:
        # Grounding guarantee: no relevant doc -> abstain, don't invent.
        raise AbstainError("no knowledge-base match above relevance floor")

    context = "\n\n".join(f"[{h.doc.source}] {h.doc.text}" for h in relevant)

🔧 Fix: Added explicit authorization checks (`slot !== 0`) before processing these authoritative full-roster snapshots, ensuring only the host client can dictate phase transitions.

  (apps/web/src/lib/backendPort.ts). The previous config also paired
  wildcard origin with credentials:true, an invalid combination per the
  Fetch spec.

  register/verify/resend/forgot-password/reset-password) and on the two
  AI-generation endpoints, tighter than the app-wide default limiter.

  across auth/engine/media/oauth/posts controllers into real
  class-validator DTO classes, closing a gap where NestJS's global
  ValidationPipe silently validated nothing for non-class body types.

- Session storage: move the auth JWT from localStorage (readable by any
  XSS for up to 30 days) to an httpOnly cookie. AuthController.login sets
  it; a new AuthController.logout clears it. JwtStrategy reads it via a
  hand-rolled cookie parser (no new dependency). The frontend now caches
  only a non-sensitive user snapshot (id/email/name/brandId/expiry) for
  synchronous UI checks; apiFetch, the upload flow, the SSE stream, and
  the three OAuth connect links all rely on the cookie traveling
  automatically instead of a client-readable token.

  path, on top of the existing allowlist checks.

  params (info-disclosure risk); log full errors server-side, show

* docs: approve the private-preview qualification policy and record H0 reviews

- QUALIFICATION_POLICY: approve private-preview-qualification-v1 (the
  baselines, thresholds, live runs, and H1-H5 gates it defines remain open)
- Fix: the deterministic test provider and recorded fixtures can never satisfy
  the Baseline/Qualification configured-provider identity
- Fix: hard guardrails now explicitly cover non-authoritative projections
  served as authoritative state (invariant 7) and unusable failure states on
  the critical journey (invariant 10)
- PRODUCT_CONTRACT: declare the merged private-preview-v1 envelope current and
  reference the approved qualification policy
- SPEC_CONFORMANCE: record the H0 current-truth, contract/design, and
  adversarial overclaim reviews (fresh-context agent perspectives, pass with
  limitation, not human sign-off) and the remaining gates: make-verify
  dispatch record, required CI on the final commit, and independent human
  maintainer/product/security/accessibility/legal reviews

Limitation: GitHub issue/PR creation and the make-verify dispatch record
require credentials unavailable in this environment; the change is staged on
main for a maintainer to file, push, and dispatch.

* feat: land the extraction-quality-v1 evaluator and corpus (h1-eval)

- tools/h1-eval: recorded mode proves the structural import gate on the
  production splitter, extraction schema, and canon validator, plus corpus and
  rubric integrity and calibration self-consistency; adversarial mutations
  must fail the versioned thresholds (per-category coverage >=80, precision
  >=80, hallucination <=20, zero chronology violations, provenance 100) and
  malformed/unsupported inputs reach their expected bounded error labels
- live mode runs the full two-stage production extraction (character + canon
  prompts) and one OpenAI-compatible judge call, then enforces the same
  thresholds fail-closed; reports record provider/model/SHA and no secrets
- corpus h1-synthetic-v1: Simplified Chinese UTF-8/GBK and English
  UTF-8/BOM-UTF-16 slices, a hostile-instructions case, a mixed-script
  splitter case, five adversarial calibrations, and five malformed labels
- CI runs the recorded gate twice and requires byte-identical reports
- novel-service: derive Clone on ExtractionResult for corpus mutation
- SPEC_CONFORMANCE 5.8: record the landed evaluator; live quality stays
  unqualified

* fix(h1-eval): close adversarial review findings before the gate can claim
extraction-quality-v1 fidelity

- hallucination ceiling rounds up: a true rate above the policy bound can
  never truncate down to a pass
- precision and hallucination now divide recorded-side matches by recorded
  facts; coverage stays expected-side per category
- live mode enforces chronology deterministically (event sequence against
  the expected table), runs the production chunk-scan/merge path, verifies
  first appearances against split chapters, and omits unverifiable
  characters like the production handler
- adversarial cases declare the exact threshold they must trip (coverage,

explanation:
fix: require message authorship for standard-channel message edit and delete (#27197)

The channel message update and delete handlers enforced authorship only on group and dm channels. On standard channels the else branch accepted any caller holding write access on the channel, so a member who could post could also edit or delete messages authored by other members. Because the update form binds content, data and meta, and the model layer never touches message.user_id, an edited message kept the original author's attribution, so another member's message could be rewritten under their name.

Write access on a channel is the capability to post, not a moderation capability, and the frontend gates the edit and delete controls on authorship (message.user_id === user.id, or admin) for every channel type. The group and dm branch already encodes this with an explicit authorship check. Apply the same rule to the standard branch: the caller must hold write access on the channel and be the message author, unless they are an admin. Pinning is unchanged, since it is exposed to every member by design.

Frontend nginx config is `frontend/nginx.conf.template`, rendered by the image's envsubst entrypoint from `${PORT}` (Cloud Run) and `${BACKEND_HOST}` (the origin `/sitemap.xml` proxies to — update it if the backend service is renamed, or the proxy 502s). This replaced the old `sed`-the-port-at-runtime hack. It also 301s the `*.run.app` hostnames to `timetify.net`, so testing a deploy on its raw Cloud Run URL will bounce you to production — hit the custom domain, or check `Host`-specific behaviour with an explicit header. Full rules in [SEO](seo.md).

**nginx `add_header` inheritance.** A `location` that declares *any* `add_header` silently drops every server-level one — which previously would have removed the CSP and HSTS headers from exactly the HTML responses that need them. The document locations therefore use `expires -1` instead of `add_header Cache-Control`; the asset locations, which do need `add_header` for `immutable`, repeat `X-Content-Type-Options` explicitly. Adding an `add_header` to a location means re-adding the security headers there too.

## Signed media URLs (post-pentest)

Media is served through **signed, expiring URLs** (`main/storage.py`, `SignedGoogleCloudStorage`), not a public bucket. Two things must be true in the environment or media breaks:

1. **The bucket must not be public.** `gsutil iam ch -d allUsers:objectViewer gs://$GS_BUCKET_NAME`. Leaving the binding in place is not merely redundant — it re-opens anonymous `storage.objects.list`, so the whole bucket stays enumerable regardless of signing.
2. **The runtime service account must be able to sign via the IAM API.** django-storages (≤1.14.6) signs with a local private key, which Cloud Run's metadata credentials do not have; `SignedGoogleCloudStorage` instead signs through IAM `signBlob`, which needs the SA to hold `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` **on itself**:

   ```
   gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding "$SA_EMAIL" \
       --member="serviceAccount:$SA_EMAIL" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator"
   ```

If signing fails the backend logs `gcs.signing_failed` at ERROR and falls back to an unsigned URL, so a missing binding degrades instead of 500ing — but that fallback only *works* while the bucket is still public. Treat that log line as "the fix is not actually deployed". URL lifetime is `GS_URL_EXPIRY_SECONDS` (default 2h).

## Other security-relevant env vars

- `ADMIN_URL_PATH` — moves the Django admin off `/admin/`. Set it to something unguessable in prod.
- `TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT` — how many proxies append to `X-Forwarded-For` (default 1, correct for Cloud Run direct). Rate limiting derives the client IP from the *rightmost* N entries, because everything left of them is caller-supplied and forgeable. Raise it if a load balancer is put in front, or per-IP throttling will key on the proxy and limit all users as one.
- `REDIS_URL` — optional. Throttle counters live in the cache; without Redis they fall back to a database cache table (created by migration `0035`). Do **not** let this fall back to a per-process LocMemCache: each Cloud Run instance would get its own budget.
- `THROTTLE_*` — per-endpoint rate overrides; see `REST_FRAMEWORK['DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES']`.

**Migration `0034` can fail on existing data.** It adds case-insensitive unique constraints on username and email. Run `python manage.py find_identity_collisions` first; it lists colliding accounts and exits non-zero, so it can gate the deploy.

                HTTP Basic authentication realm.

        description: Annotated[
            str | None,
            Doc(
                """
                Security scheme description.

                It will be included in the generated OpenAPI (e.g. visible at `/docs`).
                """
            ),
        ] = None,
        auto_error: Annotated[
            bool,
            Doc(
                """
                By default, if the HTTP Basic authentication is not provided (a
                header), `HTTPBasic` will automatically cancel the request and send the
                client an error.

                If `auto_error` is set to `False`, when the HTTP Basic authentication
                is not available, instead of erroring out, the dependency result will
                be `None`.

                This is useful when you want to have optional authentication.

                It is also useful when you want to have authentication that can be
                provided in one of multiple optional ways (for example, in HTTP Basic
                authentication or in an HTTP Bearer token).
                """
            ),
        ] = True,
    ):
        self.model = HTTPBaseModel(scheme="basic", description=description)
        self.scheme_name = scheme_name or self.__class__.__name__
        self.realm = realm
        self.auto_error = auto_error

* feat(orgs): joinTenant — the single audited writer of a foreign users.tenantId

Accepting an org invitation has to put the invitee in the Organization's
Tenant, because that equality IS the authorization check. This is the third
writer of users.tenantId in the codebase and the only one that ever points a
user at a Tenant somebody else owns, so it lives beside ensureTenant to keep
every write to that column in one audited file.

🛑 It will NOT move a user between Tenants. Hard refusal, not best-effort,
for four independent reasons:

  1. Every row the user already created is stamped with their OLD tenantId by
     ScopeStampingSubscriber and by createOrganization. Repointing orphans all
     of it — the rows keep the old tenant, so their whole history silently
     vanishes from the scope they can now see. Data loss without a DELETE.
  2. tenants.ownerUserId is UNIQUE, so an owner cannot cleanly stop owning;
     repointing leaves an owner-linked, member-less orphan Tenant.
  3. listForUser returns every Org of user.tenantId, so repointing instantly
     hides all of their own Organizations from them.
  4. The FK on users.tenantId is ON DELETE SET NULL — there is no
     database-level protection. The guard must be in code, and tested.

backfill: dragging an invitee's pre-existing private rows into the inviter's
Tenant would expose their history tenant-wide. Their own Works stay reachable
because WorkRepository filters on userId, never tenantId.

* fix(orgs): boot crash + two ways an invitee could gain unrevocable access

Three defects found by an adversarial review of this branch, all confirmed by
reading the code rather than taken on trust.

1. CRITICAL — the API would have crash-looped at boot.

   AuthSessionGuard uses constructor injection, so Nest cannot resolve it —

   module-wiring spec missed it because it only checked the flow service's
   paramtypes, not the controller's guards.

2. HIGH — accept() granted access before claiming the token.
   joinTenant COMMITS users.tenantId, and only then did tryAccept run the
   conditional UPDATE. If a revoke landed in that window the claim failed, the
   code threw, and nothing rolled back: the invitee kept TENANT-WIDE access
   with no roster row — invisible in the members list (which reads the roster)
   and not removable via removeMember (which needs one). A revoked invitation
   still granted access.

   My docblock argued for that ordering. It was wrong: it reasoned only about
   the refusal case and never considered a successful join followed by a lost
   claim. Whatever gate authorizes access has to be the atomic one, so the
   claim now runs FIRST and the grant only happens if it wins.

   The double-click path is also now precise — it checks
   acceptedByUserId === userId instead of inferring "it was me" from a failed
   re-read, which previously also matched a REVOKED invitation and reported
   success for it.

3. HIGH — joinTenant's check-then-update was a TOCTOU.
   Two invitations accepted at the same instant both observed
   `tenantId IS NULL` and both wrote, homing the user in whichever tenant
   committed last while BOTH invitations were marked accepted. Now a
   conditional UPDATE (UserRepository.claimTenantIfUnassigned,
   WHERE "tenantId" IS NULL) lets the database arbitrate; losing to the SAME
   tenant is idempotent success, losing to a different one is the existing
   refusal.

* fix(orgs): an expired invitation no longer blocks re-inviting that person forever

The partial unique index is WHERE status = 'pending', and NOTHING moves a row
from pending to expired on a timer — expireBefore exists but nobody calls it.
So an invitation that aged out still occupies the slot: re-inviting the same
address fails with `invitation_already_pending`, telling the admin there is a
live invitation when the token behind it is dead.

That was permanent. The pending-invitations list would show it, but revoking
is the only lever and revoking an invitation you were told is pending — in
order to send the same person the same invitation — is not a step anyone
would guess at.

issue() now retires the aged-out row for that one (organization, email) pair
before inserting. Scoped rather than a table sweep, so issuing an invitation
stays a bounded write, and best-effort (.catch) so a sweep failure cannot
block a legitimate invite — the index still protects correctness either way.

Verified: 20/20. Control: removing the sweep fails exactly the new test, which
also asserts the sweep happens BEFORE the insert — the other order would be
rejected by the index first and prove nothing.

* fix(orgs): stale roster on org switch, and honest failure messages

Two smaller review findings.

Switching organizations left the PREVIOUS org's roster on screen until the new
fetch resolved — real people, not in the org named above them, each with a
Remove button. Acting on that list removes somebody from an organization you
are not looking at. State is now cleared before fetching, and a `cancelled`
flag drops a response for an org already navigated away from, which also fixes
the out-of-order case (switch A→B→A and B's slower reply would otherwise land
last and win).

Removal and revoke failures both showed `errors.unknown`, whose text is
"Could not send the invitation. Please try again." — describing an action the
user did not take. They now have their own messages.

--numstat` showed 21 deletions, which looked alarming, but each is the
`unknown` line re-emitted with a trailing comma as two keys were appended
after it. A key/value comparison against HEAD across all 21 locales confirms
0 files lost any key or value.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(orgs): a failed invitation email no longer strands an unusable pending row

The invitation row commits before the mail call, and the raw token exists in
exactly one place — that email. So a send failure left a row whose token
reached NOBODY and which cannot be recovered, because the database holds only
sha256.

Left pending, that row is worse than useless: the partial unique index on
(organizationId, emailNormalized) WHERE status='pending' BLOCKS re-inviting
the address, and there is no resend endpoint. The admin is told an invitation
is pending for a token that does not exist anywhere, and the obvious
response — send it again — is refused.

invite() now revokes the invitation when the send fails, releasing the address
immediately so retrying works, and rethrows so the caller reports the failure
instead of claiming an invite went out. The revoke is best-effort: a secondary
failure while tidying up must not replace the mail error, which is the one the
admin actually needs to see.

New spec, 5/5, with two controls: a successful send must NOT revoke (or the
main assertion would pass for the wrong reason), and removing the revoke call
fails exactly the one test — verified by counting occurrences before and after
arming, 1 -> 0, because a control that quietly fails to arm looks identical to
a passing one.

Fix security findings from the August 2026 penetration tests

Cross-compared two Strix reports (timetify.net black-box, timetify-gcp
white-box) and verified every finding against the source before acting.

Confirmed and fixed:
- No rate limiting on auth endpoints (CRITICAL). Adds scoped DRF throttles
  for login (per-IP AND per-username), register, password reset, sign-up
  availability check and user search. Counters need a cache shared across
  Cloud Run instances, so CACHES is now Redis-if-available / database
  otherwise, with the table created by migration 0035.
- Public GCS bucket with unsigned URLs (HIGH). Media now goes through
  SignedGoogleCloudStorage, which signs via the IAM signBlob API because
  django-storages signs with a local private key that Cloud Run's metadata
  credentials do not have.
- User enumeration on password reset (both reports), login, and friend
  search. Constant response, generic auth error, 3-char search floor.
- Cross-tenant IDOR via writable `course` FK on Week/Exam/Assignment.
- Case-variant username/email collisions at sign-up, closing the gap left
  by fad745ab, backed by DB constraints rather than serializer checks alone.
- Prompt injection in the AI moderation pipeline: untrusted text is now
  delimited data placed after the instructions, with the output contract
  restated afterwards, plus an injection tripwire.
- Past-dated events, admin on a fixed path, missing CSP/HSTS/frame headers.

Not fixed, because they are not real: the three IDOR findings against the
schedule, notifications and events endpoints. All three views derive the
user from request.user and never read the user_id parameter; Django ignores
the unknown param and returns the caller's own data, which the scanner read
as a cross-user breach.

Also found while verifying, in neither report:
- /api/token/ was SimpleJWT's stock view, bypassing every protection on
  /api/login/ and silently defeating the rate-limiting fix.
- Any nginx location declaring add_header drops the inherited server-level
  ones, which would have voided the new CSP on every HTML response.
- CourseSerializer.parent_course had the same unvalidated-FK hole.
- Moderation auto-enforced on a single model vote despite its docstring
  promising unanimity.
- Password reset matched email case-sensitively.

Dependencies: npm 4 high -> 0; Django 6.0.2 (26 advisories) -> 6.0.7, plus
gunicorn, python-dotenv and pg8000. pip-audit and check --deploy both clean.

Adds 23 regression tests; full suite 162 passing.

Add the frontend API client and split the types module

Two pieces of foundation that have to exist before any migration slice
branches, because both are files every slice would otherwise edit.

lib/api/client.ts is the single path to the backend. It owns three things
that were each a bug waiting to happen:

  - Base URL, with a NAMED failure. EXPO_PUBLIC_* values are inlined at
    bundle time, so a missing EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL became the literal
    string "undefined" in the URL. React Native reports that as "Network
    request failed", which is indistinguishable from a real connectivity
    problem and sends you debugging the wrong layer entirely.
  - The Authorization header, read from the live Supabase session rather
    than a passed-in token, so a caller cannot send a stale one.
  - The error envelope. This fixes a live bug: create-profile.tsx read
    `errorData.error`, a field the API has never sent -- its shape is
    { statusCode, message, timestamp, path, method }. So every validation
    failure showed the generic "Failed to create profile" and threw away
    the per-field messages saying exactly what was wrong. ApiError.messages
    is now always an array whether the server sent a string or an array,
    and describeApiError() also handles non-JSON 5xx bodies, which starts
    mattering the moment this sits behind an ALB.

types/types.ts becomes types/{coach,conversation,reference,user,workout}.ts
behind a barrel at @/types. One 139-line file holding every view type meant
a guaranteed merge conflict on every slice. Same reasoning as landing the
client alone. Profile / Federation / Division / WeightClass move here out
of create-profile.tsx.

Splitting them surfaced two wrong types, which only typechecked because
Supabase's `data` is untyped:

  - Federation.id, Division.id and WeightClass.id were `number`. They are
    uuids, so strings.
  - WeightClass.sort_order was `boolean`. It is a smallint.

Correcting nullability then made strict mode reject two call sites where
the UI assumed reference-data `name` was always present. It is nullable in
the schema, so both now have a fallback -- federation falls back to `code`,
which is NOT NULL.

Verified: frontend lint and type-check both clean, tailwind compiles with

Strict meta channel recognition in server

This addresses a security vulnerability affecting user-added extensions
that implement access control for channels. These extensions typically
work by checking incoming messages whose channel is `/meta/subscribe`
and then performing some authentication routine before allowing the
message through.

However, the Server parses channels in a way that means any channel
namespaced under `/meta/subscribe` will also work as a subscription
request. For example if the client sends a message to the channel
`/meta/subscribe/x`, that will bypass most authentication extensions but
will still be interpreted by the server as a subscription request, and
the client will be subscribed to the requested channel. The client has
thus bypassed the user's access control policy.

Here we prevent this by using a strict equality check; only messages
whose channel is exactly `/meta/subscribe` will be interpreted as
subscription requests. The same pattern is applied to all other meta
channels.

Authentication Bypass For Endpoints With Anonymous Access

Using a remember-me cookie with an arbitrary username can cause Opencast
to assume proper authentication for that user even if the remember-me
cookie was incorrect given that the attacked endpoint also allows
anonymous access.

This way, an attacker can, for example, fake a remember-me token, assume
the identity of the global system administrator and request non-public
content from the search service without ever providing any proper
authentication.

The reason for this problem is that using a remember-me cookie will
always cause the user in the request context to be populated, even if
the cookie is invalid by now. This is usually no problem, except in
combination with anonymous access where anonymous authentication is
granted and the request may continue.

In such a case, Opencast's security service would just check that a user
existed in the request context and assume proper authentication of this
user, never checking if it's actually anonymous authentication.

This patch adds this additional check, falling back to the anonymous
user in case of anonymous authentication.

Add multi-tenant support: multiple restaurants, one system

Every restaurant's data is now isolated by a new Restaurant model —
tables, comandas, menu, orders, payments, coupons, help calls, audit
log and staff all carry a restaurantId and are scoped by it end to
end. This is the foundation for self-service onboarding ("reach the
market") and for a future iFood/delivery-platform channel to slot in
next to KIOSK/DELIVERY/SCHEDULED.

Architecture:
- New `Restaurant` model (id, slug, createdAt). `Settings` keyed by
  restaurantId instead of a hardcoded "singleton" row.
- QR tokens (table/comanda) and the Checkout id stay globally unique
  on purpose — that's how an anonymous QR scan resolves its own
  restaurant with no slug/login needed. Human-facing numbers (table
  number, comanda number, order number/pickup ticket, coupon code)
  become unique per restaurant instead of globally.
- User.email stays globally unique (keeps /login simple: no
  restaurant selection before the password prompt).
- Every by-id staff mutation (delete/update) now scopes on
  {id, restaurantId} via deleteMany/updateMany + a count check,
  instead of trusting a bare id — closes an IDOR class of bug that a
  single-tenant system never had to worry about.
- Realtime SSE topics ("kitchen"/"pdv") are now per-restaurant
  (`kitchen:${restaurantId}`) so one restaurant's live board never
  sees another's events.
- /totem and /pedir move to /totem/[slug] and /pedir/[slug] — the only
  public screens with no QR Code to resolve a restaurant from. New
  /signup does self-service onboarding (Restaurant + Settings + first
  ADMIN user, auto-login), also used as the isolation test's own
  second-tenant fixture.
- Data migration backfills all pre-existing rows onto one
  'rst_default' restaurant (slug "principal") — the real restaurant
  already in production, preserved verbatim.
